articleTitle: Topological Mode Analysis of PT-Symmetric Electrostatic Shear Driven Instabilities
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Topological phase refers to the notion that in a uniform system the eigenfunction in wave vector space can be characterized by an integer-valued topological invariant that describes a global property of an eigenfunction. A topological mode refers to an edge state, or topological wave, that arises at the interface between two systems with different values of a topological invariant. These ideas have had a profound impact on condensed matter theory with many important applications e.g. topological insulators, topological superconductors, and topological quantum computers. All of the condensed matter systems rely on the quantum properties, but recently these ideas have found their way into classical systems. One of the first applications was to the shallow water equations and the analysis was used to show why equatorial waves predominantly head east. Recently, these ideas have made their way into plasma physics where the quantum/classical analogy has had a long history of development. Plasmas offer a unique playground for these ideas because of their non-equilibrium natures and non-Hermitian linear operators. In this presentation, we consider a simplified model of the Inhomogeneous Energy Density Driven Instability (IEDDI) and the Electron-Ion Hybrid (EIH) instability based on the electrostatic limit of cold fluid equations. These instabilities are driven by an inhomogeneous flow perpendicular to the magnetic field and may be characterized as occurring in the boundary layer between two flowing plasmas. They have extensive applications in both space and laboratory plasmas. For example, these instabilities are known to occur in compressed plasmas such as dipolarization fronts, magnetotail current sheets, plasma sheet boundary layers, etc. and are important for anomalous dissipation, particle energization and transport. These instabilities are also both inherently non-local requiring the solution to a 1D eigenmode equation to accurately understand the driving conditions and mode properties. These instabilities are notable from a theoretical perspective because the source of free energy is contained in the inhomogeneous flow, meaning that the instability exists because there is no single frame that one is able to transform into that can globally remove the flow. This physical interpretation can also be understood through the fact that in a homogenous flowing plasma the linearized dynamics of the cold electrostatic fluid model can be described by a linear operator that can be put into diagonal form. This operator exhibits parity-time (PT) symmetry which has implications on the eigenvalues of the operator. We analyze the topological modes of this simplified linear operator in the limits of the IEDDI instability and the EIH instability and use the symmetries of the linear operator to describe the unique properties of this instability. This analysis shows the power of theoretical technique through its ability to make general statements about the instability without having to obtain the eigenmode, a task which requires assumptions about the initial conditions, and often, extensive and difficult numerical analysis.

articleTitle: An Experimental Proof of Concept for Sensing Using Hybrid Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents experimental proof-of-concept of a hybrid reconfigurable intelligent surface (HRIS) that can detect incident angles of arrivals (AoAs). Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) can improve wireless communication by reflecting the incident signal in prescribed directions. This operation, however, requires knowledge about the intended transmitter and users (e.g., their AoAs) to be available at RISs. To achieve this operation without requiring extra feedback loops or complicated channel sensing algorithms, a sensing mechanism needs to be introduced into RISs. To address this challenge, we have designed HRISs that can couple a small portion of the incident signal on a few elements of the HRIS to be used for sensing purposes. We will outline and experimentally demonstrate a compressive sensing algorithm to utilize measurements at these few sparse sampling locations for detecting AoA. The proposed HRIS can be used to implement smart and autonomous wireless communication networks, wireless power transfer, and sensing systems.

articleTitle: High-dynamic Range Radio Astronomy Systems, Interference Mitigation Strategies, and a Test Setup for Experimenting Dynamic Spectrum Sharing
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The electromagnetic spectrum is used by both ‘active’ and ‘passive’ services. Active services span a wide variety of technologies such as wireless internet and telecommunications. Passive services are remote sensing and radio astronomy. So far, distinct frequency bands have been allocated around the world for these different services. It has now been realized that this classic model cannot accommodate the demands of next-generation communications technology. One proposal to meet this mounting demand is for services to dynamically share the spectrum. Successful adoption of dynamic spectral sharing hereby hinges on implementing novel and advanced techniques and the technology that may make that possible [1].

articleTitle: Testing Spacecraft Charging Predictions as Parker Solar Probe Approaches the Sun
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Spacecraft surface charging is an important area of study for scientists and engineers to study the effect space radiation has on instrument measurements and the spacecraft itself. As spacecraft complete orbits, flybys, and experience the solar wind, electric charge from the background plasma can build up on the surface. This buildup of charge can create electric fields that can impact instrument measurements, manipulate objects (like dust), and, in extreme cases, cause damage to the spacecraft itself. Because of the possible adverse effects of spacecraft charging, careful modeling and predictions are necessary prior to the launch of any spacecraft, but particularly for spacecraft encountering sparse plasma densities, high fluxes of energetic particles, and high solar photon flux, such as spacecraft near the Sun.

articleTitle: Recent Developments on the EIGSEP Experiment for 21-cm Global Signal Detection
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Measurements of the redshifted 21-cm line offer a direct probe of the Cosmic Dawn, when the first stars and galaxies formed. This period of cosmic history is largely unconstrained, but is accessible through measurements of the global—that is, all-sky averaged—brightness temperature of the 21-cm radiation. At the early stages of Cosmic Dawn, Lyman-alpha photons from the first generation of stars couple the 21-cm spin temperature to the kinetic temperature of the hydrogen gas, which imprints an absorption feature relative to the CMB temperature in the global 21-cm spectrum. X-ray radiation heats the hydrogen gas and drives the 21-cm spin temperature to the CMB temperature, and possibly produces an emission feature, before UV-radiation reionizes the hydrogen and extinguishes the signal. The shape of this spectrum—and in particular the center, width, and depth of the absorption profile—thus probes astrophysical parameters related to the star formation rate, x-ray heating and production of Ly-alpha and ionizing photons.

articleTitle: Lunar Farside Radio Arrays for Investigations of Dark Ages and Exoplanet Magnetospheres Commission J: Radio Science from the Moon
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: An array of low-frequency dipole antennas on the lunar farside surface sensitive to frequencies ¡ 30MHz will probe for information from two of the most significant areas of astrophysics: understanding our Universe's early history during the cosmic Dark Ages and characterizing exoplanets. The Epoch of Dark Ages begins at Recombination when neutral hydrogen atoms formed, first revealed by the cosmic microwave background. This epoch is free of stars and astrophysics, so it is ideal to investigate high energy particle processes including dark matter, early Dark Energy, neutrinos, and cosmic strings. In the same band, magnetized planets produce bright, highly circularly polarized,coherent emission. This radio emission is produced at the electron gyrofrequency and thus provides a direct diagnostic of the magnetic field strength in planetary magnetospheres. Planetary magnetospheres potentially play a role in the retention of planetary atmospheres and may be a crucial ingredient for planetary habitability. This radio emission is, therefore, an important potential probe in understanding the role of magnetic fields in the habitability of exoplanets.

articleTitle: Preliminary Study of Inductive Power Transfer Compared to Capacitive Power Transfer
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Wireless charging has been growing in popularity as electronics continue to improve and global dependence on batteries has been increasing. This growth has also been fueled by a growing interest in electric vehicles. There are many benefits of wireless charging over corded charging that have been analyzed in detail by researchers. These include a reduction in battery size, reduction in the need for battery charging cables, increased convenience, increased battery lifetime (as connections that are often the source of failure are removed entirely) and increased safety from electric shock and tripping.

articleTitle: Stimulated Brillouin Scattering from Satellite Transmissions
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents details from two previous HAARP campaigns utilizing off the shelf, consumer grade VHF receivers, and a commercial satellite constellation to create nonlinear plasma interactions within the ionosphere. We are actively reviewing data to ensure accurate findings. Throughout the experiment, an emphasis is placed on utilizing low budget, beginner friendly hardware and software in order to encourage further undergraduate involvement. Data was successfully recorded, with analysis pending.

articleTitle: Ionospheric response During the 10-12 May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm and it's Connection to GICs
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The extreme ‘G5’ geomagnetic storm of 10–12 May 2024 was the largest storm of Solar Cycle 25. The space weather impacts were recorded on the ground in form of Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GICs) across the United States. In this paper, I have presented the temporal correlation of significant GICs recorded in the east coast of the US near Fredericksburg, Virginia, and the ionospheric observations derived from GNSS Total Electron Content (TEC) and Radars in the US from the SuperDARN network. I find that the largest disturbance in TEC over the United States (US) east coast occurs during the main phase of the storm and correlates with large amplitude GIC fluctuations. Two radars from the SuperDARN network observing the F-region activity over the Fredericksburg region indicate heightened activity at higher altitudes. This paper highlights the observational relationship between GICs and rise in intensity and altitude of F-region ionosphere enabled by radio observations. Further in-depth analysis is needed to understand the drivers of the ionospheric activity and peak GICs.

articleTitle: Statistical Distributions of Evaporation Duct Height and Strength Over Range and the Diurnal Cycle
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Navy regularly operates within the marine atmospheric surface layer which is a highly dynamic environment. Variations in ocean surface and atmospheric thermodynamic variables significantly impact and influence technologies that utilize radio frequencies (RF). Vertical gradients in these variables, particularly moisture, can lead to the formation of atmospheric refractive features, including evaporative ducts. These features can cause anomalous propagation such as extended detection ranges and signal holes. Therefore, understanding spatial and temporal variability in evaporation duct height and strength is necessary to accurately quantify the impact of the refractive environment on RF signals.

articleTitle: Nanosecond Differential Timing Using Inexpensive Differential GNSS Receivers DRAFT
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: To handle the ever-increasing amount of data produced, several new and planned radio telescope arrays digitize their signals at each telescope. In these systems, each telescope transmits its digitized data back to a central location where the data are correlated and/or formed into beams. This requires each telescope to accurately timestamp its data so that the antenna voltages can be combined and integrated coherently.

articleTitle: NRL SP ADE-2 Plasma Diagnostic Electronics
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Space Plasma Diagnostic Suite (SPADE) is composed of a Langmuir probe and a plasma impedance probe for high-frequency measurements and measures plasma density and plasma electron temperature in the Earth's ionosphere. A transimpedance amplifier comprises the heart of the Langmuir probe and measures the low-frequency probe current in response to a sawtooth voltage stimulus. The plasma impedance probe uses direct digital synthesis and a pair of gilbert cell mixers to measure the high-frequency probe current and voltage, from which the antenna impedance is derived. Two conductive elements comprise the active surface of the sensor, driven at the same potential for Langmuir probe measurements and used as a short dipole antenna for impedance probe measurements.

articleTitle: Gannon Storm Scintillation Observations via the NOAA Data Collection System
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The May 2024 Gannon storm disrupted the global ionosphere and caused extensive mid-latitude electron density perturbations. These disturbances resulted in rare mid-latitude radio scintillation during early phases of the storm, indicating the occurrence of irregularities at ~1 km scales. Few mid-latitude sites routinely monitor GNSS scintillation at L-band, and even fewer monitor scintillation in the more sensitive VHF and lower UHF bands. As a result, it has traditionally been difficult to corroborate the spatial occurrence of scintillation with large scale structures, such as “super plumes” or gradients at the edge of storm-enhanced density (SED) regions. This study will explore irregularity development during the Gannon storm using a novel scintillation technique-beacons of opportunity from ground transmitters to the NOAA Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Data Collection System (DCS).

articleTitle: Analyzing Historical Langmuir Probe Data Using Modern Methods
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a re-analysis of historical data collected from Langmuir probes aboard ionospheric reentry vehicles from the Radio Attenuation Measurements missions launched by NASA in the 1960s. We present the discovery of two significant inaccurate assumptions in the methods of analysis during that time, namely: methods of analyzing electron temperature, and use of cylindrical probe theory applied to conical probes. Re-analyzing this data shows that the incorrect use of electron temperature altered electron density calculations by as much as 55%. Due to insufficient cone probe theory, we develop cone probe theory for simpler cases (Langmuir probes operating within the thin sheath limit) in this paper and propose an experiment for developing cone probe theory for more complicated (thicker sheath regime) cases.

articleTitle: RF-Photonic Ultra-Wideband Instrument For Planetary Boundary Layer Sensing
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The ultra-wideband RF photonics spectro-radiometer instrument is under development for the Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) sensing. The PBL is the lower portion of the troposphere that is directly influenced by the Earth's surface. Most of the energy exchange with respect to solar heating and evaporation that drive the atmosphere and the ocean occur within PBL. Passive microwave instruments can be a critical component to a PBL observing system but the current generation microwave instruments fall well short of being optimized for near surface sensing due to limited number of spectral channels and coarse spectral resolution covering only a small portion of the spectrum of the interest for PBL sensing. It is adequate for providing thermodynamic information in both cloudy and clear air, cloud and precipitation properties and surface flux information including temperature and wind speed but not optimized for near surface sensing.

articleTitle: Testing INCUS Methods Experiment – Suborbital preLaunch Investigation of Convective Evolution (TIME-SLICE)
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The upcoming NASA Earth Venture Mission Mission INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) seeks to estimate convective mass flux over the Earth's tropical regions using a unique new reflectivity differencing technique. Therefore, validation of the INCUS products requires innovative designs for time-resolved observations of convective cores from the surface. The Testing of INCUS Measurements Experiment - Suborbital preLaunch Investigation of Convective Evolution (TIME-SLICE) is a small campaign to understand and test instruments and sampling techniques that will provide the most useful validation of INCUS products. TIME-SLICE outcomes will directly influence the development and design of the post-launch validation effort for INUCS. This presentation will focus on the Colorado component of TIME-SLICE (TIME-SLICE CO), which took place in the northern front range of Colorado during the spring of 2024 (Fig. 1). The CSU CHIVO C-band polarimetric radar collected rapid vertical slices (RHIs) of convective cores identified and tracked by the Multi-Sensor Agile Adaptive Sampling (MAAS) framework. Several profiling radars, including the S-band Snow-level Radar (SLR) and a Micro Rain Radar Pro (MRR Pro), were installed about 30 km from CHIVO to provide vertical profiles of reflectivity and Doppler velocity. Surface rainfall characteristics and amounts were collected using disdrometers and rain gauges, and special soundings were launched to characterized the atmospheric environment of the storms sampled. During the approximately eight weeks of operations, thirteen intensive operation periods (IOPs) sampled a variety of convection, from shallow to deep, fast and slow moving, weak to severe. Preliminary examination of several IOPs, as well as key lessons learned for future INCUS field campaigns will be presented.

articleTitle: Utilization of Dynamic Basis Functions in Kriging Methodology for Uncertainty Quantification in Finite Element Computation of Electromagnetic Scattering
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In computational electromagnetics (CEM) and engineering, uncertainty quantification (UQ) plays a critical role in enhancing the accuracy and reliability of analyses and designs, particularly when dealing with complex systems with unknown parameter variations. Monte Carlo simulations are the traditional method for evaluating UQ by sampling probability distributions and solving the problem using numerical techniques such as the finite element method (FEM). However, these approaches are prohibitively expensive in terms of computational cost and time; these problems are further amplified with large input data sets.

articleTitle: Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array Year 6 Data Analysis
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Observation of 21cm radio emission by neutral hydrogen from before reionization is a promising window as a probe of fundamental physics and origin of the first stars or other objects. The line temperature of intergalactic hydrogen is uniquely sensitive to the large scale flow of energy from objects forming at a time difficult to probe by other means. The redshifted line from the birth of the first stars at redshift 25 down to the end of reionization at redshift 5 is observed at wavelengths between one and five meters. The observing challenges include sensitivity for which significant collecting area is required, interference in the heavily used band, and instrumental precision which must reject unwanted chromaticity at one part in 100,000. The Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array (HERA) is a second generation 21cm experimental interferometer targeting 21cm emission at redshifts 5 to 23. HERA has reported limits on the 21cm power spectrum which constrain galaxy formation models and confirmed that x-rays were likely present to heat the early universe. After an upgrade several seasons have been recorded which are forecast to have much deeper sensitivity. The year six (2022) campaign has been partially reduced and a description has been publicly released. This reduction includes flagging, calibration, and averaging of two weeks of nightly observing. At this sensitivity small effects begin to appear. Small levels of interference become confused with otherwise unobjectionable systematics. Mutual coupling between antennas becomes visible above the noise level and transient astronomical objects are observed. These results suggest lessons which are generally applicable to other present and future instruments.

articleTitle: SDR-Based S-Band Radiometer for UAS Platforms with Spectrum Monitoring and Dynamic Allocation
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Passive microwave remote sensing is a powerful technique for obtaining information about the Earth's surface and atmosphere by detecting natural electromagnetic emissions. It plays a critical role in agriculture, water resource management, forestry, and other environmental applications. However, modern wireless communication systems pose an increasing risk of radio frequency interference (RFI) for passive sensors. To estimate accurate geophysical parameter measurements and enable the coexistence of active and passive systems, it is crucial to develop effective methods to evaluate and optimize various coexistence solutions. This paper presents the development of a spectrum monitoring system to identify available spectrum for passive radiometry in the unprotected S-band (3.2 - 3.6 GHz). Additionally, we introduce a software-defined radio (SDR)-based S-band microwave radiometer, designed to operate from unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) and capable of dynamically adjusting its center frequency to collect radiometric data from the available spectrum. Operating in the unprotected band, this system will also be used as a testbed for collecting large radiometric measurement datasets across many different interference scenarios. In this paper, we discuss the design and implementation of both the spectrum monitoring system and the microwave radiometer.

articleTitle: Sensing of Directional Ice Surface Roughness Features with GNSS-Reflectometry
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) is an opportunistic remote sensing technique, where GNSS satellites serve as transmitters and a constellation of small satellites in low-Earth orbit (LEO) capture the signals after they have reflected off Earth's surface. The power and phase of the reflected signals can be processed to obtain geophysical information about the reflection surface. Our recent work has demonstrated that the carrier phase coherence of reflected GNSS signals is related to surface deformation and roughness of the Ross Ice Shelf and entire Antarctic Ice Sheet. Figure 1 shows a map of gridded GNSS-R phase coherence for the Antarctic continent at 10 km resolution, clearly depicting the sea ice boundary, patterns in the ice shelves, and limited coherence in the interior of the ice sheet. For the Ross Ice Shelf specifically, coherence has been shown to be quantitatively correlated with centimeter-to-meter-level surface roughness, defined as the standard deviation of surface height.

articleTitle: Troposcatter: Illuminating the Black Box
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Tropospheric scattering or troposcatter is a phenomenon that causes extended radio frequency (RF) electromagnetic wave (EW) propagation at beyond line-of-sight (BLOS) ranges. Troposcatter was first described in the 1940s during World War II when signals from RF systems propagated farther than the theories of the time allowed. During the 1950s and 1960s many researchers investigated troposcatter and developed a plethora of statistical models.

articleTitle: RAE-exploring the Past: Lunar Science and the Legacy of RAE-2
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Radio Astronomy Explorer 2 (RAE-2), also known as Explorer 49, was launched in 1973 to investigate long-wavelength radio emissions from the orbit of the Moon. RAE-2 Utilized 230-meter dipole antennas to conduct pioneering observations in the 25 kHz to 13.1 MHz range. These frequencies are typically inaccessible from Earth's surface due to ionospheric interference, so this mission allowed scientists to study a wide variety of previously unstudied astrophysical effects, which haven't been studied since.

articleTitle: Design of an Electrically Small Circularly Polarized Spherical Folded Helix Antenna
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: An electrically small folded helix with an electrical size of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ka=0.29$</tex> is designed for operation in the GPS L5 band. To reduce axial ratio, parasitic elements around the equator are included in the antenna. The proposed design achieves instantaneous coverage of the L5 band with VSWR < 3:1 and axial ratio below 3 dB over nearly the entire field-of-view. Fabrication considerations are also discussed.

articleTitle: The 12 May 2021 Strong Geomagnetic Storm Viewed in the Context of Total Electron Content and Power Grid Disturbances
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We investigate the unanticipated ground and ionospheric impacts of an Earth-directed solar filament eruption on 9 May 2021 that caused most forecasting agencies to warn of increased geomagnetic activity for the subsequent 84–72 hours. The forecast verified as the first G3 (strong) geomagnetic storm of solar cycle 25 on 12 May. Despite the G3-level storm, the Dst 'peak” was a rather modest -62 nT. During mid storm, the strongest Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GICs) in five years were reported in the Austrian power grid located at noon MLT. Sub-auroral US GIC monitors, and ground-based magnetometers in the post-dawn region showed nearly simultaneous oscillatory signals. Equatorial magnetometers suggest a deep electric field penetration at low latitudes. Shortly thereafter, fast and significant fast total electron content (TEC) perturbations appeared in both hemispheres in the sunrise sector as shown in the Madrigal TEC data base.

articleTitle: A 400Gbit Ethernet Core Enabling High Data Rate Streaming from FPGAs to Servers and GPUs in Radio Astronomy
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The increased bandwidth coupled with the large numbers of antennas of several new radio telescope arrays has resulted in an exponential increase in the amount of data that needs to be recorded and processed. In many cases, it is necessary to process this data in real time, as the raw data volumes are too high to be recorded and stored. Due to the ability of graphics processing units (GPUs) to process data in parallel, GPUs are increasingly used for data-intensive tasks. In most radio astronomy digital instrumentation (e.g. correlators for spectral imaging, beamforming, pulsar, fast radio burst and SETI searching), the processing power of modern GPUs is limited by the input/output data rate, not by the GPU's computation ability.

articleTitle: REDSAW Tethered Drone-Based Meteorological Measurements
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Atmospheric duct predictions and its effect on electromagnetic wave propagation in stable boundary layers continues to be a challenging research topic. The Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in Stable Atmosphere over Water (RED-SAW) campaign investigates into the effects of stable atmosphere on radio frequency propagation. Two drone receiver systems were deployed at the Salton Sea Causeway in California during this experiment. A new system that was deployed was the tethered quad copter drone receiver system which can record electromagnetic (EM) and meteorological (MET) signals continuously for hours at a times. This extends the vertical modified refractivity profiles that can be collected by drone systems and lengthens the period of time that the drone can be in the air recording information. The objective of this research is to analyze the relationship between the atmospheric environmental conditions and the characteristics of the EM signals propagating through the Salton Sea. Preliminary MET results from the deployed drone receiver systems are shown.

articleTitle: Development of Voltage Multiplier Rectifier for Energy Harvesting Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This work describes the implementation of a RF-to-DC rectifier based on the voltage booster topology that operates at a practical 915 MHz frequency. The rectifier design is derived from the Cockcroft-Walton voltage multiplier design, which is used for lower frequency ranges, and adapted for higher RF frequencies. The rectifier achieved an efficiency about 50%, starting with a power input of 7.5 dBm and reaching a peak efficiency at 80%, with a power input of 15 dBm.

articleTitle: Quasi Static TEM Analysis of a uStrip above a Perforated Plane
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Microstrip transmission lines have been utilized for 70 years in myriad applications. Characterization of their propagation parameters has been carried out both analytically and numerically by many researchers during that time. From equations for the capacitance per unit length, their quasi-TEM characteristic impedance and propagation constants can be accurately approximated by several kinds of analytical expressions. These approximations presume a continuous, planar, conductive reference or ground plane (return path). Weight, cost and / or reliability may be factors driving the incorporation of perforations (holes) in the conductive reference plane. These perforations impact impedance, propagation constants and crosstalk. The introduction of a perforated reference plane complicates the design process of such circuits. Full-wave electromagnetic simulations of them are possible, but time-consuming and demanding of computational resources. Thus, an approximate but accurate analytical model would be of great practical value.

articleTitle: The Lunar Farside Technosignature and Transient Telescope (LFT3)
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Humanity is on the verge of being able to observe the cosmos from the moon with sufficient accuracy in order to gain a deeper understanding of astrophysical processes. This necessitates a transition from earth-based observatories to space-based telescopes. We are at a tipping point in having cost-effective access to space which will enable many nations to send experiments to the lunar surface and orbit. This provides opportunities for new science but will also bring RFI sources to the quietest remaining near-earth location. Until the moon also becomes crowded with sources of radio emission, the lunar farside offers a unique environment to measure radiation from the Universe with essentially zero radio frequency interference. We describe a multi-band telescope to be landed near the lunar antipode within five years to conduct initial baseline observations in the absence of RFI. The Lunar Farside Technosignatures and Transients Telescope (LFT3) will search the farside sky for radio emissions from known and unknown sources and create a historical record of lunar radio observations from the current pristine silence to a more crowded environment as further instruments are deployed. LFT3 is a once-in-human-history opportunity to record signals in a fully quiet environment.

articleTitle: Examination of Radar Interference Protection Criteria Power Threshold Measurement Methods
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Modern radio spectrum planning often calls for reallocating spectrum adjacent to or within existing radar bands to other radar or communication systems. At the turn of the century, the Institute for Telecommunications Sciences (ITS) developed radar interference protection criteria (IPC) power threshold (PT) measurement methods to determine how much of the other system's signal power could be tolerated (F. Sanders, R. Sole, B. Bedford, D. Franc, and T. Pawlowitz, “Effects of RF Interference on Radar Receivers,” NTIA Report TR-06-444, Sept. 2006). These measurement methods and resulting IPC/PT are widely used today.

articleTitle: A 10 GHz Parametric Amplifier for Distributed Amplification
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A negative resistance waveguide parametric amplifier is designed with a pump frequency <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(f_{p})$</tex> of 15 GHz, a signal frequency <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(f_{s})$</tex> of 10 GHz, and an idler frequency <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(f_{i}=f_{p}-f_{s})$</tex> of 5 GHz. A patch element couples the input signal to the pump and idler circuits (realized in microstrip technology) through an aperture in the ground plane. This parametric amplifier leverages a varactor diode to provide a variable capacitance. To minimize the required pump power, the feeding network for the pump is designed as an RF transformer. This maximizes the potential drop across the diode to the greatest extent possible. The design is simulated in two steps: the aperture coupled waveguide is simulated in Ansys High Frequency Structure Simulator (HFSS), and the complete amplifier circuit is simulated in Keysight Advanced Design System (ADS). The simulated gain of the amplifier is greater than 20 dB.

articleTitle: Reconnection-Driven Electron Acceleration: Guide Field Effects
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Charged-particle acceleration – a signature of the plasma phenomenon known as magnetic reconnection - has been studied in extensive detail with West Virginia University's PHAse Space MApping (PHASMA) experiment. These studies were conducted with a retarding field energy analyzer (RFEA) built to measure electron energy distribution functions (EEDFs) and to identify localized zones of energetic electron production. The results show a guide-field dependent spatio-temporal distribution of energetic electrons, which consist of field-aligned electron beams at locations with high-energy currents.

articleTitle: Fast and Accurate Method for Doppler Averaging of Rydberg EIT Signals
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Modeling the effect of Doppler broadening due to the thermal atomic motion of Rydberg sensors typically relies on sampling a large velocity class, solving the equations of motion for each velocity, and then averaging the atomic density matrix over that velocity class. This process is inexact, slow, and presents a bottleneck in simulating Rydberg sensors. We present an approach that allows for fast, exact velocity averaging just by solving the equations of motion twice. We find the “propagator” that acts on the zero-velocity solution to generate the velocity-dependent atomic state for all velocities. By averaging this propagator over the Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution of the atoms, we obtain an explicit, analytic formula that generates the averaged atomic state. This method is expected to save memory and time computational resources by one to several orders of magnitude, compared to traditional sampling approaches.

articleTitle: Statistical Analysis and Detection of Spread-F and foF2 Values Using Digisonde and VIPIR Instruments
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A comprehensive statistical study of Spread F using digisonde data from low, mid and high latitude global sites (Figure 1) has been conducted. High-latitude sites: Qaanaaq, Tromso, Norilsk, and Gakona. Mid-latitude sites: Puerto Rico, Wallops Island, Dyess, Boulder, and Vandenberg. Low-latitude sites: Jicamarca, Ascension Island, and Kwajalein. Multiple algorithms have been written to process the raw data, determine spread Es and F and detect foF2 and hmF2 values using edge detection and pattern recognition techniques. The algorithms have been tuned for different latitudes and longitudes. Vertical Incidence Pulsed Ionospheric Radar (VIPIR) data was also processed for a few of these sites for determining the foF2 values and to compare the two instruments. These foF2 values were validated with manually scaled data obtained using Standard Archiving Output (SAO) Explorer as well as comparison with COSMIC-1/FORMOSAT-3 satellite data and SAMI2 and IRI models values.

articleTitle: Toward A 2-28 GHz Reconfigurable RF Tuner with >70 dB SFDR for 2 GHz IBW
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper investigates a reconfigurable pre-select-filter-less RF tuner which can achieve 8 dB NF, 36.5 dBm IIP3, and 21.2 dB gain averaged across 2–28 GHz with a 19 dBm single-ended LO input. Simulations utilizing a fabricated and verified GaN N-path mixer core alongside COTS support components for 2 GHz IBW with 30 dB out-of-band rejection achieves average 73 dB SFDR with minimum 70 dB across the 2–28 GHz tuning range. RF tuner center frequency is digitally reconfigured by ADPLL programming and instantaneous bandwidth is reconfigured by digitally-programmed capacitor banks at baseband owing to the impedance transparency property demonstrated by prior art N-path mixer-first receivers. Compared to state-of-the-art 500 MHz IBW ELINT receivers, this work promises 7 dB enhanced NF and 12.5 dB enhanced IIP3, thus delivering a 17 dB enhanced instantaneous SFDR while providing >20 dB gain.

articleTitle: Electrically Small Ultrawideband Antenna for Wireless Power Transfer to Headstage Based Electrophysiological Recording System
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents an electrically small ultrawideband (UWB) antenna for wireless power transfer (WPT) to low-power electrophysiological signal recording systems. The proposed antenna is a slot antenna excited by a 50 Ω microstrip line-based monopole feed. The slots are cut in the ground plane, where the slot dimensions are determined to create resonance at 5, 6, and 7.5 GHz. A H-shaped resonator is added to create resonance at 9.5 GHz. The resultant antenna has a 5.5 - 10 GHz measured UWB operating frequency with 3.82 - 4.8 dBi gain. The antenna is 15 × 15 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> with an electrical dimension of 0.27 ⋋ × 0.27 ⋋. The antenna is elliptically polarized over the operating frequency and having circular polarization from 6.5 - 8.5 GHz. The antenna can receive 22.5 dBm of power without exceeding the FCC SAR limit making it suitable as a WPT receiver.

articleTitle: Measurement of Extinction Rate of Waves Propagating Through Heterogeneous Media
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Link budget analysis is an important part of the design of remote sensing and wireless communication systems. Channel attenuation is perhaps the most dominant factor in the link budget analysis. Theoretical modelling and prediction of extinction rate of a heterogeneous channel is difficult and often intractable. Moreover, theoretical predictions may not agree with measured results. Also, some of the parameters of the theoretical model may not be measurable quantities. Hence many researchers have resorted to measurement campaigns to directly estimate channel extinction rate.

articleTitle: Real-Time Computation of E-Field in Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Neuronavigation and Optimization
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive brain stimulation technique used for the treatment of depression, as well as various neurological and psychiatric disorders. There has been ongoing interest in developing fast E-field solvers that can be easily incorporated into neuronavigation systems to facilitate real-time E-field in targeted brain regions, optimizing dosing parameters.

articleTitle: Computer Vision-Generated Database of Plasma Waves in the Inner Magnetosphere
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Plasma waves like chorus, hiss, and lightning-generated whistlers (LGWs) in the inner magnetosphere play a crucial role in shaping radiation belt dynamics (Figure 1). Chorus waves are particularly important for accelerating electrons from seed energies (hundreds of keV) to relativistic energies (~1 MeV and above). Meanwhile, all of these wave types contribute to the scattering of energetic electrons into the loss cone, one of the primary loss mechanisms for radiation belt electrons. Numerous missions equipped with VLF receivers have provided valuable data on these waves, deepening our understanding of their impact on the radiation belts. The Van Allen Probes and Arase missions, for example, measured all six components of VLF waves while traversing the radiation belts within the last decade.

articleTitle: Viability of a Ground-Based Wind Profiling Radar Remote Sensing Methodology for Application in the Marine Atmospheric Surface Layer
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The use of radar to remotely sense atmospheric properties could provide accurate, high-resolution measurements that are essential for a variety of civil and military applications. Radar remote sensing within the marine atmospheric surface layer (MASL) has been performed for atmospheric refractivity (e.g., D. M. Pastore, S. E. Wessinger, M. J. Stanek, R. J. Burkholder, T. This refractivity is related to humidity, temperature, and pressure. Humidity has the largest effect on atmospheric refractivity and therefore theoretically, has the greatest potential to be inferred from radar-based refractivity. articleTitle: Ocean Salinity Measurements with L-Band Passive Airborne and Ground Based Instruments
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The accurate sensing of ocean salinity is key to enhance our understanding of the flow of ocean currents and air-sea heat flux. Passive microwave remote sensing instruments have been utilized to sense the ocean salinity such as Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity (SMOS) satellite of ESA. The spectral sensitivity of the microwave instruments to salinity is critical for accurate retrieval of ocean salinity.

articleTitle: Scientific Computing at Scale: How do we Approach a Petabyte Scale Problem?
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Current generation radio interferometers (e.g., MeerKAT, Jvla) are producing data at rates of a few to tens of terabytes per day, with the rates predicted to go up substantially (1–2 orders of magnitude) with the next generation of instruments (ngVLA, SKA). In order to keep up with the expected data rates, and to produce science ready data products on reasonable timescales, the data processing architectures must necessarily be highly parallel and scaleable.

articleTitle: Design and Simulation of a 94 GHz Resonant Horn Antenna that Detects Hidden Microscopic Defects on a PCB Board
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Hidden microscopic defects on a Printed Circuit Board (PCB) occur through one or many errors in the manufacturing process. These hidden defects can include misalignments of metallic layers, via pad misalignments, pinholes, voids and gaps, etc. Even though these hidden defects are small, they have a significant impact on the functionality of the PCB. This can equate to monetary losses due to discarding chips as well as extra time and labor spent on inspecting and correcting these defects. Currently, there are many methods to detect hidden defects based on optical, acoustic, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). However, these methods are costly and time-consuming, can only detect hidden defects at the surface, and may destroy the material.

articleTitle: Maxwell-Schrödinger Modeling of Multi-Qubit Effects in a Superconducting Circuit Quantum Device
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Creating effective modeling strategies to simulate quantum circuit initialization, control, and readout is essential for making practical quantum computers. Current modeling approaches are often limited because they utilize full-wave computational electromagnetics tools inefficiently or depend on user-intensive curve-fitting approaches, both untenable to the massive scaling up required to model useful quantum devices. In this work, we build upon previous Maxwell-Schrödinger methods (T. E. Roth and S. T. Elkin, “Maxwell-Schrödinger Modeling of a Superconducting Qubit Coupled to a Transmission Line Network,” IEEE Journal on Multiscale and Multiphysics Computational Techniques, vol. 9, Jan. 2024) by extending them to model coupled superconducting transmon qubits embedded in transmission line networks. Coupled qubits play a prominent role in quantum devices. They are essential for multi-qubit gates that generate entanglement, which is necessary for any practical quantum computing algorithm. Our method is pertinent for the common case of transmons operating in the dispersive regime where the operating frequency of the electromagnetic (EM) resonator is far detuned from the transition frequencies of the qubits coupled to it. We start from the self-consistent equations of motion developed in the original work. These equations treat the system semi-classically, meaning the EM effects are incorporated classically while the transmon dynamics are evaluated quantum mechanically. We build upon this system by incorporating the multi-qubit exchange coupling rate into the formalism. This quantity characterizes the quantum effects needed to design intentional multi-qubit gates, but also is important in assessing unintentional quantum crosstalk that occurs. This exchange coupling rate can be efficiently evaluated through our prior work (G. Khan and T. E. Roth, “Field-Based Formalism for Calculating Multi-Qubit Exchange Coupling Rates for Transmon Qubits,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.05473, 2024), where we developed a simple formula that depended on the impedance response of the superconducting quantum circuit. We then use this methodology to simulate realistic quantum circuit topologies found in the literature and demonstrate basic control operations like the cross-resonance (CR) gate (C. Rigetti and M. Devoret, “Fully Microwave-Tunable Universal Gates in Superconducting Qubits with Linear Couplings and Fixed Transition Frequencies,” Physical Review B, vol. 81, 134507, Apr., 2010.). We further show that accounting for the self-consistent interactions in our Maxwell-Schrödinger framework is key for designing high-fidelity gates, as shown in Fig. 1.

articleTitle: Pixelated Metamaterial Design with Binary Genetic Algorithm
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A binary genetic algorithm (GA) is used to create pixelated metamaterial structures to mimic the performance of an Electric-LC (ELC) resonator and a non-bianisotropic split ring resonator (NB-SRR). The ELC couples strongly to a uniform transverse electric field. In contrast, the NB-SRR couples strongly to a transverse uniform magnetic field. The GA is configured to match the magnitude and phase S-parameter response of each individual unit cell from 7 GHz to 10 GHz. This method of arranging metalized pixels in specific spatial locations to achieve a target electromagnetic (EM) response may prove to be useful in applications where using analytic solutions to determine a geometry that satisfies the target EM response is too difficult.

articleTitle: Unraveling New Indices for the Interhemispheric Asymmetry of EIA and Exploring Their Connection with Global-Scale Waves
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: When near-Earth electric and geomagnetic fields interact and create the equatorial plasma fountain in the ionosphere, ionospheric plasma is driven away from the equator, forming plasma density enhancements in the F-region. After removing plasma from the geomagnetic equator, this enhancement constitutes the equatorial ionization anomaly (EIA). Here, an interhemispheric asymmetry (IHA) index is introduced to quantitatively characterize the north-south differences of the EIA crests in terms of their strength, separations, and responses to various parameters such as seasons, solar insolation, and geomagnetic storms, utilizing ground-based Low-Latitude Sensor Network (LISN) total electron content (TEC) data. The IHA of the EIA is vital for understanding transionospheric radio propagation, predicting ionospheric processes, improving models, and mitigating space weather threats to modern technologies.

articleTitle: Evaluating the Performance Trade-Offs Between Resistively-Loaded LTI ESAs and Time-Varying Non-LTI ESAs Using OFDM Wafeforms
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The design space for electrical small antennas (ESAs) is being constantly innovated and transformed through the development of new technologies, materials, and design techniques. The thematic goal of these efforts is to balance the fundamental physical limitations imposed by the electrical miniaturization of the antenna with the application-driven need to enable broadband performance of the system. The fundamental challenges are well described by well-known limits linking the quality factor and bandwidth of the antenna (e.g., Chu's Limit) as well as the performance of any lumped, distributed, or hybrid circuit topology that may be deployed for small-signal impedance matching (e.g., Bode-Fano Limit). There are a wide range of pragmatic challenges that also exist that compound the complexity of this design space; this includes, but it not limited to, the losses and non-ideal behavior of commercial off-the-shelf components and materials and its interaction with a ground plane or the platform it is integrated onto. A recent concept using the Antenna-As-Package (AAP) has emerged in the mm-wave community to reconcile the dimensional similarities of active circuits (amplifiers, etc.) with the antennas, and it is examined here in the co-design of the ESA and a custom/co-located RFIC. This talk will include strategies explored to integrate time-varying impedance matching and large-signal matching into the ESA to maximize power radiated by the antenna when transmitting and maximize the SNR when receiving. Since typical antenna performance metrics (VSWR, etc.) becomes challenging to define in this configuration, the ESA's ability to transmit/receive phase-based digital communication schemes (N-QAM, OFDM, etc.) ais compared to an electrically large wideband antenna (horn, etc.). Simulated and measured results will be provided along with a discussion on the external limiting factors that also drive the performance of the system.

articleTitle: A Compact CPW-Fed Circularly Polarized Planar Monopole Antenna for IoT Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A flexible, compact C-shaped coplanar waveguide- (CPW-fed) circularly polarized (CP) antenna is proposed for Internet of Things (IoT) applications. The antenna is designed on a polyethylene terephthalate (PET) substrate, enabling flexibility and the potential for conformal integration. The design achieves a wide 3-dB axial ratio bandwidth (ARBW) of 5.66 GHz (79.94%) from 4.25 GHz to 9.91 GHz, demonstrating excellent CP perfor- Additionally, the antenna exhibits a broad 10-dB return loss bandwidth (RLBW) of 7.67 GHz (99.55%) spanning 3.87 GHz to 11.54 GHz, fully encompassing the ARBW. The antenna maintains a peak gain over 3.5 dB and radiation efficiency over 95% within the ARBW. This wide operational range makes the antenna suitable for a variety of wireless communication systems, including WiFi, WiMAX, and emerging 5G technologies

articleTitle: Holographic Beam Mapping for CHIME: Current Status and Future Directions
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) is a drift-scan radio interferometer located at the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory (DRAO) in Penticton, British Columbia, Canada. CHIME, operating between 400 and 800 MHz, will map the red shifted 21 cm emission of neutral hydrogen between redshifts <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z= 0.8-2.5$</tex> across the northern sky. The 21 cm line is a tracer of the large scale structure of matter, whose statistics encode a well-understood standard ruler, the baryon acoustic oscillation scale. By detecting and tracking the evolution of this scale with redshift, CHIME aims to constrain the expansion history of the Universe over this crucial redshift epoch when the overall energy density of the Universe is expected to have become dominated by dark energy.

articleTitle: Novel 1-Bit Hybrid Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface with Mitigated Quantization Lobe
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel 1-bit hybrid reconfigurable intelligent surface (HRIS) designed to sense the incident signal's angle of arrival (AoA) and redirect it toward desired directions. This device consists of independently tunable resonant patch elements loaded with PIN diodes. To introduce sensing capabilities to this geometry, a portion of the signal incident on each element is coupled to a parallel plate waveguide through small rectangular slots. Two coaxial connectors then measure the signal coupled from all elements to the parallel plate waveguide. We use compressive sensing techniques to analyze this signal and detect AoA. Further, pre-coded phase randomization is implemented by varying slot sizes to suppress undesired quantization lobes. The proposed HRIS is simple, low cost, can operate without feedback loops, and may find application in intelligent wireless communication, power transfer, and sensing systems.

articleTitle: The VLA Sky Survey (VLASS) and Beyond: Lessons, Challenges, and Future Surveys
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The VLA Sky Survey (VLASS) is a community driven program carried out by the NRAO with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array to survey the Northern Sky (33885 square degrees above Declination 40deg) in 3 complete Epochs with a cadence of roughly 32 months at frequencies from 2–4 GHz with an angular resolution of approximately 2.5 arc-seconds mid-band. The VLASS recently (Oct 2024) completed its third Epoch of observing, and we have proposed for an extension to a fourth Epoch. To carry out this survey, we pushed a number of features of the VLA system to their limits, including operating the array in an On-The-Fly mode with the telescopes scanning the sky at 3.3 arcmin/sec at an integration time of 0.45 sec. Data processing was also a challenge, due to the large data volumes and the more than 11 million pointings needed to cover one pass of the sky, as well as the presence of bright and/or extended sources in many regions impacting the dynamic range and fidelity of standard imaging. In spite of these difficulties, the VLASS was able to deliver “Quick-Look” images, of quality suitable for the detection of transient and variable unresolved sources, within around 1 month after observing a given area of sky. Our current focus is the production and delivery of higher-quality spectro-polarimetric image cubes.

articleTitle: Implementation and Validation of a Novel SAR Imaging-Based Antenna Array Calibration
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Scanned antenna arrays need to be periodically calibrated to correct for amplitude and phase errors that degrade performance. The ability to adjust complex excitations to correct for these errors requires an accurate method of determining what errors are present. Doing so often requires far-field calibration targets or sensors, additional hardware such as near-field sensors or self-sampling circuitry, or specific array configurations. These requirements are difficult to meet for arrays mounted on air/spacecraft that cannot be easily accessed during operation. Look-up table calibration approaches fail under these scenarios if operating conditions change over time, including change in the temperature, aging, and array position deformation. In [1], we show that distributed targets can be used to determine the element-to-element channel imbalances in antenna arrays through synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging. For arrays mounted on air/spacecraft, the terrestrial scene below can be used to calibrate, and is always visible. This work reports the implementation and validation of the procedure to an advanced wideband 16-element active electronically scanned array (AESA) we fabricated as a testbed. A number of scenarios are investigated, including transmit and receive arrays, over a range of signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), and with distortions to the array structure that result in uncertainties in element positions.

articleTitle: Radiofrequency Interference Issues and Mitigation for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: CMB-S4 is the next-generation ground-based cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiment, which will map the CMB's temperature and polarization to unprecedented precision, advancing our understanding of the universe. A combination of small- and large-aperture telescopes with hundreds of thousands of super-conducting bolometers will observe in broad frequency bands spanning 20–300 GHz, surveying the majority of the sky to arcminute resolution. The design is based on previous generations of successful ground-based CMB instruments, which demonstrated exceptional sensitivity and control of systematic effects. However, aspects of CMB instrument design that enable such sensitivity also leave them vulnerable to radiofrequency interference (RFI), including broad fractional bandwidths and wide fields of view. Due to this instrument design along with the stringent measurement requirements for these cosmological surveys, many typical mitigation techniques for RFI used in radio astronomy are not feasible, including frequency rejection.

articleTitle: A FMM Bidomain Boundary Element Method for Modeling Electromagnetic Brain Stimulation of a Pseudo-Realistic Cell
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Brain cells known as neurons transmit electrical signals by controlling the transport of chemical ions across their membrane. The presence of an electric (E-) field generated by an external device modulates these brain signals, producing therapeutic effects. Electrodes and coil technologies have been developed to use E-fields for treating psychiatric disorders, smoking addiction, and tremors from Parkinson's disease.

articleTitle: LibRA: A Scientific Software Library of Radio Astronomy Algorithms
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: LibRA is a scientific software library with implementations of both existing and new algorithms for interfer-ometric calibration and imaging in the Radio Astronomy (RA) community. Derived from the CASA code base, LibRA has been developed into a standalone, open-source library with its own independent reposi-tory. The primary goal of the LibRA project is to provide direct access to RA algorithms, targeting research groups, university departments, and individual researchers, including faculty, students, and postdoctoral re-searchers. This library offers production-quality implementations of core algorithms that are user-friendly, easily deployable, and modifiable to suit specific needs. The fundamental scientific principles behind such telescopes share commonalities with other domains that rely on indirect imaging, such as Magnetic Res-onance Imaging (MRI) and ultrasound imaging. To make RA algorithms accessible, a strong requirement driving the software design is to keep the interface simple, the software stack shallow, and the software de-pendency graph small. To achieve these primary goals, LibRA provides interfaces through C++, Python, and command-line options. In this talk, we will outline the software architecture, current capabilities, and in-terfaces of LibRA. We will also discuss how these can be leveraged in other software development projects and by end-users for scientific applications. Additionally, we will illustrate the use of LibRA by parallel computing in large-scale distributed networks for calibration and imaging of ngVLA/SKA-sized data sets. The talk will also cover ongoing collaborations with computing, RA, and medical imaging groups, as well as future development plans.

articleTitle: Linearization of Nonlinear Power Amplifier Effects on BPSK Waveforms
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Contemporary communication systems demand continual improvements in power efficiency, motivating the operation of their power amplifiers in increasingly nonlinear regions. To mitigate the associated waveform distortion, a linearization technique is often implemented. While linearization is typically performed on transmit, it is also possible to perform at the receiver as a Digital Post-Distortion (DPoD) correction (N. Naraharisetti, et al., “Efficient Least-Squares 2-D-Cubic Spline for Concurrent Dual-Band Systems,” in IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, vol. 63, no. 7, pp. 2199–2210, July 2015). Previous results have shown success in the use of DPoD techniques for waveforms that have non-constant amplitudes. However existing DPoD techniques are inapplicable for correcting any distortions in constant amplitude waveforms such as Binary Phase-Shift Keying (BPSK).

articleTitle: Development of a Low Mutual Coupling Antenna for Future 21 cm Interferometers
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The epoch of reionization (EoR) and Cosmic Dawn are the last periods of the cosmological timeline that has not been directly observed. The most notable probe of these periods is the redshifted 21 cm spectral line of neutral hydrogen. Interferometry is crucial to understanding the spatial structure of neutral hydrogen during these periods. Current EoR experiments that use interferometers to observe the hydrogen signal, such as the Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array (HERA), struggle from instrumental systematics that limit their sensitivity. Crucially, mutual coupling between neighboring antennas greatly reduces instrument sensitivity. Models for mutual coupling have been developed in the hopes of calibrating these effects, but simple re-radiation models used lack precision and do not account for scattering on objects such as dishes. Although these calibration schemes improve instrument sensitivity, they still lack the sensitivity levels needed for 21 cm observations. Electromagnetic simulations of attempts to minimize mutual coupling by means of lowering feeds or adding structures between antennas have also been made but these did not show considerable promise. Instead of mitigating mutual coupling in current arrays, we propose designing a new antenna altogether with low mutual coupling as one of the main design requirements. A prototype slotted ground plane antenna in the 10 GHz band has been designed in the electromagnetic simulation software FEKO. This antenna was designed similar to antennas used in Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiments that exhibit favorable mutual coupling figures. We then compared the HERA antennas with our own, using mutual coupling figures of merit such as transmission coefficients (S21), beam deviations and most importantly, induced fields on neighboring antennas. We have found that without any optimization, our prototype antenna experiences significantly lower mutual coupling than HERA. These findings will be discussed in this talk.

articleTitle: Design of an Antenna Synthesis Algorithm for Application with a Reconfigurable Phased Array
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: As demand for spectrum has increased, it has become a more scarce and valuable resource. Even so, the management of spectrum remains largely rigid. Consistent with the management approach, technology used to implement wireless transmitters is often rigid and unable to maximize performance while adjusting operating frequency. To move towards a future of more flexible spectral co-existence, there must be innovation in the underlying technologies. For instance, while the signals in the elements of a traditional, fixed-geometry phased array can be phase-shifted to change beam direction, there are many other parameters that are typically fixed in the design and cannot be altered during use while maintaining acceptable performance, such as frequency, bandwidth, beam pattern, and power. While sparse arrays can provide more control over array geometry, they are very application specific and may not be applicable in general use cases. Instead, a more adaptable and reconfigurable array that can change its electrical and physical properties to meet varying specifications could provide a much more flexible solution for dynamic spectrum use scenarios.

articleTitle: Re-Channelizing Quantized Polyphase Filter Banks
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)

abstract: I will present a fast, Fourier-transform based algorithm to invert the effects of Polyphase Filter Banks (PFBs). Data channelized with a PFB is usually quantized, causing difficulties with the inverse, which greatly am-plifies quantization noise. I will present two practical methods for dealing with quantization noise: (1) by applying a Wiener filter, and (2) a maximum-likelihood conjugate-gradient based approach.

articleTitle: Screen-Printed Wearable Textile Antennas Using Ag/Cu Inks
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Wearable industry is rapidly expanding, and is projected to grow at an annual rate of 15.9% (Brophy et al., The Future of Wearable Technologies - Guder Research Group 2021). The devices that are integrated onto these wearables that provide seamless communication with the external world are of paramount interest for both commercial and military applications. In such applications, some of the challenges include designing lightweight, less obtrusive and flexible devices that consume minimal power. In this study, we consider the design, fabrication and testing of screen-printed antennas that operate in Citizens Broadband Radio Service (CBRS) band which is within the range of sub 6 GHz 5G.

articleTitle: Direct Antenna Binary Phase-Shift Keying through Ferrimagnetic Loading
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study proposes the use of Yttrium Iron Garnet (YIG), a ferrimagnetic material, as part of the substrate for a Cband patch antenna. It was observed that the phase of the radiated signal from the patch antenna can be tuned by adjusting the magnetic bias field strength. By selectively switching between two magnetic bias fields that give 180 degree phase difference in the radiated signal, a direct antenna binary phase shift keying (DA-BPSK) is realized. Simulation results from HFSS and ADS are used to demonstrate the feasibility of the idea. Such direct antenna modulation (DAM) system can be instrumental for onchip electrically small antennas

articleTitle: Whistler-Mode Waves on Magnetic and Density Shelves
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Very-low and extremely-low frequency (VLF/ELF) whistler-mode waves are crucial in the dynamics of energetic electrons within the Earth's radiation belts, primarily through wave-particle interactions. The propagation of these waves in the magnetosphere is affected by variations in the background plasma density and magnetic fields, referred to as density and magnetic ducts. Recent observations from the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission and NASA's Van Allen Probes (RBSP) have revealed that VLF/ELF whistler waves can become trapped and guided by field-aligned irregularities in plasma density and magnetic fields, known as density shelves (n-shelf) and magnetic shelves (B-shelf). These structures form ducts that enable the waves to travel long distances in the Earth's magnetosphere with minimal attenuation.

articleTitle: Large Aperture Telescope Sidelobe Issues and Mitigation for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Large aperture telescopes (LATs) require exquisite control of systematic errors to make high resolution measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and Galactic foregrounds, using multiple observing frequency bands spanning roughly 20 to 280 GHz. In particular, far-sidelobe contamination is an important consideration for CMB measurements by LATs on large angular scales. Ground pick-up is particularly con-cerning because the complex and time-varying nature of the signal makes it difficult to remove from the data without also suppressing cosmological information. Such sidelobe signals can be produced by diffraction from gaps between panels in segmented telescope mirrors, and by the interactions between light scattered in the receiver optics and the surrounding telescope enclosure.

Over a 4-day exposure period, fibrosarcoma growth rates were modulated in the presence of low-level alternating current (AC) magnetic fields at a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10 \mu \mathrm{T}$</tex> amplitude at 13.5 Hz to 30 Hz frequency, superimposed on a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$45 \mu \mathrm{T}$</tex> static background field.
