articleTitle: A GNSS-T and LiDAR Fusion Approach to Generate Large Scale Vegetation Optical Depth Map
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Accurate measurement and analysis of vegetation optical depth (VOD) are essential for understanding vegetation water content and its spatial distribution. This paper investigates the use of GNSS-T (Global Navigation Satellite System Trans-missometry) techniques for non-destructive VOD measurement. While GNSS-T is effective, scaling VOD measurements to larger areas remains a challenge. We address this issue by proposing methods to enhance the scalability of VOD assessments. Specifi-cally, we utilize LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) scans to generate features corresponding to satellite positions at various azimuth and elevation angles. These features are then used with pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) models to predict VOD values, with GNSS-T measurements serving as ground truth. This approach aims to improve the upscaling of VOD measurements and advance our ability to monitor and manage forest ecosystems effectively.

articleTitle: Exploring the Crosstalk Properties of the CHIME Telescope
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) is a drift-scan radio interferometer located at the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory (DRAO) in Penticton, British Columbia, Canada. CHIME, operating between 400 and 800 MHz, will map the redshifted 21 cm emission of neutral hydrogen between redshifts <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{z}=0.8-2.5$</tex> across the northern sky. The 21cm line intensity map traces the large-scale structure encoded by the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) scale. By detecting and tracking the evolution of this scale with redshift, CHIME aims to constrain the expansion history of the Universe over this crucial redshift epoch when the overall energy density of the Universe is expected to have become dominated by dark energy.

articleTitle: Metamaterial Antenna Design to Enhance Near Field Inductive Coupling for Biomedical Implants
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a concept for a double negative metamaterial (DNM)-based antenna to simultaneously enhance Wireless Power Transfer (WPT) and reduce Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) here for a network of distributed brain microim-plants. The DNM copper coils are integrated in a FR-4 substrate, which has a dielectric constant of 4.3 and tangent loss <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\delta)$</tex> of 0.025. Occupying a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2 \times 2\text{cm}^{2}$</tex> area, the DNM structure is introduced into our target wireless brain-machine interface (BMI) system operating at 915 MHz. Preliminary HFSS simulations show it provides 2 dB WPT enhancement and a 20% SAR reduction. We believe the work has the potential to address the WPT/ SAR co-optimization challenges for biomedical implants in general.

articleTitle: Pioneering Ultra-Long-Wavelength Radio Science with LuSEE-Night
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Explorer at Night (LuSEE-Night) experiment will reach the lunar farside in 2026 to observe the sky in frequencies between 0.1 and 50 MHz. The radio sky below 20 MHz is largely unexplored, since the ionosphere blocks ground-based observations. LuSEE-Night will observe these new skies from a site remarkably isolated from terrestrial radio interference.

articleTitle: Compact Dual-Band Planar Wireless Power Transfer (WPT) System
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A compact dual-band planar wireless power transfer (WPT) system is presented in this paper. The planar structure is set to be 30-by-30 sq. mm to make it suitable for the Internet of Things and implantable medical devices applications. Furthermore, the system operates on two distinct frequencies, 0.9 GHz and 1.8 GHz, providing the potential for both data and power transmission. The desired resonances are achieved by varying the design parameters. Finally, the planar WPT with a 13 mm transfer distance reaches a PTE of 74% at 0.9 GHz and 66% at 1.8 GHz. Moreover, the influence of misalignment on the planar WPT is assessed, revealing the system's resilience to displacement within specific ranges at two frequencies.

articleTitle: NRL SPADE-2 Measurements of Ionospheric Plasma Parameters
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Space PlasmA Diagnostic suitE (SPADE) instrument, developed by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), is a plasma impedance probe designed to monitor background space plasma conditions and provide early warning of the onset of hazardous levels of spacecraft charging. SPADE operated on the International Space Station (ISS) from May 2019 until November 2021 as part of the Department of Defense Space Test Program's STP-H6 mission. The SPADE experiment consisted of two dipole antennas, one active antenna that is used to excite the local plasma and another passive dipole antenna that observes the excitation. The active probe is swept across a range of frequencies and DC voltage biases to determine the plasma impedance spectrum. The impedance measurements yield properties of the plasma, such as density, plasma potential, and electron temperature, while also providing data indicating the charging level of the ISS relative to the local plasma. SPADE responds to slight changes in the plasma sheath that forms around a charged object, providing a unique method for the early detection of charging. SPADE active dipole measurements of ionospheric plasma parameters, ISS charging, and comparisons to measurements made using other in situ and ground-based diagnostics will be presented.

articleTitle: Preliminary Range-Dependent Measurements During the Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in Stable Atmosphere Over Water Campaign
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Study of stable atmospheric conditions and the corresponding effect on radiowave propagation is the focus of the Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in Stable Atmosphere over Water campaign. Among other systems, our group collected range-dependent propagation loss measurements using a remote controlled JetYak and Twin Otter aircraft. The preliminary measurements are discussed.

publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The demand for spectrum is growing and to fully utilize this limited resource dynamic spectrum-sharing (DSS) systems need to be developed and deployed at scale. In 2021, Verizon spent $45.5 billion for a subset of spectrum licenses in the C-Band [1]. This demonstrates the economic impact of increasing the number of services that can use a given frequency at the same place and time. Sensing and reconfigurable circuitry can be used in DSS systems to prevent interference between concurrent services by providing spectrum agility in four domains: time, frequency, direction, and power. Directional modulation enables a dualfunction radar communication systems in which a single antenna array can transmit both communication and radar waveforms in different directions simultaneously.

articleTitle: Design, Implementation, and Experimental Characterization of a non-LTI Electrically Small HF Antenna with Improved Bandwidth-Efficiency Product
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present the design and experimental characterization of a non-linear-time-invariant (i.e., non-LTI) electrically small antenna (ESA) operating at the high-frequency (HF) band. This non-LTI ESA is designed to overcome the problems associated with the fundamental bandwidth-efficiency product limitations that govern the performances of passive, linear-time-invariant (LTI) ESAs. The antenna comprises an electrically small radiator and a class-E switch-mode inverter and can transmit multiple types of digitally modulated waveforms in the HF band. Due to the large wavelength of electromagnetic waves in the HF band, practical HF antennas are usually electrically small. Because of their limited dimensions, passive electrically small antennas suffer from large quality factors and are hard to impedance match over wide bandwidths. The physical limitations that govern the bandwidth-efficiency products of ESAs are well known (e.g., the Chu, Wheeler, and Gustafsson limits) and have been thoroughly investigated and confirmed by many ESA designs. Different techniques, such as non-foster impedance matching, active matching, and direct-antenna modulation among others, have been investigated to overcome these limitations. These techniques do not violate the laws of physics. Rather, they violate the linear-time-invariance or passive operation assumptions used in the derivation of the fundamental physical limits. In a recent work (N. Behdad, D. Ludois, M. Mirmozafari, and M. Liben, “A class-E, switched-mode, non-LTI electrically-small transmit antenna design for overcoming the fundamental bandwidth-efficiency product limits,” 18th European Conf. Antennas Propag., Glasgow, UK, 2024), our team presented the design of a non-LTI ESA that integrates a switched-mode amplifier with an electrically small radiator. Through simulations, we demonstrated that this ESA is expected to be capable of radiating wideband, digitally modulated waveforms with bandwidth-efficiency products that exceed the fundamental limits. In this work, we present experimental results of a fabricated prototype of this non-LTI ESA. The prototype consists of a 1-m long monopole as the radiating element integrated with a class-E switch-mode circuit employing a GaN transistor switch. Digitally modulated waveforms are directly generated at the antenna stage by controlling the duty cycle of the gate driver signals applied to the switch-mode circuit. Amplitude, phase, and frequency control can be achieved by controlling the duty cycle, timing, and frequency of the gate driver signals. In this non-LTI ESA, the tasks of RF carrier generation, modulation, amplification, and radiation are all performed in a single device and only DC bias and gate driver control signals are supplied to the system. We have conducted system-level over-the-air (OTA) experiments using the non-LTI ESA as the transmitter and a conventional receiver system. The bit-error-rate (BER) and error vector magnitude (EVM) of the communication system are measured for a link operating at 10 MHz. We have also conducted similar OTA experiments using a conventional LTI ESA transmitter that uses the same radiating element in conjunction with an impedance matching network and a commercially available power amplifier. We will present the results of these two experiments and compare the bandwidth-efficiency product of the non-LTI ESA with that of its LTI counterpart. Finally, we will also present the initial designs of the next generation of this non-LTI ESA employing a closed-loop control system allowing for more efficient pulse shaping of the radiated siganls.

articleTitle: A Study of the Fields Excited in a Cylindrical Cavity by Multiple Longitudinal Apertures
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A semi-analytical solution for the electric field in a finite-length cylindrical cavity with a longitudinal aperture based on a dyadic Green's function formulation is available in past work (S. E. Dogan, J. T. Johnson, R. J. Burkholder, “On the Electromagnetic Fields Excited in a Finite-Length Circular Cylindrical Cavity by Plane Wave Incidence on a Longitudinal Aperture,” IEEE Transactions on Electromagnetic Compatibility, vol. 65, no. 6, pp. 1972–1980, Dec. 2023). This solution provides the field inside the cavity as a summation of discrete orthogonal modes satisfying appropriate boundary conditions on the cylindrical conducting surface. The aperture that excites fields inside the cavity is modeled with an equivalent source determined by solving a separate slot excitation problem. Power losses in the cavity due to the aperture and the wall conductivity are introduced to the solution via perturbative correction through the quality factor of each resonant mode. Past comparisons with numerically exact methods showed the approach to provide reasonable accuracy while significantly improving efficiency. It also provides physical insight into the effect of cylinder and aperture dimensions and material parameters on the collective power loss, and therefore the quality factor of each mode.

articleTitle: Spectrum Sensing Using Dispersive Delay Line Structure in Real-Time
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We investigate the generation of a local oscillator (LO) sweep across the 2–4 GHz frequency range with a sweep time on the order of several hundred nanoseconds. We introduce a new prototype for a fats LO sweep network that utilizes a dispersive delay line (DDL) structure. This prototype features a precision multi-stage cascaded DDL, which is implemented using coupled strip-line embedded within a delay loop. The delay loop incorporated a high-gain, high-linearity amplifier stage, enabling it to support numerous loops with enhanced frequency resolution, making it suitable for real-time spectrum sensing.

articleTitle: Pointing the South Pole Telescope with Machine Learning
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The South Pole Telescope (SPT) is a millimeter/sub-millimeter telescope primarily used to characterize the cosmic microwave background. The SPT's ability to point accurately at the sky depends on its structural imperfections, which are impacted by the South Pole's harsh weather. Pointing errors are particularly detrimental to SPT participation in Event Horizon Telescope observations, which require stricter pointing accuracy than typical SPT observations. Here, we present our efforts to improve the SPT's real-time pointing accuracy by using machine learning. We train two XGBoost models on data compiled from archival observations made during standard operation. The models learn a mapping from current weather conditions to two telescope drive control arguments that correct for errors in azimuth (az) and elevation (el), respectively. Our models achieve root mean squared errors on test data of 3.01” in az times cosine el and 3.57” in el, well below our goals of 5”. We deploy our models on the telescope and perform additional testing. Our models result in significantly reduced pointing errors: for sources where the models are best trained, average total error improved 33%, from 15.9“ to 10.6”. These improvements, while significant, fall shy of our goal yet serve as proof of concept for further development.

articleTitle: Modelling the Effective Vegetation Optical Depth and Scattering Albedo for Coniferous Forests from P- to Ka- Band
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Vegetation optical depth (VOD, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau$</tex>) and scattering albedo <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\omega)$</tex> are key radiative transfer properties for microwave radiometry of vegetated land. articleTitle: Development of Next Generation Very Large Array Tropospheric Calibration
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present on the development of calibrations strategies for the next generation Very Large Array (ngVLA). The ngVLA is the planned large scale interferometric array that will be primarily based in the American Southwest, but will include outlying sites across the United States, Mexico and Canada. The continental sized baselines available to the array, combined with a densely populated core, will enable ngVLA to be an order of magnitude more sensitive than the current VLA, while being able to achieve sub-milliarcsecond-resolution. Temporally variable water vapor in the troposhpere will introduce delay error to observations made with ngVLA. Calibration of this delay error is essential to ngVLA meeting science requirements.

articleTitle: The Magnetic Imprints of Coronal Currents: Remote Sensing of Remote Currents
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Carl Gauss speculated that the diurnal variations in the geomagnetic field were produced by currents flowing in a conducting layer in the Earth's upper atmosphere. In 1839 he developed a decomposition to separate the vector magnetic field observed on the Earth's surface into two components: one that is produced by the Earth's dynamo and a second produced by currents in this mysterious conducting layer. On the sun, the structure of the coronal currents is key to understanding solar eruptions. However, solar corona is optically thin and dense measurements of coronal magnetic field for computing J=curl(B) are presently impossible. We have applied Gauss' technique to vector magnetograms from the solar surface (photosphere) observed by the Solar Dynamics Observatory Helioseismic Magnetic Imager. This approach reveals, for the first time, the magnetic imprints of coronal currents in the photosphere. We discuss the properties of coronal currents in active regions and the implications of this 186 year old technique for predicting solar eruptions.

articleTitle: VLF and ELF Remote Sensing of the Lower Ionosphere During Total Solar Eclipse Conditions
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Solar eclipses offer unique opportunities to investigate the rapid electron density changes occurring in the ionospheric D-region. Previous research has demonstrated that the D-region's electron density decreases when the moon obscures solar radiation, but the detailed gradients and spatial structure of this density have not been fully understood. In this study, we take advantage of the total solar eclipse over the eastern United States on April 8, 2024, to gather new multi-point ELF and VLF measurements and compare to measurements made during previous eclipse events. VLF observations are made of the amplitude and phase of VLF communication transmitters. ELF observations are made of impulses from lightning discharges. By deploying ELF and VLF receivers in configurations that optimize transmitter-receiver alignments relative to the eclipse's path, we aim to refine the spatial resolution of prior studies. Our goals are to (1) assess the steepness of electron density gradients near the path of totality, (2) analyze ionospheric disturbances when the totality zone passes near a strong VLF transmitter, and (3) determine the lower ionosphere's response time to localized perturbations caused by the eclipse.

articleTitle: Electromagnetic Noise and Radiation Mitigation in Power Delivery Networks
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A growing interest in AI and deep learning applications necessitates the development of efficient power delivery networks (PDNs) to manage broadband impedance in high-speed switching environments. This paper evaluates the electromagnetic performance of horizontal, vertical, and embedded PDNs in fanout packages, with particular emphasis on vertical and embedded configurations, both less explored for noise mitigation. Simulations indicate that embedded PDNs significantly reduce commonmode (CM) and differential-mode (DM) radiation, achieving levels between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$20-78 \ \text{dB} \mu \mathrm{V}$</tex>. Additionally, measurements show that embedded PDNs maintain a lower electric field strength of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.9\ \mathrm{V}/\mathrm{m}$</tex> for DM radiation as compared to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.7 ~\mathrm{V}/\mathrm{m}$</tex> for horizontal PDNs and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$11.4 ~\mathrm{V}/\mathrm{m}$</tex> for vertical PDNs. Advanced shielding with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$5-\mu \mathrm{m}$</tex> thick Cu-CoNiFe layers further reduces magnetic field emissions by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${30 - 45} \text{dB}$</tex>. These findings demonstrate that embedded PDNs are a more effective solution for electromagnetic interference (EMI) mitigation in future electronic systems, offering superior noise control and reduced crosstalk.

publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) is a NASA Earth Venture mission (EVM-3) led by PI Susan van den Heever of Colorado State University (CSU), in collaboration with NASA/Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), Blue Canyon Technologies, and Tendeg Systems. The successful EVM-3 proposal to NASA's Earth Science Division relied on the prior success of two pathfinder CubeSat missions: RainCube, the first weather radar on a CubeSat, led by NASA/JPL, and the Temporal Experiment for Storms and Tropical Systems - Demonstration (TEMPEST-D) mission, led by CSU, producing the first global (up to 58 degrees latitude) observations from a multi-frequency microwave radiometer on a CubeSat, operating for nearly three years in LEO.

articleTitle: Design, Modeling, and Characterization of the Antenna Module for the LuSEE-Night Project
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The “Dark Ages” refers to the cosmic era between the last scattering of the cosmic microwave background and “Cosmic Dawn,” the time when the first stars and galaxies formed. Only cold, non-luminous hydrogen gas existed during the Dark Ages, which emits at 21 cm (f = 1420 MHz). Through the expansion of the universe, this signal has been redshifted to low radio frequencies that are inaccessible from earth due to distortions of our ionosphere and significant terrestrial radio-frequency interference. This era is therefore largely unexplored and remains one of the least constrained frontiers of modern cosmology.

articleTitle: Forecasting Global VTEC Data from VISTA with High Spatial and Temporal Resolution Using a Transformer-Based Deep Learning Model
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Accurate forecasting of global Vertical Total Electron Content (VTEC) is essential for numerous space-based technologies. This project aims to leverage deep learning models to enhance our ability to predict VTEC on a global scale. It addresses the challenge of forecasting VTEC with high spatial resolution, using a 1 °x 1 ° grid for latitude and longitude, and a temporal resolution of 5 minutes across various geographical regions. The goal is to extract geographic coordinates of interest from the predicted VTEC data, allowing real-time analysis and assessment of specific areas.

articleTitle: Metasurface-Backed Luneburg Lens for Backscatter Data Exfiltration
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: An additively manufactured Luneburg lens is combined with a spatially-tunable dynamic metasurface to create a low-power backscatter communicator. The device reflects signals back to an interrogator and can modulate the waveform's phase to communicate data. We experimentally show that the spatial control over the metasurface allows different bit streams to be communicated in varied directions while the lens provides gain and prevents would-be eavesdroppers from receiving information.

articleTitle: Status of the MIST Global 21-cm Experiment
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Observations of the redshifted 21-cm signal absorbed and emitted by neutral hydrogen offer one of the most promising methods to study the conditions of the early universe. The birth of the first stars and galaxies during cosmic dawn is imprinted on the globally-averaged signal as an absorption feature, which contains key information about the physics driving their formation. In 2018, the Experiment to Detect the Global EoR Signature (EDGES) collaboration claimed an anomalous detection of the cosmic dawn feature, finding it much deeper and wider than expected, leading to explanations that have variously invoked instrumental effects or the possibility of new physics. The EDGES detection was challenged in 2022 by the Shaped Antenna measurement of the background Radio Spectrum 3 (SARAS-3) team, which rejected the EDGES result with approximately 2σ confidence. The competing results motivates the need for independent teams to apply unique approaches to resolve the tension.

articleTitle: An Approach for Obtaining Hours of GIC Predictions from a Single, Short FDTD Simulation Having a Time-Step Increment on the Order of ~1 μ s
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method is a numerical technique for directly solving the full-vector form of Maxwell's time-dependent curl equations (both Faraday's and Ampere's laws). It has been used extensively to study electromagnetic wave propagation behavior for a wide variety of applications, such as wireless communications, antenna design, biomedical imaging, bio-photonics, remote sensing, and so on. Additionally, the FDTD method has been applied to geophysical applications, including electromagnetic propagation in the Earth-ionosphere waveguide, high frequency propagation through the ionosphere, and studying the impacts of space weather events on the operation of electric power grids. For this last application, of particular interest is the coupling of ionospheric currents to electric power grids via geoelectric fields and geomagnetically induced currents (GICs).

articleTitle: A Conformal Microwave Measurement System for Imaging Buried Anomalies
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Microwave imaging has long been reported for locating buried anomalies inside a bulk object as relying upon external measurements of microwave data. The approach is non-invasive, low-cost, portable, and the use of non-ionizing radiation makes it popular for biomedical applications. In this work, we explore the experimental feasibility of a conformal microwave imaging system, where the antennas are mounted on or very close to the imaging object. Our proof of concept setup entails 12 antennas surrounding a plastic cylindrical frame in free space with two dielectric cylinders used as anomalies. S-parameters were measured using a network analyzer and a 12- port switching matrix. For imaging, we used the Born Iterative Method, where the data equation was replaced with the S-parameter sensitivity formula. Simulation and measurement results show good quality image reconstruction, asserting the feasibility of the proposed conformal imaging setup. Future work will incorporate tissue-emulating materials to ultimately develop a stable and wearable imaging system.

articleTitle: Direct Comparisons of Whistler Mode Excitation Between an Electric and Loop Dipole Antenna in a Laboratory Plasma
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: High energy electrons from either solar wind or from human activity may become trapped inside the Van Allen radiation belts or create an artificial radiation belt that can persist for long periods of time. Spacecraft flying through these belts are susceptible to damage from these trapped electrons. Whistler waves are known to precipitate electrons into the atmosphere, so a proposed solution is using spacecraft to carry compact electron beams or antennas to remediate these trapped electrons. This remediation effort has picked up momentum with knowledge gained from recent space missions such as the Van Allen Probe spacecraft which collected data on electron loss mechanisms. Additionally, the recently completed Demonstration and Science Experiment (DSX) satellite mission conducted experiments on the efficiency of injecting very low frequency (VFL) waves in space with their novel 82-meter tip to tip electric dipole antenna. However, based on these missions and existing laboratory studies, there is still no clear candidate as the best generator of whistler waves for the purposes of a spacecraft-based radiation belt remediation mission.

articleTitle: Characterization of Whistler Mode Waves Launched by Phased Array High-µ Core Magnetic Loop Antennas*
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Small diameter, large aspect ratio, high-µ core magnetic loop antennas are a promising development as compact, low-power transmitters for the direct injection of electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) mode and whistler mode waves in the ELF/VLF frequency range in space plasmas. These waves play important roles in the inner radiation belt regions due to their ability to interact with high-energy trapped radiation belt particles. Antennas that can efficiently generate these waves from a space platform would be valuable for investigating key wave-particle interactions in space with laboratory-like precision.

articleTitle: Grounded Coplanar Waveguides for Material Characterization
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: When designing microwave frequency sensors mounted on human tissue, electrically accurate models of tissue, i.e. phantoms, are necessary. For applications in measuring internal body temperature, material parameters at 1-1.5 GHz are of particular interest (P. Momenroodaki et al., “Noninvasive Internal Body Temperature Tracking with Near-Field Microwave Radiometry,” IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, vol. 66, no. 5, pp. 2535–2545, Dec. 2017). Previous research suggests the use of transmission lines to extract the effective permittivity from S-parameters (W. B. Weir, “Automatic measurement of complex dielectric constant and permeability at microwave frequencies,” Proceedings of the IEEE, vol. 62, no. 1, pp. 33–36, Jan. 1974). A grounded coplanar waveguide (GCPW) was chosen for the transmission line due to ease of construction and small form factor. From the measured effective permittivity, the filling factors are necessary to obtain the relative permittivity of the material under test. These filling factors are found using a conformal mapping (J. Hu et al., “A grounded coplanar waveguide technique for microwave measurement of complex permittivity and permeability,” IEEE Transactions on Magnetics, vol. 42, no. 7, pp. 1929–1931, Jul. 2006).

articleTitle: Utilizing Low-Elevation Wideband GNSS Signals for Ionospheric TEC Estimations
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study explores the use of wideband, low-elevation satellite signals to retrieve ionospheric Total Electron Content (TEC) from Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) data. Monitoring ionospheric conditions is crucial for GNSS precision and space weather research, especially in polar regions where ground stations are sparse. Traditional GNSS systems often ignore low-elevation data due to noise, but this study demonstrates a method to utilize these signals, nearly doubling TEC measurements in key latitude bands. By analyzing data from GNSS stations in Hawaii and Alaska, the study shows that single-frequency wideband signals can reduce noise by 3–8 times compared to dual-frequency methods. This technique could significantly enhance ionospheric monitoring in poorly covered areas.

articleTitle: Michael Faraday and the Quantum Field Theory
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Trevor S. Bird's discussion in IEEE Antennas and Propagation magazine (December 2023) provides an excellent overview of Michael Faraday's role in one of the most important aspects of the development of electromagnetic (EM) theory. In the nineteenth century, at a time when electric and magnetic fields were considered separate phenomena, Faraday's work laid the foundation for all modern electromagnetic technologies that we use every day. In addition to forming the basis for key aspects of all EM theories, the influence of Faraday's work can also be directly linked to subsequent work by Maxwell. The purpose of this paper is to describe the connection between Faraday's research in the 19<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> century and subsequent developments in the 20<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> century as well as contemporary research.

articleTitle: Commission J: Radio Science from the Moon Lunar Odyssey: ROLSES-1 Data Analysis
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: As part of the NASA Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the lunar lander Odysseus touched down on the Moon's south pole near a crater called Malapert A in February of 2024. On board this lander was an instrument with four monopole stacer antennas called Radiowave Observations at the Lunar Surface of the photoElectron Sheath, or ROLSES-1. Despite setbacks due to the orientation of the lander, ROLSES-1 managed to collect data from its four antennas, one en route to the Moon, and the other three from the lunar surface.

articleTitle: Evidence for Uncorrected Gain Factors in Galactic Synchrotron Template Maps
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Accurate models of Galactic synchrotron emission are critical for our understanding of astrophysics and cosmology. For example, this emission is a bright foreground in observations of the redshifted 21-cm line and the Cosmic Microwave Background. It also serves as a probe of the astrophysical properties of our Galaxy such as its magnetic field. Galactic synchrotron emission is often modeled by anchoring to the 408 MHz Haslam map. While the map has been extensively analyzed over the past few decades and several of its known issues have been corrected, there are still uncertainties regarding the absolute calibration of the flux scale that are made apparent when compared to other maps of diffuse radio emission.

articleTitle: Simultaneous Observation of a Daytime Arietids Meteor Head Echo at VHF and UHF Frequencies
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: On June 11th, 2024, simultaneous meteor observations were performed using two radar instruments at Jicamarca Radio Observatory, including the main 50 MHz array which transmits 2 MW of power, and the smaller AMISR-14 445 MHz array which transmits approximately 150 kW. The main array is far more capable of observing head echoes, but larger meteoroids can produce head echoes detectable via both instruments, and multi-frequency observations of head echoes are valuable due to their scarcity. At around 6 am local time, a bright head echo was observed with velocity of 44.9 km/s and peak signal strength of 56 dB and 50 dB (above the noise floor) as measured by the main array and AMISR-14, respectively. Using the interferometric capability of the main array, the head echo trajectory was identified consistent with the Daytime Arietids meteor shower. Particle-in-cell plasma simulations and finite-difference time-domain scattering simulations are underway to estimate meteoroid mass using the radar results.

articleTitle: Solar System Radiophysics from the Farside of the Moon
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The NASA/DOE LuSEE Night experiment (Bale et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.10345) will be deployed on the lunar farside in early 2026 to make full-Stokes spectral measurements of the radio sky below 50 MHz using a simple crossed-dipole antenna system. LuSEE Night will be a pathfinder for future farside observatories, demonstrating many of the (quite ambitious) technologies required to make synoptic, radio quiet measurements throughout the lunar night. Additionally, a second experiment LuSEE Lite will make direct measurements of the DC electric field on the lunar surface which is thought to be a controlling factor for the electrostatic dust levitation which gave rise to the lunar ‘horizon glow’ observed by the Apollo astronauts.

articleTitle: Enhanced Adaptive Learning Model for Accurate Dual-Polarization Radar Rainfall Mapping
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study investigates the generalization capability of a deep learning model for dual-polarization radar-based quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE). The model is built upon a ShuffleNet architecture and trained using an extensive dataset, including radar reflectivity, differential reflectivity, and specific differential phase, from the KMLB radar in Florida covering the years from 2017 to 2021. Rain gauge data was also incorporated to enhance accuracy in estimating surface rainfall rates. Although the model demonstrates great performance in Florida, its adaptability was assessed by testing it in two contrasting regions: Oklahoma and California. Oklahoma, with its complex weather systems influenced by topography and the nearby Gulf of Mexico and Rocky Mountains, presents unique challenges for QPE models. Similarly, California's diverse precipitation patterns, ranging from coastal rain events to mountainous snowfall, offer another rigorous testing environment. The model's performance in these regions was validated against high-precision rain gauge measurements, providing key insights into its strengths and limitations. The results indicate that while the model performs well in its training region, accuracy challenges arise when applied to areas with differing climatic conditions, highlighting the need for adaptive learning techniques or region-specific model adjustments to improve QPE performance across diverse environments.

articleTitle: Anomalous Diffusion of a Strongly Magnetized Plasma in a Simulated Spacecraft Wake: Experimental Observations and Modeling
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The movement of objects, from satellites to the International Space Station, through the local geospace environment can significantly impact plasma conditions. These disturbances lead to the formation of wakes, which can interfere with measurements of electric potentials, electric fields, and even serve as a mechanism for generating waves and instabilities. The development of scaled laboratory studies can provide valuable insights for understanding satellite observations.

articleTitle: Plasma Impedance Tomography (PIT): Results of Measurement and Inversion Method
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Plasma Impedance Tomography (PIT) is a form of 2D plasma density mapping, using mutual-impedance measurements from an encircling array of dipole antennas. The method and algorithms build upon the broader established field of Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT), while tackling the unique challenges of measuring and inverting a plasma medium. The benefits of PIT include: 1) its non-intrusive approach for mapping a plasma distribution at relatively low-densities (~10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">8</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup>), 2) the contribution of information along current paths that may be outside the direct line of sight, and 3) the possibility of isolating the probe from the plasma, through a dielectric window. We believe PIT has applications in a broad range of research areas, including: electric propulsion, hypersonics, fusion, ionosphere sensing, plasma processing, and general laboratory plasma.

articleTitle: Software-defined Radio (SDR) Configuration Pitfalls and Reference Signal Coherence Experiments
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Software defined radios (SDRs) are devices which apply digital signal processing to implement many functions traditionally performed by radio frequency (RF) circuits. The availability of relatively inexpensive SDRs, and their ability to facilitate the recording and processing of signals, makes them a valuable tool for research. The ETTUS N210 is a low-cost, but highly capable, SDR that is routinely used by the scientific and engineering communities. As part of an experimental setup, the SDR internal clock is ideally disciplined with a high-quality 10 MHz reference source, which is often derived from global positioning system (GPS) signals. However, when using an ETTUS N210, there are several options for discipling clocks in the event that an external reference signal is not available. During a recent experiment using the BasicRX daughter cards, an outage occurred where the external 10 MHz reference was not available for a period of time. During this time, the SDR had defaulted without warning to using its internal clock source for discipling, despite the software being set to use an external source. An inspection of the data acquired during the outage of the external reference revealed that signals collected during these times had a linear phase drift, while generally retaining favorable coherence properties. The ability to maintain phase coherence between multiple receive channels is particularly important for phased-array applications. Following these observations, the software was modified to interrogate the SDR prior to data collection, in order to verify the detection and use of external reference signals as prescribed. In addition, a series of tests were performed to understand the difference in the coherence properties of signals acquired using external and internal sources. While it was anticipated that confirming external clock state and use would be trivial, this was not the case in practice. After navigating through several software configuration obstacles, invaluable lessons were discovered which would be beneficial to discuss with a broader technical community. After resolving the software configuration issues, a series of laboratory tests were conducted with a controlled input sinusoid fed into two separate N210 receiver channels in different SDRs. To evaluate the influence of the different reference sources, the phase difference between the input signals as sampled by the two ADCs (analog-to-digital converters) on the separate SDRs, was analyzed as a function of time, reference signal source, and SNR (signal-to-noise ratio). It was found that with the external reference source, the difference between the phase of the signals remained largely constant with a time variance that was dependent on input SNR of the RF input test signal. For the internal reference signal, we found that the phase difference changed linearly as a function of time in a manner that was surprisingly well behaved and predictable.

articleTitle: F-Engine Development Towards a CHORD Pathfinder Array
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio transient Detector (CHORD) is a next-generation radio telescope which will observe most of the northern sky in the coming decade across 300–1500 MHz. CHORD will be composed of a central array of 512 six-meter dishes located at the Dominion Radio Astrophyiscal Observatory (DRAO) near Penticton, B.C., Canada, and two outrigger sites in the United States positioned at continental baselines from the main array, each equipped with 64 CHORD dishes enabling ≾10 mas localization of radio transients. CHORD will focus on a wide variety of science objectives, including improvements in our understanding of dark energy through 21-cm intensity mapping of the large scale structure (LSS), increased fast radio burst (FRB) detection rates across a wide frequency range, a vast increase in 21-cm galaxy detection compared with previous observatories, and precision measurements of pulsars.

articleTitle: VLF Scattering and Polarization at HAARP
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The detection of Very-Low Frequency (VLF, ~3-30 kHz) propagating waves is a widely used method in the field of remote sensing because of the sensitivity to changes in electron density, which has been used for the observation of a variety of Ionospheric Disturbance events. Given that propagating waves travel vast distances (> 10,000 km) with little attenuation, reception of these waves can give us insight of effects that transpire along the path of propagation. A method of observing these changes is through the polarization of the scattered propagating waves. A recent paper (Burch & Moore, 2023, “Scattered Field Polarization for VLF Remote Sensing of Transient Events”) demonstrated changes in the apparent direction of arrival of a known VLF propagating wave corresponding with a Lightning-Induced Electron Precipitation (LEP) event. This is presumably due to the event itself moving as the event transpires. Furthermore, the polarization parameters of the VLF signal changed significantly during the LEP event, which we believe can be caused by a change of the shape of the scattering body itself. We seek to determine the possibility of these two ideas in a controlled environment.

articleTitle: An Eclipse-Ballooning Study of Shadow Bands During the April 2024 Total Eclipse
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We planned a comprehensive study of shadow bands for the 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse. These mysterious low-light-level bands of light and dark have been observed dating back to at least the 9th century. They appear to travel rapidly on the ground, parallel to the direction of the Sun's crescent, minutes before and after totality.

articleTitle: Optimizing DC-Stabilized Direct Antenna Modulation Transmitters for Electrically-Small Antennas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Linear time-invariant (LTI) electrically small antennas have high radiation quality factors, leading to a challenging tradeoff between efficiency and bandwidth. Bandwidth limitations distort broadband signals, limiting overall data throughput. To circumvent the narrowband limit of LTI antennas, researchers have investigated non-LTI systems. In this paper, we study one time-varying antenna technology called direct antenna modulation (DAM), which is based on storing and releasing energy on a small, capacitive, dipole-like antenna synchronously with an input digital sequence. One challenge in DAM systems is parasitic oscillations that occur when the antenna is switched between states. This ringing significantly influences signal quality in DAM transmitters and leads to spurious radiation. To mitigate the ringing and ensure better transmitted signal quality, the use of an auxiliary DC source was recent proposed to stabilize the parasitic ringing during state transitions. In fact it has been shown that this DC-DAM technique can improve key signal quality metrics like EVM by as much as 10 dB. However, little work has been done to optimize the DC source for best performance in a variety of scenarios.

articleTitle: Track After Detection of Inert Space Objects in Conjunction with Satellite-Based Plasma Wave Sensors
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Techniques have been developed to track small objects in space using plasma waves produced by orbital debris as they pass through the ionosphere. Computer simulations and laboratory measurements provide predictions and validation of this technique to detect objects that are not seen by optical and radar systems. In situ observations that confirm the presence of these plasma waves have been made during space sensor conjunctions with known space objects. Small space objects, when they pass through a structured environment, can also be detected with ground sensors and remote satellite instruments. Space debris and satellites moving through plasma irregularities excite electric and magnetic emissions such as whistler, compressional Alfvén, or lower hybrid waves. A whistler wave disturbance is generated by conversion of orbital kinetic energy into an electromagnetic plasma oscillation when a charged space object encounters a region of field aligned irregularities (FAIs). Whistlers propagate undamped at around 9000 km/s from the source regions and can be detected at large ranges over 100 km. Fast magnetosonic waves have been detected out to these ranges of 100 km in situ electric field probes on the Canadian CASSIOPE/Swarm-E spacecraft. After detection, space debris geolocation is required to update orbit prediction models. In situ measurements from host sensors can provide both range and angle-of-arrival from measurements of electromagnetic (EM) plasma waves in space. The angle of arrive needs a vector sensor of the EM fields to give both the electric (E) and magnetic (H) vector components of the incident signal from the space debris. Forming the E × B Poynting flux from the target object, yielding its source direction. A time history of this direction allows estimation of the target trajectory has it passes by the host sensor platform. When charged target debris crosses a field aligned irregularity, it launches a dispersive waveform as a whistler down-chirp or a magnetosonic up-chirp. Propagation from the source point causes temporal dispersion in these signals that stretch in both time and spatial extent. Matched filter processing of the measured signals with wavelet-like, plasma waveforms allows determination of the range to the source at specific generation time.

articleTitle: Circular Retrodirective Arrays Making Use of Self-Interference Cancellation Properties of Butler Matrices
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Circular retrodirective arrays (RDAs) extend the well-established retroreflection functionality to 360° in azimuth. Conventional beamforming networks (BFNs) in the open literature include directly connecting elements across the diameter (D.E.N. Davies, “Some properties of Van Atta arrays and the use of 2-way amplification in the delay paths,” Proc. af the IEE, vol. 110, issue 3, Mar. 1963) or Van Atta style (L. C. Van Atta, “Electromagnetic reflector,” U. S. Patent 2908002, Oct., 6, 1959) connections of modes of a circular modeforming network (H. P. Coleman, “Circularly symmetric retrodirective antenna system,” IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag., vol. 19, issue 6, Nov. 1971). However, these BFNs do not consider the impact of mutual coupling, or self-interference, in the array aperture. When self-interference is taken into account, the retrodirective action breaks down.

articleTitle: Validation of EDGES Software Suite Using 10 Days of EDGES-3 Data
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Experiment to Detect the Global Epoch of Reionization Signature (EDGES) is a single antenna low frequency radio telescope designed to study the era of Cosmic Dawn and Epoch of Reionization. This precision cosmology radio instrument was the first ever telescope to have detected the redshifted 21 cm signal (Bowman+18., Nature Astronomy), albeit an absorption feature deeper and broader than the fiducial model. Since the initial detection, there have been efforts from many researchers, theorists and experimentalists alike to gather more evidence and analysis techniques to test the results. EDGES-3 is the third iteration of the instrument, and was deployed in Nov 2022 at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory with significant changes from the previously operational EDGES-2 system. Notable changes include a bigger ground plane (50m by 48m) and in-situ receiver calibration, which allow calibration of the absolute temperature and noise waves of the system periodically in the field.

articleTitle: Multi-Wave Generation Studies Using Beat Mode Excitation at HAARP
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The interaction of electromagnetic waves with very low frequency (VLF) plasma turbulence is an important disruptor of communication systems that propagate through the ionosphere. These systems include over the horizon radars and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) surveillance and navigation systems. The main objective of this research is to predict optimal conditions for generation of VLF and electron-cyclotron (EC) waves in the ionosphere F layer due to parametric beat wave interaction of two HF pump waves with different frequencies. The difference in the two HF transmissions should be in the VLF or electron cyclotron frequency range. Two experimental setups were used. In the first setup, when we are interested in excitation of VLF waves with frequencies close to a Lower Hybrid (LH) frequency in the F layer, pump waves were directed north. The second series of experiments focused on beat wave excitation of EC waves. These experiments injected two HAARP pump waves from the split array along the magnetic field of the Earth (or with a small angle to the magnetic field). Pump waves can be two Omodes, two X modes or combination of O and X modes. The experiments also attempted to define the minimum necessary power in split antenna array for detection of excited beat waves on the ground. These series of experiments will allow to determine what pump waves polarization is preferable for excitation of VLF and EC modes and what are necessary wave amplitudes of the pump waves.

articleTitle: Lightweight and Battery-Less Multichannel Wireless Sensor for Swine Biopotential Recording
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Continuous neural recording provides vital information to map the focus of seizures in epilepsy patients. For the first time, we validate our novel packaged battery-free and multichannel wireless neurosensing system (mWiNS) in large animals (swine). The implant is miniaturized by employing a multilayer 3D printed design that includes a shorting pin to reduce antenna size by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 50 \%$</tex>. Measurements indicate reliable recovery of neural signals, demonstrating the capabilities of our proposed wireless system in recording neural epilepsy indicators.

articleTitle: Unambiguous Phase Modulation Approach for SDR LPD Waveforms
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The rapid evolution of wireless millimeter-wave (mm- Wave) links has provided impetus to develop low-power and secure ultra-wideband (UWB) transceivers. Notably, UWB wireless links enable interference immunity using spread spectrum modulation in conjunction with complex digital modulation techniques.

articleTitle: On RIS Bandwidth: Bandwidth Discussion and Trade-Offs for a Dual Resonant, Dual Linearly Polarized Element
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Bandwidth for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) is difficult to quantitatively define and measure due to their reconfigurable nature. This paper discusses the types of bandwidth associated with RIS and their trade-offs. Then it proposes a dual linearly polarized, dual resonant varactor-based design for a unit cell with increased bandwidth. This design's simulated results lead to an estimated 14 % gain bandwidth for a full RIS implementation.

articleTitle: An Overview of REDSAW and its 2024 Field Campaign
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in Stable Atmosphere over Water (REDSAW) project investigate effects of atmospheric conditions on Radio Frequency (RF) propagation particularly within the stably stratified atmospheric surface layers. The primary objectives of REDSA Ware: 1) To identify the key parameters of the atmosphere and the sea that affect the near-surface vertical profiles of water vapor as a result of surface evaporation and turbulence mixing; 2) To quantify the physical processes near the sea surface that lead to radio ducting (evaporation ducts), impacting maritime communication and low-flying target detection by radar; 3) To determine the most effective methods for representing evaporation ducts in stable surface layers and their impact on radio wave propagation; and 4) To understand the development of marine stable internal boundary layers and their effect on evaporation ducts in coastal regions. The REDSAW science team comprises researchers and students from multiple universities, Navy research laboratories, and private industry partners.

articleTitle: Polarization and Spectral Content of ELF/VLF Transients
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Scientists have investigated the sources of impulsive radio transients in the extremely-low-frequency (ELF, 3–3000 Hz) and very-low-frequency (VLF, 3–30 kHz) bands since the beginning of radio. In the 1930's, Appleton and Chapman, as well as Watson-Watt and others, presented records of a wide variety of ELF/VLF signatures associated with lightning. In the 1960's, Ogawa and colleagues performed careful ELF/VLF radio observations in order to provide much needed categorization of the types of impulses observed. In the 1990's, Boccipio and associates related sprite-causative lightning with so-called Q-bursts. Most recently, in 2022, detailed measurements by Flint determined that Q-bursts were more frequently associated with gigantic jets and N-bursts were more frequently associated with sprites. Much of the impulse categorization effort has focused on the spectral content of the ELF/VLF transient. For instance, Q-bursts are identified as having strong ELF content, but weak VLF content, whereas N-bursts are identified as having strong ELF and VLF spectral content. In such a categorization, thresholds are required, and they can be somewhat arbitrary.

articleTitle: Detection and Statistical Modeling of the Effect of Mima Mounds on Bistatic Radar Scattering
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Several bistatic scattering models for global navigation satellite system reflectometry (GNSS-R) radar scat-tering have been developed. One such model is the Improved Geometric Optics with Topography (IGOT) model (A. Melebari et al., Remote Sensing, 15, 1880). This model has been validated using data from the NASA Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) in several locations including the San Luis Valley of Colorado, the Walnut Gulch Experimental Watershed in Arizona, and the Jornada Experimental Range (JER) in New Mexico. It was observed that the match between modeling predictions and CYGNSS observations over certain regions of JER is significantly worse than that over the other validation sites. The model tends to overestimate the received signal in areas of JER that contain mima mounds, which are regu-larly occurring dirt mounds. The mima mounds of JER range in height from 0.5 to 2 m and range in diameter from 2 to 10 m. They could be a significant error source because their size is smaller than the resolution limit of the elevation data used in the IGOT model, which is from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM). This work uses high resolution lidar elevation data to characterize the mima mounds. Analysis of the lidar data provides the probability density function (pdf) of the mound slopes and the total area of the mounds. These parameters can be estimated using on-the-ground measurements, making this approach applicable to other sites.

articleTitle: L-Band Scintillation Characteristics During the 2024 Gannon Storm
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We use a network of “high-rate” geodetic Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers and Ionospheric Scintillation Monitoring Receivers (ISMR) to characterize ionospheric irregularities and scintillation at high-latitudes during the 2024 Gannon storm. We especially focus on the available data from American Longitude sector covering Alaska and Canada. We show that presence of L-band diffractive scintillation observed at L1, L2, and L5 bands, with fading exceeding 10 dB. The scintillation was observed during several local time sectors possible indicating the scintillation-producing irregularities residing in the SED plume, polar cap patches, and auroral structures. We analyze the strength of the observed scintillation in terms of elevation/filed-aligned aspect angle, TEC, TEC gradients, decorrelation times, and local time occurrence. The spatial localization of scintillation-producing structures is aided by High latitude Ionospheric Data Assimilation 4D (H-IDA4D) TEC outputs at 5-minute time resolution. H-IDA4D assimilated slant-TEC data from 250 high-latitude ground-based GNSS receivers into IRI and E-CHAIM background models.

articleTitle: Tomographic 3D Imaging for UAV Lunar Penetrating Radar Using Geometric Optics
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for planetary subsurface exploration using unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms. These UAVs act as probes, where one sends the RF signal and the others collect the backscattered signals from multiple angles. This multistatic approach increases resolution and sensitivity for subsurface characterization. The method combines tomographic and ray-tracing techniques for image recovery, enabling the simultaneous capture of data from diverse geometries to improve resolution and mitigate vacuum-ground effects. This paper demonstrates that bistatic tomographic approaches can form images of subsurface objects more accurately.

articleTitle: Coherence Modeling of Land Cover Observations from Repeat Pass Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The phase change of repeat-pass Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) observations has found applications to monitoring of surface deformation, forest biomass, soil moisture and snow water equivalent. The InSAR phase measurement accuracy depends on the interferometric coherence of radar signals from repeat passes. The temporal decorrelation of radar signals can be influenced by many factors, including the signal to noise ratio of radar observations and geometry offset as well as natural variability of terrain surfaces, such as surface elevation, snow and vegetation cover within the radar footprint.

articleTitle: Design and Study of a Transient Plasma Array with Static Magnetic Fields for Detection of Multispecies Interactions in Hypervelocity Impact Plasmas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Complex plasmas with highly time variant and inhomogeneous property distributions are generated from hypervelocity impacts (HVIs). Even when low momentum transfer HVIs driven by small impactors preclude mechanical damage to targets, HVIs are hypothesized to be responsible for electrical anomalies on spacecraft through RF generation during and after expansion of the plasma. Plasma expansion theories generally disregard the complex multispecies interactions involved in this process. Instabilities driven by multispecies interactions may drive changes in bulk plasma properties including temperature and density while also creating local regions with divergent properties and non-Maxwellian distributions.

articleTitle: CSCMR WPT Systems for Wearable Devices
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Traditional wireless power transfer (WPT) utilized for wearable medical devices exploits Inductive Power Transfer (IPT) utilizing Magnetic Resonant Coupling (MRC) methods. IPT can deliver very high efficiencies with the main drawback being the short distance (between 1 and 3 cm). Unfortunately, beyond the 3 cm threshold the efficiency significantly diminishes, as its attenuation rate becomes proportionate to l/r<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>, As a result, for WPT applications requiring longer-range IPT is a challenging way to go. On the other hand, MRC systems can be used for extended WPT ranges being insensitive to interference from non-resonant objects. The Strongly Coupled Magnetic Resonance (SCMR) WPT method is undeniably the most efficient, providing the longest range. Specifically, in a traditional SCMR system both the transmitter (TX) and the receiver (RX) employ two loops each. For the TX element these are a source loop and a resonator loop, and for the RX element, these are a load loop and a resonator loop. The only drawback of SCMR systems against their very high efficiency is their size posing a significant challenge for case where deployment in confined spaces is chosen. That is the reason that SCMR requires miniaturization to boost its applicability. The Conformal Strongly Coupled Magnetic Resonance (CSCMR) method which was recently introduced in (K. Bao, et al.,doi: 10.1109/ ACCESS.2019.2945319) can do exactly that. Specifically, contrary to conventional SCMR systems that require a physical separation between the source and the resonator loop for TX (or load and resonator loop for RX), in CSCMR the source/load loops are coplanar with their respective TX/RX resonator loops. Thus, the volume is significantly reduced, while high efficiency is maintained. However, even though SCMR is very efficient for power transferring, the maximum dimension of its resonators is also the maximum limit for range of operation. This challenge was addressed by a novel technique introduced in (J. Barreto et al., doi: 10.1109/OJAP.2020.2999447) effectively extending the range of operation. Specifically, a U-loop resonator which is a repeater resonator was introduced, enabling the extension of the range of WPT to distances equivalent to the size of this U-loop. Finally, continuous research on WPT for wearable applications has produced several advances in the last few years. For example, in (K. Bao, et al., doi: 10.1109/LAWP. 2019.2906069) a substantial range but also miniaturized and highly efficient (60 mm and up to 80%) wireless power system was designed for wearable applications. More recently, (Juan Barreto, Abdul-Sattar Kaddour, Hyeon Seok An, Robert F. Shepherd, Constantinos L. Zekios, and Stavros V. Georgakopoulos “Liquid Metal Nanoparticles-Infused Wearable CSCMR WPT Systems”, in IEEE NRSM 2024 Boulder, Colorado 9 – 13 January 2024) presented a novel technique where conductive threads can be doped using liquid metal nanoparticles through infusion increasing the efficiency of traditional wearable CSCMR systems over six times. In this work, we present our study when our WPT system is next to a human body as shown in Figure 1. These simulations were carried out using Sim4Life software(https://zmt.swiss/sim4life/). “This work was supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research under grants FA9550-19-1-0290 and FA9550-24-1-0004.”

articleTitle: Textile-Based Incognito RFID for Patient Tracking
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The advancement of wireless technologies enabled the use of radio frequency identification (RFID) tags at an increasing rate in the past decade. In retail, RFIDs are placed in tags on merchandise for analysis of supply chain, inventory, and loss prevention (K. Finkenzeller, RFID Handbook: Fundamentals and Applications in Contactless Smart Cards, Radio Frequency Identification and Near-Field Communication, 3rd ed. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley, 2010.). However, in healthcare applications, RFIDs are not only used for item tracking but can also be utilized for patient tracking. When treating patients with memory impairment, RFID placement must be done in a noninvasive and unobtrusive way so as to not frighten the patient with the applied technology (R. Nayak, A. Singh, R. Padhye and L. Wang, “RFID in textile and clothing manufacturing: technology and challenges”, Fashion and Textiles, vol. 2, no. 9, June 2015.),(J. Lundquist et al., “Textile-Based Inkjet-Printed RFIDs: Exploring wearable antennas in the real world [Bioelectromagnetics]”, in IEEE Antennas and Propagation Magazine, vol. 66, no. 1, pp. 50–62, Feb. 2024.).

articleTitle: Novel Yagi-Uda Direction Finding Antenna Backed by Software Defined Radio
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A novel two-element front-end of squinted-beam monopole Yagi-Uda antennas is proposed to perform amplitude-only direction finding from 3.1 GHz to 4.2 GHz. The system makes use of the inherent beam squint resulting from diffraction from a finite ground plane. The beam squint and peak directivity are stabilized across frequency, varying less than 4° and 1.5 dB, respectively. Simulation results indicate a 74° unambiguous field-of-view over the band. Amplitude only direction finding with software defined radio receivers is also discussed.

articleTitle: Growing a Spectrum Paradigm: Toward Adaptive and Reconfigurable Spectrum Sharing
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: With the increasing number of wireless applications, systems, and devices, the spectrum is becoming congested. This congestion requires a paradigm shift in how spectrum is managed and used: a shift from rigid spectrum use to adaptive and reconfigurable spectrum use. In rigid use, spectrum is pre-assigned, and devices and systems are designed to operate at the same frequency with little need to respond to their spectral environments. As such, devices and systems are pre-characterized to ensure functional operation before deployment, and can operate in an open-loop fashion. In adaptive and reconfigurable spectrum use, devices can adapt to the needs of the overall spectral environment and can reconfigure their operation for successful operation at different frequencies (potentially different bands) and potentially in different directions to ensure coexistence. In this case, devices and systems must be continually assessed, in real-time, after deployment. This provides closed-loop operation and optimization of system performance.

articleTitle: The Design of an Ultra Low-Noise, Ambient-Temperature Amplifier for the DSA-2000 Using Automatic Differentiation
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The advancement of ambient-temperature receivers has been a pivotal feature in the development of the DSA-2000. Foregoing cryogenics allows us to build a much larger system for lower cost, while maintaining best-in-class sensitivity and survey speed. The heart of this receiver lies in the ambient-temperature low-noise amplifier, first demonstrated in the DSA-110 (Weinreb and Shi, 2021). Since then, we have been developing a wideband design for the DSA-2000 (Shi and Weinreb, 2023). While certainly successful, there is always an incentive to improve the noise performance, as any reduction in the system noise temperature results in an exponential increase in survey speed.

articleTitle: Repeatability of Internal Body Temperature Measurements via Microwave Radiometry
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Microwave radiometers offer a non-invasive method for measuring internal body temperature, with several applications in the medical field (P. Momenroodaki et al., “Noninvasive Internal Body Temperature Tracking with Near-Field Microwave Radiometry,” IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, vol. 66, no. 5, pp. 2535–2545, Dec. 2017). The knowledge of internal body temperature can be helpful in detecting cancer, diagnosing heat stroke in athletes and soldiers, as well as monitoring brain temperature during cardiac surgery (J. Lee et al., “A 1.4-GHz GaAs MMIC Radiometer for Noninvasive Internal Body Thermometry,” in IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, vol. 72, no. 1, pp. 759–770, Jan. 2024). While existing research has demonstrated the potential of microwave radiometry for measuring the temperature of internal tissue layers, there have not been sufficient studies of the reliability across different patients or conditions. This work evaluates the repeatability and limitations of the temperature measurements using a radiometer.

articleTitle: Characterization of Dielectric Nonlinearity in High-permittivity Materials for High Power mmW Devices
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The growing demand for next-generation, high-throughput wireless communication systems necessitates the development of high-power transistor topologies operating well into the millimeter-wave (mmW) frequencies. These new devices are based on wide bandgap GaN and AlGaN semiconductors that incorporate high-k dielectric materials, such as Barium Titanate (BaTiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) and Titanium Dioxide (TiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) into the transistor topologies in the form of thin-film gate insulators. A critical requirement for effectively designing and fabricating such high-power transistors is a precise understanding of the dielectric permittivity and loss characteristics of the materials under high electric fields. This knowledge directly impacts performance optimization for better energy efficiency and higher operating speeds, particularly at mmW frequencies.

articleTitle: Drone-Based Antenna Beam Calibration for ALBATROS
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Array of Long Baseline Antenna for Taking Radio Observations from the Seventy-ninth parallel (ALBATROS) is an interferometer that aims to map Galactic foregrounds at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq 30\text{MH}z$</tex>. In its current phase, ALBATROS is a pathfinder for future experiments that will observe the cosmic ‘dark ages' through the 21-cm neutral hydrogen signal. The era of the cosmic dark ages occurs prior to the cosmic dawn and after the period of recombination. Due to the expansion of the universe, the 21-cm signal emitted during the cosmic dark ages is redshifted to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq 30\text{MH}z$</tex>. However, terrestrial observations in this frequency range are challenging due to ionospheric attenuation and refraction that corrupt the incoming sky signal as well as the presence of man-made radio frequency interference (RFI).

articleTitle: Latency Budget for Spectrum Sharing with Airborne Radars
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this study, the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) conducted a latency analysis of a simulated citizens broadband radio service (CBRS) instantiation. Since the CBRS architecture is a potential solution for future spectrum sharing scenarios with airborne radars and it is critical for CBRS devices (CBSDs) to vacate the frequencies required by the incumbent as quickly as possible, this study is designed to determine all contributions to the latency budget. This will allow other researchers to further investigate the latency and to investigate optimizations for sharing with airborne radars. Latency is composed of three parts: a) the time required for an environmental sensing capability (ESC) to detect the radar signal, b) latency in a spectrum access system (SAS), and c) latency in 5 G system. Figure 1 shows a block diagram of CBRS system architecture.

articleTitle: AERO: Remote Sensing of Auroral Radio Emissions from a Small Satellite Using Electromagnetic Vector Sensors
