publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Earth's aurora has a complexity and richness in both energetics and spatial/temporal structure that is of intense interest for community understanding of space physics. Auroral radio emissions from the ionosphere in the LF to HF range (<= 5 MHz) form a powerful space physics observational tool because they provide a means to remotely sense auroral ionospheric plasma conditions and processes and to resolve long standing mysteries on the auroral acceleration process. For instance, auroral kilometric radiation (AKR) is the most important energetic radio source in the aurora, radiating up to 1 % of total auroral energy, but open questions exist on its appearance below the ionosphere. Electromagnetic vector sensor antenna (VSA) systems provide a potent method to advance knowledge of these features by accomplishing direction finding capability from a small compact sensor.

articleTitle: Climatology of Large-Scale Traveling Ionospheric Disturbances Observed with 14 MHz Amateur Radio Using a Novel Automated Detection Technique
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present a multi-year climatology of Large Scale Traveling Ionospheric Disturbance (LSTID) period oscillations observed using 14 MHz amateur (ham) radio data. Traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs) are quasi periodic electron density perturbations in the F region ionosphere that affect radio communications and can help with understanding energy transport throughout the coupled magnetosphere-ionosphere-neutral atmosphere system. These are seen, in daytime, as variations in contact ranges in 14 MHz amateur radio communication reports recorded by automated monitoring systems such as the Weak Signal Propagation Reporting Network (WSPRNet), the Reverse Beacon Network (RBN), and PSKReporter. A new deterministic and fully automated method was developed for identifying and quantifying these disturbances. This technique, which filters for TID wave periods between 1 and 5 hours and curve fits a sinusoidal function to the first hop skip-distance edge of observed communication ranges, provides both TID amplitudes and periods. In this study, we present full year climatologies of LSTID events over the continental United States (CONUS) using RBN, WSPRNet, and PSK observations from 2016–2021. Results are organized as a function wave period, amplitude, and season. We find that LSTIDs increase in winter and decline during the fall and spring, with slight enhancements in the summer and occasional brief declines in LSTID winter activity. This seasonal pattern shows consistency with previous studies and observations of LSTIDs and medium scale TIDs that suggests this behavior may be associated with neutral wind filtering in the middle atmosphere, sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) events, and multi-step vertical coupling (MSVC) processes. MSVC is a process where gravity waves (GWs) from the lower neutral atmosphere propagate upwards, break, and produce new, higher-order GWs in the thermosphere and TIDs in the ionosphere.

articleTitle: FDTD in Computational Electromagnetics and Quantum Transport
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method used in computational electromagnetics (CEM) and quantum transport are investigated. In CEM, FDTD is applied to coupled electric and magnetic fields based on the Maxwell's equations. In quantum transport, FDTD is implemented to coupled real and imaginary components of the electron wavefunction based on the time dependent Schrödinger equation. To have a better understanding of CEM and quantum transport, FDTD formulations and simulations of plane wave propagation in free space and electron scattering in metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) are presented. A comprehensive observation of electromagnetic and quantum techniques can be obtained through discretization of the time-dependent Maxwell's equations and Schrödinger equation.

articleTitle: On the Use of Ionosonde Return Pulse Amplitudes
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present novel observations of HF amplitudes from the return pulses of ionosondes, which have been largely ignored in prior ionosonde research. A strong correlation is observed between ionosonde-inferred absorption of HF signals, and VLF-inferred D-region absorption, suggesting that D-region propagation contributes a measurable portion of the return pulse absorption.

articleTitle: Bistatic GO Solution to the Mean RCS of an Object Above a Rough Surface: 2D TE Case
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The bistatic mean radar cross-section of a object above a randomly rough surface in the geometrical optics (GO) limit is presented. A four-path model is invoked to simplify the scattering problem, and a decoupled method used to combine the independent contributions of both object and surface and to model their interactions. A high frequency approximation of surface scattering effects is also made to simplify the formulation.

articleTitle: Characterizing Clutter via a Time-Varying Troposcatter Signal
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Over-the-radio-horizon propagation is of particular interest to today's telecommunication engineers, for both network planning and interference analysis. At distances over 100 km, the primary mechanism for propagation is the forward scattering of the electromagnetic waves interacting with the turbulence-induced inhomogeneities within the troposphere. This tropospheric scattering, or troposcatter, can result in large swings, often exceeding 20 dB, in the power at the receiver depending on the conditions of the atmosphere, which makes measuring its effects inherently a long-term study of variability.

articleTitle: Effects of Weather Events on Wireless Power Receiver Arrays
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This talk describes environmental testing of a 5×5 array of 10-GHz patch antenna rectifier antennas (rectennas), composed of unit cell modules (Montgomery et al., European Microwave Conference, Sept. 2024). These arrays can be scaled to larger sizes, including up to 25×25 elements to form a one meter by one meter array. The main substrate of the array is flexible PTFE foam, chosen for its hydrophobic properties and ability to withstand a wide range of temperatures. For the ground plane, a copper fabric is chosen for mechanical flexibility. The top substrate with metallization for the antennas and circuitry is polyamide with copper cladding, with silicon Schottky diodes soldered to rectify the received RF incident waves and deliver power to a dc load. The motivation for the design of the scalable rectenna arrays is to quickly provide power in energy denied environments regardless of conditions such as weather or time of day. The rectenna array therefore needs to be able to withstand a variety of weather conditions with little to no deterioration in its operation.

articleTitle: Metasurface-Infused Sky Radio Quiet Zone for Mitigation of Radio Frequency Interference
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio frequency interference (RFI) from non-geosynchronous orbit (NGSO) satellite communication systems (SCSs) to a ground radio astronomy system (RAS) is addressed using a combined use of sky radio quiet zone (SRQZ) and novel metasurface-based antenna. We integrate a lightweight, unilayer metasurface lens, consisting of subwavelength circular patches imprinted on both sides of a dielectric sheet, into a regular horn antenna to regulate the amplitude and phase of electromagnetic waves. The proposed antenna reduces sidelobes by 34 dB compared to conventional air-filled horns, ensuring better radiation pattern control. Additionally, the average RFI results demonstrate that the design meets RFI constraints with a much smaller communication outage area than existing methods.

articleTitle: The Role of Cold Oxygen Ions in the EMIC Wave Growth
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) waves are electromagnetic emissions with frequency range of Pc1-Pc2 (0.1-5 Hz) geomagnetic pulsations, generated by ring current ion temperature anisotropy <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\mathrm{T}_{1}/\mathrm{T}_{\Vert})$</tex> in the Earth's magnetosphere. EMIC waves are parallel propagating waves with left-hand polarization below cyclotron frequency of each ion species and can be divided into three bands based on the ion cyclotron frequencies in the Earth magnetosphere: hydrogen <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\mathrm{H}^{+})$</tex>, helium <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\text{He}^{+})$</tex> and oxygen <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\mathrm{O}^{+})$</tex> bands, respectively. They play a vitally important role in the acceleration and precipitation of relativistic electrons in the radiation belt. EMIC waves can resonate with relativistic electrons(~MeV) by gyroresonance and produce a rapid scattering loss of radiation belt electrons. The electrons with relatively low energy, from tens to hundreds keV, can interact with EMIC waves via bounce resonance and be scattered significantly in pitch angle.

articleTitle: Dish Surface Characterisation for CHORD and HIRAX Using Metrology and Electromagnetic Simulations
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Hydrogen Intensity and Real-time Analysis eXperiment (HIRAX) and the Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector (CHORD) are next-generation radio interferometers designed to measure baryonic acoustic oscillations through 21-cm intensity mapping and also act as powerful platforms for studying fast radio bursts, pulsars, and cross-correlation studies. HIRAX and CHORD are being developed for deployment in the Karoo desert, South Africa, and the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory (DRAO) in Kaleden, Canada, respectively, and operate in a drift-scan mode with manual adjustments in zenith angle within ±30° to build up sky coverage. HIRAX operates within a frequency range of 400–800 MHz, corresponding to a redshift range of 0.8 < <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex> < 2.5, while CHORD covers a broader bandwidth from 300 to 1500 MHz, focusing on redshifts < 3.7. HIRAX and CHORD will consist of 256 and 512 elements, respectively, and both utilize six-meter diameter parabolic composite dishes with a focal ratio of f/0.21.

articleTitle: Interference Monitoring with NRDZ-as-a-Service at Spectrum Experimentation Events
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio Dynamic Zones (RDZs) provide automatic spectrum management mechanisms to control the electromagnetic environment (EME) in a surrounding area. As part of the NSF SII-NRDZ program, MITRE's NRDZ-as-a-Service (NaaS) will enable the technology and operational paths necessary for robust RDZ creation to protect spectrum incumbents and experimental participants from RF interference (RFI). The NaaS infrastructure, as shown in Fig. 1, includes an RDZ Integrity System designed to protect spectrum incumbents by maintaining the RDZ boundary integrity. This system ensures RF spatial, spectral, and temporal situational awareness through sensing systems capable of discerning potential RFI sources. Key components include the RDZ Monitor Network (RMN), which performs situational awareness via spectral measurement sensors and information-bearing sensors for interference reporting. This RDZ Integrity System reacts to deviations from the experimental plan by comparing observed execution against orchestrated events, creating a “safety net” to prevent harmful interference during RDZ deployment.

articleTitle: A Digital Calibration Source for 21 cm Cosmology Telescopes
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio surveys of the red-shifted 21 cm emission line from neutral hydrogen provide a means to measure statistical cosmological signals that cannot be measured through other means. Many past experiments have shown that the major challenge for carrying out 21 cm measurements is the presence of bright foregrounds from the galaxy, and suppressing these foregrounds has become vital in 21 cm Cosmology. Attempts to separate signal and foreground components have led to new developments in hardware specifically dedicated to instrument calibration. The measurement of the instrument beam is implemented by flying radio calibration sources over an interferometric array to measure beam pattern. The calibration sources currently used in literature are broadband incoherent sources that can be detected as total power only, and no direct phase sensitivity is recorded. As a result, these instruments must contend with signal-to-noise issues where the beam has low response as well as the lack of a direct phase measurement without a reference antenna.

articleTitle: Fading Measurements From a Maritime Mobile Troposcatter Link
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Tropospheric scatter, also known as troposcatter, communications has been around since the 1950s but has recently received interest as a means for long distance beyond line-of-sight (BLOS) communications. According to the literature, Rayleigh fading is expected for troposcatter links. In this paper, measurement results are presented for a long-distance maritime link in the coastal area of Southern California; however, the measurements indicate that the observed fading was not Rayleigh. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first reported finding of non-Rayleigh fading for a troposcatter link and demonstrates the need for further investigation of troposcatter channels.

articleTitle: Quantized Tensor Trains for Simulations of Plasma Waves
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The quantized tensor train (QTT) is a low-rank computational framework that may enable solving partial differential equations with significantly reduced cost. In this work, we investigate the effectiveness of using QTTs to solve the Vlasov equation by measuring the QTT rank required to achieve the desired accuracy for a wide range of electrostatic and electromagnetic test problems. We also compare the performance of the QTT solver when using different basis representations and different time integrators, providing insight into preferred numerical methods and also demonstrating the flexibility of the QTT framework.

articleTitle: Nonlinear Model Excitation by VLF Transmitters
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Very low frequency (VLF, 3–30 kHz) transmitters broadcast signals that propagate large distances (≥10,000 km) around the globe within the Earth-ionosphere waveguide. It is well-known that the transmitter signals heat the overlying ionosphere and can scatter other radio waves propagating near the heated ionospheric patch, for instance. It is not well-known, however, that the heating of the ionosphere can change the propagation characteristics of the signal that was transmitted itself. In this paper, we present careful measurements of VLF transmitter signals observed using the North American VLF (NAV) Array. These measurements monitor the amplitude and phase of narrowband signals during power on periods of the VLF transmitters at receiver locations across the contiguous United States and receivers along the same propagation path are compared by means of transfer functions. From this, we demonstrate nonlinear waveguide excitation effects as a function of VLF transmitter power level.

articleTitle: The Dawning of Radio Astronomy from the Moon
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The first robotic commercial lunar lander, Intuitive Machines' Odysseus, successfully touched down on the Moon in the South Pole region on 22 February 2024. This mission was part of NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program. Odysseus carried with it the first NASA radio astronomy telescope to the surface of the Moon - Radiowave Observations at the Lunar Surface of the photoElectron Sheath (ROLSES). ROLSES collected engineering and science data in cislunar transit using one of four antennas prior to entering lunar orbit, as well as data from the lunar surface over multiple days using all antennas, despite the tilting of the Odysseus lander. ROLSES was built by NASA-GSFC in collaboration with the University of Colorado. The ROLSES spectrometer obtained spectra over the range 2 kHz - 30 MHz with 8-sec time resolution. The science goals included measuring the electron density of the near-surface plasma, detecting terrestrial anthropogenic and Earth's Auroral Kilometric Radiation, and measuring the Galactic background below 30 MHz. In this talk, I will describe the outcomes from ROLSES including initial science results. In addition, two follow-on lunar missions scheduled for 2026 including an upgraded ROLSES-2 and LuSEE-Night will be described. LuSEE-Night will be the first low frequency radio telescope on the lunar far side to explore the frequency band associated with the unexplored Dark Ages of the early Universe - selected as the Discovery Area for Cosmology in the Astro2020 Decadal Survey. Finally, I will discuss the NASA-funded FarView project, an early-stage concept for a large, low-frequency radio observatory, manufactured in-situ on the lunar far side using metals extracted from the lunar regolith and designed to observe the redshifted 21-cm power spectrum from the Dark Ages (Polidan, Burns, et al. 2024, Advances in Space Research, 74, 528). It consists of 100,000 dipole antennas in compact subarrays distributed over a total area of 150 km<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, with a dense core that is ≈4 km square and an outer halo extending to a diameter of ≈12 km. I will describe our efforts on developing model predictions for the power spectrum and on sensitivity forecasting. The development of FarView was supported by the NIAC program via grant 80NSSC23K0965 and internal funding from Lunar Resources, Inc.

articleTitle: Thomson Scatter with L band Radar and Potential New Multi-Frequency Ionospheric Radar Utilization
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Perturbations in the ionosphere caused by human-created objects such as space debris have been studied recently and are measurable with ground-based radar. While these perturbations are actively being researched as an alternative method of detecting and characterizing debris, their presence interferes with geospace radar measurements in the UHF band. Multi-frequency radar techniques enable a broader sampling of the spatial scales in the ionosphere and may distinguish between natural and man-made effects. Relatively few radars sites in the world exist with multi-frequency transmitters at the megawatt-hectare level and with useful center transmission frequencies., given known ionospheric plasma scattering responses. Haystack Observatory, jointly operated by MIT Lincoln Laboratory and MIT campus and located at northern mid-latitudes in the American longitude sector, has co-located large aperture high power radars in the UHF and L bands (seen in Fig. 1), providing the capability of simultaneously observing common volumes in the ionosphere. In this talk, we present preliminary results showing that the operational Millstone Hill L band satellite tracking radar is capable of recovering an altitude-dependent collective Thomson scatter spectrum, which can jointly be measured by the UHF system currently used for ionospheric measurements. While this tracking radar was used decades ago for ionospheric profiling, only recently our tests verified that the system retains the sensitivity for that capability in its current configuration. Ongoing joint characterization between the UHF and L band radars has the potential to open up a new multi-wavelength experimental capability for fundamental ionospheric science and debris perturbation studies driven by a need to understand the increasingly crowded low earth orbit environment.

articleTitle: Design and Performance of the DSA-2000 Antennas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The DSA-2000 will consist of 2,000 5 m dia telescopes operating in over 0.7 to 2 GHz spread over a 15 km x 19 km area. The instrument is designed to map the whole available sky every three months with high sensitivity and fidelity and produce images with a sensitivity of 1 µJy, even for rich fields with sources as bright at 1 Jy. Producing the images with a real time Radio Camera pipeline places stringent requirements on the array configuration and antennas to avoid false detections and to minimize imaging artifacts.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Networks to Estimate Electric Fields From Noisy B1 Maps
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Deep learning networks have shown promising results in estimating electric fields from B1 maps. Some recent studies have shown that 2D analytical solutions can quickly generate data to be used as potential data augmentation with numerically simulated data. Since the ultimate goal is to have the developed deep learning networks able to operate with experimentally acquired data which might be affected by noise, in this study we have developed and tested the ability of these 2D networks to accurately predict the electric fields from noisy B1 maps. The networks could predict well the electric fields also in presence of noise, with a maximum NRMSE of 13.6%.

articleTitle: Retraining Meta's Segment Anything Model for RFI Segmentation and Flagging
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio Frequency Interference (RFI), unwanted radio signals from electronics, permeates through astronomical observations using radio telescopes. The interference results in lower sensitivity and higher noise when present. Existing methods, such as TFCrop and RFlag, flag RFI to prevent the contamination of observations. However, these approaches are not fully automatic and require significant manual input to correctly flag RFI. We explore artificial intelligence methods using Meta's Segment Anything Model (SAM) and its parameter space in segmenting RFI. From this, we have developed an open-source pipeline called SamRFI, which segments and flags RFI from measurement sets. We trained SAM's masking weights from Hugging Face to fine-tune the model using VLA data and synthetic waterfall plots injected with RFI. We define a metric, calcquality, to measure the performance of our models based on sensitivity, over-flagging, mean shifts, and standard deviation shifts. Three RFI segmentation models were trained: the synthetic model trained with Gaussian persistent and intermittent RFI, and two models trained with the P-Band publicly available measurement set 3C147. The training data consists of 256 by 256 patches from waterfall plots that are stretched by logarithm with base 10 or square root for the models with P-Band data, then normalized by the median. The ground truth masks in the training data are clipped from the P-Band patches using 5 median standard deviations per patch. The synthetic model uses the synthetic RFI for the ground truth masks. A separate P-band dataset, 3C129, was used for validation testing for each model. Calcquality demonstrates throughout all three models that the flags generated increased sensitivity and decreased noise. Retrained SAM models identify RFI structure and allow for further exploration in RFI segmentation.

articleTitle: Multi-Watt GaN MMIC Power Amplifiers for 32 GHz Deep Space Communications and Radio Science
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The RF communications of spacecraft-ground and spacecraft-spacecraft play an essential role in space exploration and space science. Radio science instruments commonly utilize existing RF communications channels to extract scientific information from radio wave propagation (Asmar, Sami, et al. “Convergence of Technologies Enabling Radio Crosslink Missions for Planetary Atmospheric Structures.” 2024 IEEE Aerospace Conference. IEEE, 2024). For future missions into deep space, communications at Ka-band carrier frequencies may significantly increase the data rate and measurement resolution to maximize the scientific return when compared with S and X-bands. The goal of this project is to enhance the efficiency and output power of power amplifiers (PAs) at the MMIC level to improve solid-state transmitters for use in deep space communications. Using advanced fabrication processes including WIN 120nm and Qorvo 150nm GaN on SiC, two Ka-band (32GHz) PAs are designed using different power combining techniques to achieve between 5–10 W of output power.

articleTitle: Aggregate Interference Analysis of a LEO Satellite Constellation into the Radio Astronomy Observatory
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: One mechanism to provide worldwide internet coverage is to deploy low Earth orbit satellite megaconstellations. Increasing the number of satellites in space increases the risk of harmful interference on radio astronomy observatories (RAOs). In this study, the aggregate interference induced on an isotropic RAO is investigated. Analysis is performed for a single orbit and for multiple orbits with 36 satellites on each orbital path. In all orbital path cases, aggregate interference exceeds the damaging interference threshold of -104.9 dBm (computed using (5) and (6)) which causes operational issues on the RAO.

articleTitle: Assimilative Coupled Modeling of the Gannon Superstorm
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Modern Modular Model for Space Data Assimilation (M3SDA, pronounced ‘mahs-da’ like the automotive manufacturer) is used to model the global evolution of the ionospheric electron density over the duration of the May 2024 Gannon superstorm. M3SDA is an ionospheric data assimilator which combines ionospheric measurements with background models to estimate the most likely state of the ionosphere. M3SDA can be run using either a three-dimensional variational assimilation (3DVar) or Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) algorithm to minimize the cost function.

articleTitle: Extreme Low-Latitude Scintillation Structure Evolution
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Ionospheric equatorial spread F (ESF) structure has been associated with a two-component inverse-power-law spectral density function (SDF) for decades. The support comes from intensity scintillation measurements, in-situ measurements, and hight-resolution physics-based simulations, which also reveal that the two-component structure develops when ESF depletions pen-etrate the F-region peak density. By using a new radio diagnostic measurement technique based on irregularity parameter estimation (IPE) applied to back-propagated GPS complex scintillation data, we have measured EPB SDF structure evolution. Recent measurements obtained during an Ascension Island campaign, which included the Gannon Storm, have provided examples of extreme scintillation. This presentation will review the new analysis procedure and measured EPB structure evolution.

articleTitle: Elves as the Optical Signature of Lightning Precursor Discharges in the Lower Ionosphere
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Narrow bipolar events (NBEs), initial breakdown pulses (IBPs), and energetic in-cloud pulses (EIPs) are compact intracloud discharges, with spatial extent of 100s of meters, that usually precede lightning flashes. There is growing evidence that these discharges are associated with elves [Neubert et al, Science, 367, 183,2020; Nature, 589, 371,2021; Østgaard et al., JGR, 126, e2020JD033921, 2021]; a type of transient luminous event observed at altitude <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 80–95 km as laterally expanding rings of light. Elves are produced when electromagnetic pulses from high peak current lightning discharges interact with the lower ionosphere [Fukunishi et al., GRL, 23, 2157,1996; Inan et al., GRL, 24, 583, 1997]. In particular, Marshall et al, [GRL, 42, 6112, 2015] show that compact intracloud discharges with peak currents of 200 kA can reproduce the optical signatures of elves. Observations have also shown elves associated with discharge events with peak currents as low as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 50\mathrm{k}\mathrm{A}$</tex> [Børge-Ingeland et al., JGR, 129, e2023JD039849, 2024]. Although estimates of source peak current of compact intracloud discharges are available, the exact current waveforms have not been directly measured. We recently calculated the source current waveforms of NBEs from their wideband electric field measurements [Pervez et al., GRL, 51, e2023GL107789, 2024]. In this work we apply the electromagnetic fields from such current waveforms to the lower ionosphere at elve altitudes, and use a plasma fluid model to study the dynamics of the charged species. In particular, we quantify optical emissions resulting from excitation processes due to collisions between the electrons energized by the discharge electromagnetic field and the neutral atmospheric species.

articleTitle: Plasma Irregularities at the Equator (PIE) Mission Concept
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present a Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) mission concept to study mid to low latitude ionospheric irregularities. This mission investigates the formation of equatorial plasma bubbles (EPBs) and the distribution of medium scale (100-300km wavelength) traveling ionospheric disturbances (MSTIDs). EPBs are thought to be caused by the generalized Rayleigh-Taylor instability (GRTI). GRTI growth rates replicate the climatology of EPB occurrence very effectively, but they do not replicate day-to-day variability. One likely source of variability is the seeding of the instability. We will examine MSTID activity in the bottom-side F-region as a possible seeding mechanism for EPBs. By looking at both the growth rates and the seeding in situ, we can determine their relative contribution in EPB formation. There are two major types of MSTIDs: gravity wave driven, which mainly occur in the daytime, and electrified MSTIDs, which mainly occur at night. By examining MSTID activity in the evening we can determine which mechanism is dominant in this local time sector.

articleTitle: Design and Optimization of 4.7-Tesla RF Coils and Associated Circuits for Use in High-Field Strength and High-Larmor-Frequency Magnetic Resonance Imaging
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has become an indispensable tool in medical diagnostics, with high-field strength <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(B_{0}\geq 3\mathrm{T})$</tex> MRI systems offering major advantages in image resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and scanning speed. However, these benefits come with technical challenges, particularly in the design of the radiofrequency (RF) coils responsible for generating the RF magnetic field pulse <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\mathrm{B}_{1})$</tex>. At these high field strengths, the increased Larmor frequencies (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$[\geq 127.74$</tex> MHz) necessitate more advanced coil designs that differ from those used in traditional MRI scanners operating at lower field strengths and frequencies, such as 1.5 T.

articleTitle: Experimentally Overcoming Fundamental LTI Bounds via Periodic Temporal Modulations
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The introduction of time as a new degree of freedom in electromagnetic structures has witnessed a surge of research interest in recent years due to their potential applications and theoretical promise. More specifically, numerous research efforts have focused on the use time-varying structures to overcome conventional electromagnetic performance limits. While these studies have revealed strong theoretical performance of time-varying structures, their experimental demonstration across any frequency spectrum has been slim. In this talk, we will focus on the limit on electromagnetic absorption, also known as the Rozanov bound. (K. N. Rozanov, “Ultimate thickness to bandwidth ratio of radar absorbers,” in IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation, vol. 48, no. 8, pp. 1230–1234, Aug. 2000).

articleTitle: Channel Scaling Limitations to Spurious Free Dynamic Range for 2-18 GHz Hybrid Digital Array Architectures
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper covers spurious free dynamic range (SFDR) improvement factor limitations in ultra-wideband hybrid digital arrays when scaling channel counts to larger apertures. A brief theory is provided to establish the differences between signal chain SFDR and analog-to-digital converter (ADC) specified SFDR. Then, measurements are performed with a 2–18 GHz digital array testbed to validate the theoretical coherent channel combining expression. This model can be applied to arbitrary digital arrays to establish a limit to the expected SFDR improvement factor. A representative hybrid beamforming architecture used for the presented analysis is shown in Figure 1. This figure captures the major subsystems required for signal conditioning, up/down conversion, digitization, and processing.

articleTitle: Detecting VHF Satellite Emissions Using the Orville Wideband Imager
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are experiencing rapid growth, a trend which is likely to continue with the on-going expansion of the Starlink, OneWeb, and Kuiper constellations. The telecommunications satellites in these constellations produce both intentional in-band Radio Frequency (RF) emissions as well as unintended out-of-band emissions. These emissions can be detected from radio astronomy telescopes and are a possible source of interference, particularly when the emissions occur at frequencies outside of a licensed satellite communications band. Out-of-band RF emissions from the Starlink constellation have been observed at radio astronomy telescopes such as the LOFAR array in the Netherlands (Vruno, et al. 2023) and the SKA-Low prototype station in Australia (Grigg, 2023.)

articleTitle: Broadband Scattering from the HAARP-Disturbed D-Region Ionosphere
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The HAARP facility's HF ionospheric heater can be used to modify the electron temperature of the D-region ionosphere (60–100 km) to temperatures near 3000 K within 30 µs. This heating occurs over a patch ~20 km in diameter from 75–85 km in altitude, within which the conductivity tensor is modified. Scattering of VLF transmitters (3–30 kHz) from this patch was previously observed [1] [2], but we present here scattering of broadband sferics, originating from distant lightning strokes, from the HAARP-modified ionopshere.

articleTitle: Dual-Polarized Multi-Emitter RF Propagation Collection with Large Vertical Array at the Salton Sea
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A 40-element, 10-meter vertical array receives horizontally and vertically polarized signals from multiple Cband sources located several kilometers away, across a sea surface known to exhibit stable ducting conditions. The dense datasets resulting from the multi-week collection are suitable for developing new models for atmospheric refractivity in stable conditions.

articleTitle: Design of an HF Scimitar Antenna
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Scimitar antenna is a bi-directional radiator constructed as a flat metal plate with a wide end on one side and a narrow point on the other. Once the antenna turns on, it maintains uniform impedance characteristics over a wide range of frequencies, however, the radiation patterns are not stable over the same bandwidth (W. P. Turner, “The Scimitar Antenna,” in The Sixth Symposium on the USAF Antenna Research and Development Program, 1956). When fed at the narrow end and grounded at the wider end, the antenna presents a nominal impedance of about 200 Ω. To match it to the standard 50 Ω one needs a 4: 1 impedance transformer. Moreover, due to the small flare angle at the feed region the fabrication may be somewhat challenging. Thus, increasing the flare angle is a reasonable approach to reduce the Scimitar's nominal impedance (Meinke, H. “Research on Antennas.” Tech. Annu. Summary Report, Munchen, Germany: Air Force Avionics Laboratory, Sept 1963) while providing more attachment real estate. In addition, a wider flare angle reduces the frequency at which desired pattern characteristics manifest and stabilizes the radiation patterns to some degree. Simulations show that when the flare angle is increased from 65° to 130°, the nominal impedance of the antenna is reduced from 200 Ω to 50 Ω, the bandwidth with the stable pattern is increased from 84% to 128%, and the start of the band for a 5.1 m tall scimitar antenna is lowered from 7.65 MHz to 3.75 MHz. The curve describing the outline of the proposed antenna is given in (1), where the values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$k$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex> are 3.65 and 0.2, respectively.

articleTitle: The Sea State Sensitivity of GNSS-R Ocean Wind Speed Measurements
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) is a form of bistatic radar that relies on GNSS navigation signals and measures their forward (specular) scattering by the Earth surface. Modifications to the strength of the navigation signal by the scattering process contain information about the surface roughness. Over the ocean, surface roughness is related to near surface wind speed, which can be estimated from the scattered signal strength. Near surface ocean wind data products are routinely produced by the existing constellations of GNSS-R satellites (CYGNSS, Spire, Triton, FY-3, and Muon). The wind speed is typically estimated using a Geophysical Model Function (GMF) that relates the wind to the normalized bistatic radar cross section (NBRCS) of the ocean surface. Notably, contributions to the NBRCS are made across a range of wavelengths of the surface roughness spectrum that includes both smaller capillary waves and longer swell waves. Stress at the ocean surface caused by wind imparts energy into the surface roughness at capillary-scale wavelengths and turbulent energy cascade transfers the energy from shorter to longer wavelengths. After a sufficient length of time, the complete roughness spectrum will reach an equilibrium referred to as a fully developed sea. Prior work has shown that the time scale of this energy cascade is of order 1 hour. However, if the wind has changed in the ~1 hour prior to a measurement of the NBRCS, the capillary waves will have reacted to the change more quickly than have the swell waves, and the relationship between NBRCS and the wind at the time of the measurement may not be consistent with that assumed by the GMF. In this presentation, we examine the dependence of GNSS-R wind speed retrieval bias on wind persistence (defined as the change in wind speed in the recent past). There is found to be a very strong dependence, with the wind speed bias increasing with increasing change in wind speed in the recent (~1 hour) past, prior to the GNSS-R measurement of NBRCS. This sensitivity to wind persistence is not generally observed with other remotely sensed ocean wind products such as radar scatterometers and passive microwave imagers, which are much less sensitive to the longer (swell) wavelength portion of the roughness spectrum of the ocean surface.

articleTitle: Investigation of Guided Power Expressions for Symmetric Dielectric Slab Waveguides
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This manuscript explores various phase constant candidates for computation of guided power in symmetric dielectric slab waveguides. Prior studies on guided power calculation have been marred by ambiguity in definition of the phase constant. In this study, we establish the relationships between electric and magnetic fields for both Transverse Electric (TE) and Transverse Magnetic (TM) modes by evaluating numerous phase constant candidates regarding the computation error of guided powers traversing the cross-sectional area of a three-dimensional (3D) waveguide. As a numerical example, we analyze a dielectric slab waveguide comprising a silicon core encased by a silicon dioxide cladding, and compare the calculated fields and guided powers in TE and TM modes, validated by simulation results.

articleTitle: Impact of Surface Temperature Representation in a Mesoscale Numerical Weather Prediction Model on Electromagnetic Propagation Modeling over an Inland Water Body
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Frequent fine-scale spatial and temporal variations of scalar parameters and wind in the marine atmospheric boundary layer contribute to a dynamic refractive environment. Prediction of this environment with modern numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems remains challenging due to limitations of resolution and the initial values, among other factors. These environmental variables contribute to the characteristics of refractive features such as evaporation ducts. These features can lead to anomalous propagation of electromagnetic (EM) and radio frequencies (RF). The modeling of electromagnetic frequency propagation through the atmosphere using NWP systems is of critical importance for users of such technologies (Kammerer et al., 2018). The variability of the above mentioned oceanic and atmospheric fields along propagation paths are also of critical importance (Greenway et al., 2024). Properly configured NWP systems with robust data assimilation are a valuable tool in modeling refractive conditions through the atmosphere and thusly the impact of the atmosphere on EM RF propagation.

articleTitle: Improved Radio Astronomy Interference Characterization Using DevOps
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In order to increase spectrum sharing and protect Radio Astronomy against ever increasing Radio Frequency Interference (RFI), it is important to constantly monitor and analyze the radio frequency environment. This research improves upon a Software Defined Radio (SDR)-based testbed deployed at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory for over a year now with real time monitoring through DevOps tools. Utilizing Docker, Ansible, Prometheus, and Grafana in addition to improvements on the code created to run these continuous radio frequency surveys, measurements are calculated and displayed within seconds. Ensuring the health of these devices both from tampering and time/wear is also of utmost importance given the nonstop data collection. To that end daily status checks, alerting, and daily liveness checks have also been implemented. All of this ensures the constant monitoring of RFI is reliable, allowing for improved data gathering and analysis.

articleTitle: Multiplexed Detector Readout Technology for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present the design, development plan, and predicted performance of the readout system for the CMB-S4 receiver focal planes. CMB-S4 will be a ground-based observatory conducting a millimeter-wave survey of the southern galactic sky across observing bands ranging from 20 to 300 GHz. It will significantly enhance sensitivity compared to current ground-based cosmic microwave background (CMB) surveys, aiming to search for cosmic inflation and relic particles, study the distribution and flows of matter in the universe, and detect millimeter-wave transient events.

articleTitle: Impact of May 2024 Geomagnetic Superstorm on the Submarine Cables
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: During the first half of May 2024, solar active regions (ARs) 3663 and 3664 produced numerous solar flares, SEPs, and associated CMEs, which created major geospace disturbances. Specifically, the CME associated with the aforementioned ARs caused G5 geomagnetic storms, pushing Kp beyond 9 and Dst below -400 nT, creating a superstorm. During the storm, we observed large fluctuations in the magnetospheric and ionospheric current systems, recorded by space-borne and ground-based instruments such as magnetometers, coherent radars, and ISRs. Previous studies reported possible hazards of storm induced ground electric fields (GEF) and associated geomagnetically induced currents (GICs). While magnetic superstorms are known to be known to permanently damage ground-based transformers and lead to blackouts [1], we have not had a clear vision of the impact of these superstorms on underwater electrical equipment such as submarine cables, due to the low accessibility of underwater measurements. The March 1989 storm, the largest superstorm of the last century, caused widespread effects on power systems, including a blackout of the Hydro-Quebec system, and created rapid fluctuations on submarine cables [2, and references therein]. Due to the lack of underwater measurements, the general understanding of submarine cable risk and vulnerability during superstorms is limited. We have recently developed a capability to model (SCUBAS) the impact of storm-driven GICs on underwater cables [3]. In this study, we will leverage this capability to estimate the voltage fluctuations during the May 2024 superstorm and compare them with the March 1989 superstorm. We will also include the variability in the model parameters and uncertainties in the inputs to create ensemble outputs from SCUBAS to quantify the uncertainties. This study will be the steppingstone towards validating the SCUBAS estimates during extreme space weather events and will provide insight into the health of the underwater electronics during these types of space weather hazards.

articleTitle: Electromagnetic Field-Induced Modulation of Antioxidant Responses in Cancer Cells: Frequency-Specific Investigations and Bioengineering Implications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study explores the modulation of antioxidant enzyme activities in HT-1080 human fibrosarcoma cells under low-intensity radiofrequency (RF) electromagnetic field (EMF) exposure, specifically in the 2–5 MHz range at 20 nT. The investigation focuses on the bioengineering and quantum biological mechanisms driving these effects. Significant frequency-specific changes were observed in key antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione (GSH), and peroxidase, highlighting the resonance effects between weak RF fields and biological macromolecules. This suggests that even weak RF fields can trigger notable biological responses.

articleTitle: Stopband Investigation of Leaky-Wave Antenna Based on Microstrip Line with Circular Apertures
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The design and analysis of a simple leaky-wave antenna (LWA) based on a microstrip line with radiating circular apertures is investigated, which can suppress the open stopband when the beam is scanned through broadside. In this design, open-stopband suppression is achieved by adjusting the distance between two circular apertures in the unit cell. A simple analysis of the stopband suppression of the proposed L W A design is discussed. An almost complete elimination of the stopband is possible for relatively small slots. The proposed design has the benefits of having a simple structure, low cross polarization, and an ability to achieve a wide range of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha/k_{0}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Radio Interferometric Imaging on High Throughput Computing Systems
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The increasing data volumes from observations with the current radio telescopes and the prospects for several orders of magnitude increase in data rates with the next generation of radio telescopes have motivated the development of a high performance and high throughput data processing model to enable data processing rates to be compatible with data acquisition rates.

articleTitle: Radar Beam Blockage Correction for Improved QPE Over Complex Terrain
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In weather radar data, partial beam blockage is caused by the obstruction of the beam filling by mountains or buildings, which often leads to incomplete and/or distorted radar quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE). In this paper, a novel deep learning approach using Generative Adversarial Networks to correct radar beam blockage effects is presented and demonstrated using radar observations over complex terrain in Northern California. The model is trained and tested using historical radar data collected during a number of precipitation events. The testing results show that the precipitation patterns are better captured by the beam blockage corrected data, and the corrected radar reflectivity measurements agree better with ground-based disdrometer data. In addition, radar QPE products are derived using radar reflectivity before and after correction, and the QPE results are evaluated using rainfall rates derived from the disdrometer data. The improved QPE indicates the potential of the proposed beam blockage correction model for quantitative applications over complex terrain regions.

articleTitle: A Reconfigurable 2-Bit-Phase-Shifting Reflectarray Antenna Utilizing Two PIN Diodes per Unit Cell
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Electronically reconfigurable reflectarray antennas (RRAs) with discrete phase quantization have gained attention for next-generation wireless communication systems due to their dynamic beamforming capabilities and relatively affordable costs. Compared to ideal reflectarrays with continuous phase correction, l -bit, 2-bit, and 3-bit RRAs experience quantization losses of approximately 3 dB, 0.6 dB, and 0.2 dB, respectively. Considering that each additional bit comes with extra switches (e.g., PIN diodes) and more complicated control circuitry, 2-bit RRAs offer a balanced compromise between the antenna gains and system complexity. While various unit cell designs for 2-bit RRAs have been reported, most of them require more than two PIN diodes to realize the four discrete phase states. Only a few works managed to achieve the 2-bit operation using two pin diodes (Han et al., IEEE Transactions on Industrial Electronics, 2022; Li et al., IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, 2023), which is the minimum number of switches needed to provide four operating states for the unit cell. These designs are based on tuning the resonant frequency of the unit cell structure and typically provide a 2-bit phase shift over a narrow frequency range. Indeed, both studies only characterized the beam-scanning performance of the RRAs at a single frequency point and did not report the operating bandwidths of the unit cells. Therefore, new 2-bit RRA unit cell designs that allows for extending the operating bandwidth as much as possible while maintaining the minimum number of switches (e.g., 2 PIN diodes) are highly desirable.

articleTitle: Multidimensional Load-Pull Extrapolation for Accelerated Computer-Aided Design (CAD) Simulations
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) is widely used in the design and optimization of power amplifiers. Often CAD tasks require many simulations and the time required can be a limiting factor. Additionally, there are many difficulties with characterizing the behavior of high-power and high-frequency power amplifier devices. The work presented reduces the time required for CAD simulations and can use data collected from a device in a measurable region to approximate behavior under difficult-to-measure operating conditions. This work improves on the Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (WGAN) Load-Pull Extrapolation network trained for 2d load-pull extrapolation (A. Egbert, C. Baylis, and R. J. Marks, “Extrapolation of Load-Pull Data: A Novel Use of GAN Artificial Intelligence Image Completion,” IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, vol. 70, no. 11, pp. 4849–4856, Nov. 2022) and extends it to support a 3<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">rd</sup> dimension, input power. This work can extrapolate as few as 16 simulation queries to 24,176 output powers while predicting the optimal reflection coefficient over changing input power to within a median vector error of 0.1098.

articleTitle: Using Automatic Differentiation to Simplify Ionospheric Specification with Signals From a Network of HF Beacons
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A high-frequency (HF) beacon network has been deployed in Peru and another in Alaska. The (HF) beacons and other instruments like GPS and sounder receivers are used to reconstruct the ionospheric electron number density regionally. The continuous wave HF signals employ unquantized random phases code with pseudorandom noise (PRN) encoding, and the observables include propagation time or pseudorange, Doppler shift or beat carrier phase, and amplitude. A forward model based on geometric optics in an inhomogeneous, anisotropic, lossy plasma relates plasma number density to the observables. Plasma number density is parametrized with a modified Chapman profile in the vertical and biquintic B-splines in the horizontal. Sensitivity analysis is needed to model the ray amplitudes and solve the two-point boundary problem for each ray. We perform sensitivity analysis here with reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Specifically, we use an LLVM compiler (Clang), the corresponding OpenMP library, and the Enzyme Automatic Differentiation Framework plugin to compute ray endpoints' sensitivity (gradients) concerning initial bearings. The algorithm exhibits no performance penalty compared to variational sensitivity analysis and is relatively simple to implement.

articleTitle: Estimation of Statistics of Long Range Millimeter-Wave Propagation in Rain Based on Full-Wave Analysis
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The problem of electromagnetic (EM) wave propagation in random media composed of a heterogeneous mixture of different scattering particles in a background medium is encountered in many practical applications. Scattering and propagation of light through fog or murky water are familiar examples of such problems. The scattering and absorption by the particles are responsible for the wave attenuation and the scattering alone is responsible the wave phase front aberration and the field spatial fluctuation. The scattering phenomenon becomes important as the size of the constituent particles become comparable or larger than the wavelength. In this talk we consider the problem of EM wave propagation and scattering in rain at millimeter-wave (MMW) part of the spectrum because of its importance in radar remote sensing of precipitation as well as the emerging MMW 5G and 6G communication and the use of MMW radars for autonomous vehicles. The analysis of EM wave interaction with rain as a random medium is important since at MMW band, the size of the rain particles are comparable to the wavelength which can result in considerable scattering. Knowing the specific statistical characteristics of wave propagation such the attenuation rate through rain enables more accurate link budget planning for communication and radar systems. Also information about the statistics of the phase and amplitude fluctuations of the waves in rain enables better performance analyses of antenna arrays used in communication and radar systems. Analytical models based on single scattering theory are inadequate for the prediction of long range wave propagation characteristics in such media, as the effect of multiple scattering among particles become important. To account for the effects of multiple scattering a full-wave simulation must be considered which is quite challenging considering the size of the computational domain. Considering the fact that the statistical nature of the wave propagation properties, as opposed to exact field quantities for a specific medium configuration, is of desire, a novel computational model based on S-matrix is developed. The attributes of the S-matrix method are as follows: 1) it is based on full-wave analysis, 2) it is applicable to dense or sparse random media, 3) it tracks the polarization of the wave along the propagation, 4) it tracks phase aberration to the phase front needed for assessing the performance of coherent imaging systems such as SAR or MIMO radar operating in random media, 5) it can be used for any random media with arbitrary shaped scatterers. In the presentation, the formulation for the S-matrix method and its application for predicting the attenuation rate and wave fluctuation statistics will be presented. The model is validated by comparing the simulation results with the existing attenuation rate measurements reported in the literature.

articleTitle: Get Away Special Radio and Antenna Transparency Satellite (GASRATS) Payload
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Utah State University's Get Away Special (GAS) Student Satellite Team is a student-run CubeSat team to provide university students unique opportunities to learn, develop, and launch CubeSats. The main payload of the current CubeSat project, Radio and Antenna Transparency Satellite (GASRATS) mission, is an optically transparent, circularly polarized, S-band patch antenna integrated on the solar panel of a 3U CubeSat. The merit of such a payload is clear, because such an integration resolves the issue of antenna competing with solar cells for the limited surface real estate on a small satellite. The object of GASRATS is to perform technology demonstration through an on-orbit data link of such an integrated solar panel antenna, and to collect data for future deployment of the transparent antenna technology.

articleTitle: Multi-Scale Estimation and Parameterization of Severe Storm Impacts at High Latitudes
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Gannon storm generated severe high-latitude geomagnetic disturbances. Understanding and preparing for space weather events in this context is critical for our technology innovations that operate in the near-earth space environment and/or rely on trans-ionospheric and skywave signal propagation. Safety-critical radio-based applications include satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), HF radar, and VHF communications. These systems deliver assured PNT and global connectivity for billions of users worldwide, with rapidly growing downstream markets for autonomous services driving ever more rigorous safety and integrity standards. Here we discuss ionospheric disturbances and parameterization of associated real-world impacts during this storm event via data-driven modeling approaches.

articleTitle: Reconfigurable Nonlocal Metasurface for Tunable Frequency, Quality-factor, and Geometric Phase
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a reconfigurable bilayer non-local metasurface capable of frequency-selective wavefront manipulation, featuring tunable geometric phase and quality factor through varactor diode tuning. Simulations demonstrate dynamic beam steering, quality-factor control, and resonant frequency tuning, while achieving transparency at out-of-band frequencies, offering significant potential for advanced, multifunctional, recon-figurable cascaded metasurface systems.

articleTitle: Design and Modeling of High-Power Density Stacked Coil for WPT in a Lossy Seawater Environment
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: For successful undersea exploration and marine resource development, providing reliable power and stable communication to devices like undersea sensors, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) is critical. The operational endurance of these vehicles is limited by their onboard energy storage. This research proposes a subsea-grade, high-power-density coil pack designed for subsea and marine wireless power transfer systems, enabling the underwater recharging of ROVs and AUV s. By facilitating high-speed, contactless high-power charging without the need for docking, this technology maximizes operational efficiency while reducing the costs and complexities associated with long subsea charging cables.

articleTitle: Impact of Notch Filtering on Radar Target Detection: Problems and Proposed Solutions
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Over time spectrum usage has been increasing at an exponential rate. This increased usage has presented radars with increasingly congested spectral environments. Congested spectral environments can cause radars many issues such as radar processing errors due to signal distortion through saturation of the low-noise amplifier (LNA) and decreased signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR). Excessive interference power on a receiver's front end can cause nonlinear distortion of a received waveform. A useful solution to these issues for ultra-wideband radars (UWB) are notch filters, which effectively block out known interferers prior to the LNA. Adding a notch filter prior to the LNA avoids saturation and alleviates other radar processing issues. While adding a notch filter into a UWB radar system may help block out interferers as well as their undesired effects, the notching will introduce new issues mainly when detecting a target. This presentation discusses the challenges introduced to the UWB radar system when performing target detection techniques, as well as possible solutions to alleviate this issue.

articleTitle: Inverting Soil Moisture From GNSS-R Reflectivity Using a Semi-empirical Model
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study presents an initial investigation in estimating near-surface soil moisture from GNSS reflection signal-based reflectivity observations. A semi-empirical model is implemented firstly under coherent reflection principles, parameterizing reflectivity's interaction with soil moisture, vegetation, and surface roughness. We applied this model to a track of Spire reflection data over Australia to invert soil moisture measurements, which agree well to the collocated SMAP observations with a root mean square difference (RMSD) of 0.05 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>• CYGNSS reflectivity observations are used as well to generate gridded maps of soil moisture. Using three-day CYGNSS data over Australia, the resultant averaged soil moisture map depicts a similar spatial variation pattern as SMAP data, with a RMSD of 0.06 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>. Our results are promising for using GNSS reflection data to semi-physically invert soil moisture, serving as an independent data source for scientific research and applications.

articleTitle: Toward Binary Reconfigurable Holographic Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents the design of a reconfigurable holographic surface (RHS) using binary control for electronic beamforming. We employ a symmetrical unit-cell design with a compact topology of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda/6$</tex> periodicity at 6.2 GHz. PIN diodes are used as radio frequency (RF) switches to electronically tune the RHS unit cells, resulting in 1-bit modulation of the surface impedance. The RHS features a symmetrical design along both the x and y axes, making it scalable for large-scale apertures. Numerical results of a 440-element RHS show gain of 11.3 dB and a sidelobe level of -10 dB. Additionally, the RHS can achieve beam scanning of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm 70^{\mathrm{o}}$</tex> in both azimuth and elevation angles and allows for polarization control.

articleTitle: The Computational Burden of Next-Gen Terahertz SDR and Algorithmic Paths for Solutions
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The terahertz (THz) bands, which are also typically referred to as the spectrum beyond 100 GHz, are emerging thanks to the abundant spectral resources, including continuous bands of spectrum that may be wider than 20 GHz. The availability of spectrum with bands over 20 GHz is an exciting opportunity for ultra-broadband wireless systems, including next-generation communications, networking, and sensing systems. As the carrier frequencies being considered continue to increase, the wavelength correspondingly reduces, in turn leading to smaller antennas with increased bandwidths. Even a narrowband patch antenna at 400 GHz could have more than 20 GHz of bandwidth even though the fractional bandwidth is only 5% of the center frequency. This leads to exciting new capabilities in broadband digital signal processing (DSP) and software defined radio (SDR) systems when used at such high carrier frequencies.

articleTitle: Optimization Metrics for Minimizing Error in Array Transmission Pattern
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: As the wireless spectrum grows increasingly congested, more transmitting systems need to be compatible with frequency-sharing techniques. To effectively use adaptive frequency-sharing techniques, transmitting hardware must be able to operate efficiently over a wide range of frequencies. While wideband hardware does achieve this requirement, gain performance is always degraded according to the Bode-Fano limit. Reconfigurable narrowband transmit hardware, however, comes with its own difficulties. Antenna arrays are particularly affected by these challenges, due to effects like mutual coupling, fixed element spacings at varying wavelengths, and the need for tuning every element in the array independently.

articleTitle: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface-Assisted Beam Management for AI Signal Classification in mmWave Networks
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Millimeter wave (mmWave) communications are vulnerable to blockages and node mobility due to the highly directional signal beams. Reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) has emerged as a competitive solution to the blocking problem. However, due to the passive nature of the RIS, obtaining channel state information (CSI) for RIS-assisted mmWave communication systems is rather difficult. Automatic modulation classification (AMC) could improve the transmission efficiency of mmWave wireless communication systems, as it can adaptively select the most suitable modulation method according to the current communication environment, under the condition of unknown prior information, such as CSI, thus improving spectral efficiency and reducing the power consumption in NextG wireless communications systems. Deep learning (DL) has been widely used for AMC in sub-6 GHz wireless networks due to its capacity for feature learning directly on raw radio front-end data.
