articleTitle: Compact Development Platform for Wideband Digital True Time Delay Beamforming and RFI Cancellation
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: As processing bandwidths for passive receivers and communication systems increase, digital beamformer systems become increasingly resource-intensive with respect to their computational requirements. One approach to dealing with the high computational burden is a heterogeneous architecture with processing steps distributed between networked FPGAs and GPUs.

articleTitle: Scintillation and High-Rate TEC Observations at Mid Latitudes During the Gannon Storm
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present scintillation and ionospheric total electron content (TEC) measurements made by a network of low-cost GNSS based monitors distributed over North and Central America during the May 2024 super geomagnetic storm. The observations show severe TEC gradients and fluctuations occurring over the US that persisted for several hours between May 10 18:00 UT and May 11 12:00 UT TEC fluctuations were quantified using the rate of change of TEC index (ROTI). Amplitude scintillation was quantified using the 1-minute S<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> index. Despite severe TEC perturbations, only weak to moderate amplitude scintillation events were observed. Additionally, the observations show that while ROTI increases persisted during several hours, S<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> increases were observed for only a few minutes.

articleTitle: Assessment of a Humidity and Temperature Retrieval Technique Using Refractivity Measurements
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Air properties influence the propagation of electromagnetic waves in the marine atmospheric surface layer (MASL) through several mechanisms such as absorption, scattering, and refraction. At X-band, atmospheric refractivity is the main factor influencing the propagation, but at higher frequencies, air properties such as temperature and humidity can also directly influence propagation. Many existing technologies including numerical weather prediction, similarity theory, or in-situ atmospheric measurements are used to make estimates of temperature and humidity, but each of these technologies have their own limitations. Remote sensing technologies that estimate air properties are generally applied over broad vertical spatial scales at coarse resolution; however, refractivity inversions based on radar data have been used to estimate vertical profiles of refractivity in the MASL at fine vertical resolution. These methodologies commonly use propagation loss measured from bi-static X-band radar or ocean surface clutter paired with machine learning algorithms or look-up tables to inversely determine these vertical profiles of refractivity. However, these inversion technologies are currently limited to estimating refractivity; extension to other air properties would enable their remote sensing at fine resolution within the MASL. Thus, this work explores the development of an inverse technique for retrieving temperature and humidity from modified refractivity measurements. Such measurements can be inferred from refractivity inversion techniques based-on radar measurements. With this extension, inverse methods offer an additional tool for remotely estimating vertical distributions of temperature and/or humidity in the MASL.

articleTitle: Improving the Modeling of Artificial Periodic Inhomogeneities for the Entire Ionosphere Regions
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Artificial Periodic Inhomogeneities (API) are periodic structures in the electron plasma density generated by heating the different layers of the ionosphere using powerful HF waves emitted from ground-based radio frequency transmitter facilities. Since their first detection was reported by Belikovich et al., 1975, the formation of these types of inhomogeneities has been extensively studied across different ionospheric regions. Backscatter signals from these structures provide valuable information about the medium from which they originated and serve to study a broad range of ionospheric phenomena (see Bakhmetieva et al., 2022). To understand the API formation, we need to establish the interaction between the propagating powerful HF wave sent by the heater and the ionospheric medium. Moreover, we need to identify the exact physical mechanism resulting from this interaction at each ionospheric region and produce these artificial perturbations. Due to the range variability of the formation mechanism, the development of a single theory for the full range of altitudes is still absent.

articleTitle: Theoretical and Practical Aspects of Frequency Up-Conversion in Linear Time Varying Plasmas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In recent years, researchers have shown a lot of interest in the interaction of electromagnetic (EM) waves with linear time-varying media. Changing the constitutive parameters of a medium, such as dielectric per-mittivity and permeability, results in a myriad of applications such as non-reciprocity, wideband impedance matching, frequency conversion, etc. Among various possible materials, a potential candidate for studying as a time-varying medium is a gaseous plasma. One can change the number density of electrons (or the plasma frequency) in time and thus vary the dielectric constant of a gaseous plasma as a function of time. As a result, theoretically it is possible to achieve frequency up-conversion with a plasma that is switched in time, with a plasma frequency that increases in value with time up to a nominal steady-state value. However, experimental studies in this area have been limited so far.

articleTitle: Signatures of Ionospheric G-Condition Observed During 2017 and 2021 Total Solar Eclipses
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We investigated the photochemical and dynamic processes driven by eclipses and the subsequent impact on the plasma density. Total solar eclipses have been reported to adversely affect over-the-horizon propagation of High Frequency (HF: 3–30 MHz) radar and communication signals. While previous studies focused mainly on the macroscopic effects on the IT response to eclipses, the detailed features controlling the ionospheric density including the plasma transport from the conjugate hemisphere remain poorly understood. We observed ionospheric G-condition during 2017 Greate American Eclipse (GAE), which observed near middle latitudes. Since then, there have been a few eclipses observed at different latitudes, specifically 4th December 2021 Antarctic Eclipse. We utilized the Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN) and ionosondes to investigate how the evolution of G-condition at different latitudes. We compared the observations from midlatitude radar observations from 2017 and 2021 eclipses to evaluate how eclipse geometry impacted ionospheric G-condition. We used GITM and WAM-IPE model simulation to understand the G-condition impact, which adversely affected the HF propagation.

articleTitle: Development and Validation of a Limb-to-Disk Algorithm for Mapping Radio Occultation Measurements of Scintillation to the Vertical Propagation Geometry
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Modern radio occultation (RO) receivers can routinely provide high-rate observations during ionospheric scintillation events. The high-rate data enables direct measurement of the amplitude and phase scintillation indices (S4 and sigma-phi) as well as indirect (model-inferred) estimation of turbulence strength integrated along horizontal radio-occultation ray-paths. While useful, a ground-based user of satellite radio services would generally prefer to know the scintillation indices along a space-to-ground propagation path. Under the COSMIC-2 calibration/validation program, Boston College developed a limb-to-disk (L2D) algorithm for mapping scintillation along radio occultation ray-paths from the horizontal to the vertical propagation geometry. Since turbulence strength and propagation distance both contribute to the measured S4, it is necessary to first geolocate the irregularity region before the mapping is performed.

articleTitle: Hunting for Electromagnetic Solitons in the Laboratory
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The near-Earth space environment is growing ever more cluttered and has led to an exponential growth of orbital debris. Collisions with these objects traveling at orbital speeds has resulted in serious malfunctions or the disabling of satellite systems. Orbital debris down to a cm are catalogued and tracked to aid in collision avoidance. However, NASA reports that a collision with an object as small as a millimeter traveling at orbital speeds can be mission ending. Consequently, there has been a concerted effort to develop innovative detection techniques that can track the multitude of sub-centimeter sized debris and provide enough warning time for a satellite to react.

articleTitle: Double-Layer Lightweight Linearly Polarized High-Gain Transmitarray Antenna Design at Ka-Band Based on Ultra-thin Kapton Membrane
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The growing need for compact, high-gain antennas in space communication and remote sensing radar systems, particularly for CubeSat integration, has led to the development of a compact and lightweight transmitarray antenna (TA). Our novel design uses two layers of ultra-thin (0.5 mil) Kapton membrane, allowing for both low mass and easy deployment. The S-shaped metasurface geometry enables asymmetric transmission and facilitates 90° linear polarization conversion while offering full <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2\mathfrak{n}$</tex> phase coverage and maintaining high transmission efficiency for linearly polarized feed source. Simulation results indicate that the 10 cm diameter TA design can achieve 29.6 dBi directivity and 63% aperture efficiency at 35.75 GHz, showing great potential for future millimeter-wave space communication applications.

articleTitle: Ionospheric Diagnostics Using AM Radio and Non-Directional Beacon Signals Received at Sondrestrom, Greenland
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Dartmouth College operated a receiving system covering 100–3100 kHz at the incoherent scatter radar facility in Sondrestrom, Greenland, for many years prior to station closing in 2018. The system used five antennas spaced on baselines up to 500 meters to enable direction finding; signals were received with a custom-built digital receiver mounted in a vault in the antenna field, with resulting data transmitted approximately one kilometer to a computer in the station for storage and analysis. The principal science goal was to measure radio emissions of natural auroral origin, but local non-directional beacons and AM radio signals from Greenland, North America, and Europe were also detected. Region 1 radio stations (North America) were easily distinguishable from region 2 (Europe). Relatively local Greenland stations and beacons, few in number, could be individually identified. A typical pattern was observed whereby reception of European AM radio signals was shifted to earlier times relative to reception of North American AM radio signals, according to development of nighttime conditions on the respective propagation paths. This spatial separation of the signal paths in principle allows localization of disturbances in propagation caused by auroral activity, which is most commonly centered equatorward of Sondrestrom, which is near 75 degrees invariant magnetic latitude. Disturbances in propagation could include absorption or bearing deflection. Data from years of operation of the Dartmouth College receiving system enable statistical and case studies investigating use of these propagation effects as ionospheric diagnostics. Other measurement techniques employed at Sondrestrom during these years, including incoherent scatter radar, complement these propagation studies.

articleTitle: Ground-Penetrating Radar for Lunar Exploration
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Ground-Penetrating Radar (GPR) is widely used for subsurface imaging to support investigations in geology, hydrology, agriculture, engineering, mineral resources, unexploded ordnance, and archaeology. These diverse applications require investigation depths spanning several centimeters to kilometers, with corresponding frequencies of several GHz to a few MHz, respectively. Early GPR development began in the mid-20<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> century, but the first major application was the Surface Electrical Properties (SEP) experiment on the Apollo 17 lunar landing. We review key previous work in lunar GPR and discuss several approaches to future exploration.

articleTitle: Switching between Whistler-Mode Waves inside Density and Magnetic Ducts
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Observations from NASA Van Allen Probes and Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) satellites demonstrate that whistler-mode waves can be trapped and guided by the field-aligned irregularities of the plasma density and the magnetic field. These irregularities can be formed by the depletion of the plasma density or the magnetic field (these are low-density or low-B ducts), enhancement (high-density or high-B ducts) and shelf-like density and magnetic field structures. The ducting of the whistler-mode waves explains their propagation in the Earth's magnetosphere over a significant distance with a little attenuation, which was observed in recent experiments with the DSX satellite.

articleTitle: A Principal Component Analysis of Convective Environments, and Their Relationship to Satellite-Observed Storm Characteristics
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: There are many unknowns surrounding why convective storms occur exactly when and where they do, including environmental impacts on storm morphology and processes. One of primary science objectives of NASA's upcoming INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) satellite mission is to quantify relationships between a storm's environment and its convective mass flux. To do this, we seek to distill the somewhat nebulous concept of a “convective environment” into a small number of scalar variables. In this study, as a first step towards those goals, we leverage 25 years of spaceborne radar observations from TRMM and GPM to evaluate how the depth and width of precipitating convective storms are related to large-scale environmental variables obtained from ERA5 reanalysis. Using random forests, we identify eight variables that are useful for distinguishing between global convective storm modes. We then show that principal component analysis can collapse most of the information in these variables into just two dimensions. The top two principal components effectively separate the environments of the deepest convective features from the environments of other convective features (Fig. 1).

articleTitle: A Study on RFI Detection and Mitigation for UAS-Based P-Band SoOp System
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: P-band has emerged as a spectrum of special interest for soil moisture estimation due to its longer wavelength and higher penetration depth into the soil. But to properly utilize this spectrum using Signals of Opportunity-Reflectometry (SoOp-R), interference from the system itself and external sources need to be identified and mitigated. In this study, a workflow has been formulated to identify the instrument-generated radio frequency interference (RFI) in an uncrewed aircraft system (UAS) based SoOp-R system designed to estimate surface reflectivity using P-band. Spectral kurtosis has been identified as a possible method for external RFI detection and the Front-End GNSS Interference eXcisor (FENIX) algorithm has been proposed as a possible RFI mitigation technique in a P-band SoOp system. The effect of RFI mitigation on surface reflectivity estimation will be validated in a digital twin of the system in a simulated environment.

articleTitle: Off-Axis Laser-Radiation Detection Using Intensity Interferometry: Signal-to-Noise Ratio
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We describe some aspects of a method for detecting indirect laser light (the weak off-axis or back-scattered radiation of a laser beam scattering in the atmosphere or from a rough surface) in the presence of low coherence (primarily solar) background. Unlike in most existent methods, which detect laser light based on its monochromaticity or intensity, the proposed approach uses a high degree of temporal coherence as the distinguishing property of laser radiation. It also utilizes intensity interferometry, which, in our case, amounts to the measurement of correlations of time-averaged photocurrents generated by two photodetectors located within the correlation range. Those correlations are proportional to the radiation's co-herence time, hence are sizable for the scattered laser light and negligible for the background. However, the low-coherence background does contribute to the noise (understood as statistical fluctuations of the current correlation); additional large noise components come from intensity fluctuations of the scattered laser radiation itself. We carry out a rigorous calculation of the signal and noise, the latter involving high - up to eighth - moments of the scattered field. The derived expressions allow us to determine the preferred range of the detector parameters, maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio (which can be sizable even for detection of a single pulse) and minimizing its sensitivity to the background.

articleTitle: TRIDENT: A Novel HF Radar System for Measuring Traveling Ionospheric Disturbances
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs) are electron density fluctuations that travel as waves through the ionosphere. TIDs are thought to be the ionospheric manifestation of atmospheric gravity waves and can emerge due to a wide variety of natural and anthropogenic causes, including earthquakes, thunderstorms, and rocket launches. With detailed measurements of TIDs, the scientific and operational community can better understand the ionosphere's response to these phenomena and predict the impact of the disturbed ionosphere on technological systems. Amongst other instruments, TIDs can be observed by ground-based HF radars. Orion Space Solutions is developing a next generation HF radar system for measuring TIDs called the Traveling Ionospheric Disturbance Evaluation Tri-wave (TRIDENT) sensor.

articleTitle: Enabling Direct Imaging Radio Telescopes and Precision Cosmology with pyFHD
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A new generation of sensitive radio observatories are being developed with ever increasing numbers of antennas to pursue cosmology, fast transients, astrophysics and near-earth space physics. The extreme data rates required for these telescopes has led to the development of direct imaging correlators that scale much more modestly than traditional correlators. However, standard radio astronomy tools cannot process data from direct imaging correlators, making it difficult to propose new direct imaging telescopes.

articleTitle: Polarized Atmospheric Properties and Modeling for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Detection of inflationary B-modes with the Cosmic Microwave Background Stage-4 (CMB-S4) experiment will require exquisite experiment sensitivity in polarization measurements and thorough handling of contaminating signals. One such contaminating signal is polarized atmospheric emission, which originates from ice crystals in the atmosphere. These ice crystals scatter and emit millimeter-wave radiation, detected as a Stokes Q polarized signal by cosmic microwave background (CMB) telescopes. This signal is largest on the scales relevant for inflationary B-mode searches (> 0.5 degrees). We present the first detection of polarized atmospheric emission at the South Pole using data from the South Pole Telescope (SPT). We offer a complete characterization of this signal in SPT data, including its frequency scaling, spatial scaling, elevation scaling, and amplitude across four Austral winter observing seasons. This model of polarized atmospheric emission will inform the design and forecasting of CMB-S4.

articleTitle: First Results from an Array for VLF Imaging of the D-Region Ionosphere
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A new array of VLF receivers is now online to advance sub-ionospheric remote sensing of the D-region ionosphere. As a part of bringing this array online, the drifting phase from the NLK (24.8 kHz) and NML (25.2 kHz) VLF transmitters has been characterized with a drift rate of -0.07885 ± 0.00079 °/s and -0.07201 ± 0.00012 °/s (2σ), respectively. We show that detrending using these drift rates recovers true phase shifts along transmit- receive great circle paths and can be used to recover phase measurements when a known reference is unavailable. A case study of two solar flares is presented, characterizing the peak phase change as a function of solar zenith angle for flares originating at different radial distances from the center of the solar disk.

articleTitle: Multi-Modal Sensing Aided RIS Communications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as one of the key enabling technologies for beyond 5G and 6G networks due to their capability to create virtual line-of-sight (LOS) paths between transmitters and receivers in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) environments. However, to achieve narrow beams and significantly enhanced received power, RIS must incorporate a large number of elements. This, in turn, presents a challenge due to the substantial beam training overhead required for optimal beam selection, particularly when dealing with larger RIS arrays. In this work, we propose a novel approach that leverages multi-modal sensing data to guide the beam selection process in RIS, especially in mobile environments where frequent beam alignment is necessary. This approach is motivated by promising results from recent research (G. Charan, T. Osman, A. Hredzak, N. Thawdar and A. Alkhateeb, “Vision-Position Multi-Modal Beam Prediction Using Real Millimeter Wave Datasets,” 2022 IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference (WCNC), 2022, pp. 2727-2731; U. Demirhan and A. Alkhateeb, “Radar Aided 6G Beam Prediction: Deep Learning Algorithms and Real-World Demonstration,” 2022 IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference (WCNC), 2022, pp. 2655–2660), which demonstrated that multi-modal sensing, combined with machine learning, can effectively extract wireless channel information and map it to optimal mmWave beams in vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication scenarios. These findings suggest that sensing data from co-located sensors and mmWave systems can significantly reduce the beam training overhead in mmWave communication, with minimal impact on system performance.

articleTitle: Unprecedented Nightside Ionospheric Dynamics Observed by GOLD During the 10-11 May 2024 Gannon Storm
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: During the intense geomagnetic storm of May 10–11, 2024, NASA's Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk (GOLD) imager revealed unprecedented changes in the nightside ionosphere. One of the most striking observations was the poleward expansion of the Equatorial Ionization Anomaly (EIA). The northern and southern crests of the EIA extended significantly, reaching around 38°N and 35°S magnetic latitude (Mlat), respectively. This poleward movement indicated the presence of a super plasma fountain effect. The southern EIA crest moved at speeds up to 450 m/s over a broad longitudinal range and merged with the aurora australis. Additionally, the southern crest drifted westward, forming a distinctive ‘V’ shape near 400W, which coincided with the peak of geomagnetic activity at that longitude as it neared sunset.

articleTitle: The Continuing Contribution of Roger Lang to the Measurement of the Dielectric Constant of Sea Water
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Roger Lang has been a pioneer in the measurement of the dielectric constant of sea water to support microwave remote sensing of sea surface salinity. The dielectric constant is the parameter through which salinity and temperature enter microwave models for emission from the surface and an accurate model is critical for passive remote sensing.

articleTitle: Identifying Regions of Large Propagation Variability via Principal Component Analysis
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Many radar and radio-frequency (RF) communication systems operate within the first ~1000 m of altitude over the ocean surface, a region known as the marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL). The MABL is a highly complex environment due to the sharp gradients of humidity which varies radio refractivity, creating large deviations from “standard” propagation. These day-to-day or even hour-to-hour propagation variations are driven by refractive ducting features (i.e., evaporation, surface, and elevated ducts) which trap and carry RF energy at ranges farther than expected from the transmitter. Due to the highly dynamic nature of the MABL, refractive conditions, and thus EM propagation, vary on short timescales (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim O \ 10$</tex> minutes) and relatively small spatial scales <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\sim \ O \ 10 \ \text{km})$</tex>. An ongoing area of research is capturing these small-scale variations using numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts of refractivity input to RF propagation solvers. While high temporal resolution in refractivity forecasts is sometimes necessary, conditions can also remain relatively stable for hours or even days in certain geographic regions and seasons. Incentive for intelligently adapting to those time scales is high, because the prediction of RF propagation is computationally expensive. Whenever possible, it is desirable to use similar, previously predicted refractive environments and their associated propagation predictions. Doing so decreases computational load and frees up limited bandwidth and radar-operator resources.

articleTitle: Dual-Band Matching and Decoupling Network Design for Asymmetric Two-Element Antenna Arrays
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In-band full-duplex (IBFD) systems have the potential to significantly enhance spectral efficiency by allowing simultaneous transmit and receive on the same frequency. With rapid advancement of wireless communication technology, there is a growing demand for IBFD systems that support multi-band operation in various wireless applications. However, there have been very few simultaneous transmit and receive (STAR) designs for multi-band IBFD antennas, due to the increased complexity of the design problem. The main challenge lies in achieving two independently controlled operating bands while maintaining the high isolation between transmit and receive channels. A widely used solution for mitigating antenna coupling in IBFD systems is to use matching and decoupling networks (MDNs). While several previous works have focused on dual-band MDN designs for symmetric antenna arrays, the asymmetry in the antenna elements adds significant complexity to the design process. To the best of our knowledge, no previous work systematically addresses the design of dual-band MDNs for asymmetric two-element antenna arrays, or provides an analytical method for calculating the element values of such an MDN.

articleTitle: Evolving Antennas for Directional Radio Sensitivity
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This work presents a genetic algorithm that evolved antennas with specified directional sensitivity. The algorithm constructs antennas by combining geometric shapes like building blocks, where the fitness is determined by the directionality of the antenna's radiation pattern. This paper demonstrates that the algorithm is capable of evolving antennas towards maximizing gain in desirable directions while simultaneously minimizing gain in undesirable directions for single-frequency (300 MHz) and broadband (200 MHz to 800 MHz) applications.

articleTitle: An Analysis Framework of Supplemental Coverage from Space (SCS) and Radio Astronomy System (RAS) Interference
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Low earth orbit (LEO) satellites have become a growing component of commercial radiocommunications over the last decade and are considered by some to be an integral part of 5G and beyond radiocommunication development (Xie, H.; Zhan, Y.; Zeng, G.; Pan, X. “LEO mega-constellations for 6G global coverage: Challenges and opportunities.” IEEE Access 2021,9, 164223–164244). The potential of a satellite constellation to bridge the digital divide is enormous, as providing service to any location is as easy as pointing a phased array beam at the desired location. However, this advantage of LEO satellites poses a risk of radiofrequency interference to radioastronomy systems (RASs) that have historically relied on the choice of remote locations for part of their interference protection.

articleTitle: Mitigating Mutual Coupling in an Antenna Array in the Digital Domain
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The impact of mutual coupling on the performance of antenna arrays can be significant as it can alter active impedance and the radiation patterns of embedded elements. This paper introduces an effective method for mitigating mutual coupling in the digital domain using Virtual Load Theory (VLT). Instead of real-time impedance adjustments, VLT utilizes precomputed compensation coefficients derived from the array's impedance (Z) or scattering (S) matrices. These frequency-domain matrices are then applied to the input signal vector, effectively decoupling antenna elements and restoring their Embedded Element Patterns (EEPs) as standalone elements within the array. Simulations of monopole and dipole arrays show that VLT significantly reduces mutual coupling, thereby enhancing the overall system performance.

articleTitle: Reference HOPS Calibration Pipeline for the Event Horizon Telescope
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a global network of millimetre and sub-millimetre wave radio tele-scopes that has produced the first resolved images of the supermassive black holes M87 and Sgr A* using Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). The EHT-HOPS calibration pipeline extends the capabilities of the Haystack Observatory Postprocessing System (HOPS) with routines specific to the reduction of EHT observations (L. Blackburn et al., 2019, ApJ, 882, 23). We present a new version of the EHT-HOPS pipeline which has been refactored with a goal to calibrate multiple years of EHT data and observations from similar VLBI arrays, providing reference calibrated data products under a common automated framework.

articleTitle: Miniaturized, Tri-Band (2.4 GHz, 5.2 GHz, and 5.8 GHz), and Self-Matched Antenna Design for Future Earbud Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Wireless earbuds have been widely popular since their launch due to their convenient design, and enhanced mobility for body wearable applications. Bluetooth (2.4 GHz to 2.4835 GHz) has been a standard technology adopted for wireless earbuds until now, however, it comes with its limitations. Wireless earbuds lack features such as high-resolution audio, simultaneous connection with more than one device, enhanced spatial sound technology implementation, and generally suffers from a limited amount of bandwidth. Moreover, mobile phones nowadays are already utilizing higher frequency bands like Ultra Wide Band (UWB), Wireless Fidelity 6 GHz Band (Wi-Fi 6E), and Near Field Communication (NFC) for various applications such as device location tracking, augmented reality, low latency gaming, improved network performance, and features such as NFC tags, and tap-to-pay. This gap can be filled by the implementation of multi-band wireless earbuds by the use of higher frequency bands such as the Unlicensed National Information Infrastructure (UNII) bands, mainly UNII-1 (5.150 GHz to 5.250 GHz) and UNII-3 (5.725 GHz to 5.850 GHz). The 5 GHz UNII bands offer more non-overlapping channels compared to the 2.4 GHz band and thus experience less congestion and interference from non-Wi-Fi devices while supporting higher data rates. The aforementioned UNII bands have a higher prescribed Effective Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) as regulated by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), e.g., UNII 1 (EIRP of 1W for client device and 4W for master device) and UNII 3 (maximum EIRP of 4W). A higher EIRP allows for a larger coverage distance, stronger signal strength, better penetration in urban environments, and improved link margins. The integration of a new radiating element into the earbuds to support the additional UNII bands can help offer the higher data rate required for hi-resolution audio, distinguish and deliver time-sensitive notifications and alerts from different devices through the earbuds as part of an extended Internet-of-Things (IoT) environment, and help create a new realm of applications that have not been envisioned yet for an earbud use case. The development of new integrated chips in the coming years to support this infrastructure can help create a new area of applications for wireless earbuds.

articleTitle: A Prototype Millimeter-Wave Reflectionless Diplexer Based on Silicon Micromachining
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Millimeter and submillimeter wave instrumentation operating above 100 GHz typically utilizes rectangular waveguide as the primary propagation medium and, consequently, is limited to operation over restricted bands bound by the cut-off frequencies for single- mode propagation. Diplexers provide an option for overcoming the band limitations imposed by conventional waveguide-based instruments. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first implementation of a prototype “quasi-reflectionless” diplexer based on the reflectionless filter concept developed by Morgan, operating at millimeter-wave frequencies, and utilizing the integration of passive elements onto a silicon-on-insulator platform.

articleTitle: Two-Dimensional Radar Studies of Post-Midnight Equatorial F-Region Irregularity Development
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Since July 2021, new two-dimensional (2D) observations of ionospheric F-region irregularities have been made at the Jicamarca Radio Observatory (JRO) with a 14-panel version of the AMISR system (AMISR-14). AMISR-14 is configured to capture coherent backscatter echoes off centimeter scale size irregularities within a field of view (FoV) that extends, at F-region heights, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 400$</tex> km in the geomagnetic East-West direction. The wide FoV expands the observational capabilities of the JRO, allowing us to generate sequences of 2D images which unambiguously show the development of irregularities associated with equatorial spread F (ESF) events. We present and discuss results from our analyses of these 2D images to describe the development of post-midnight ESF events. The results include occurrence statistics/rates that distinguish between “local” and “non-local” post-midnight events.

articleTitle: Broadband Impedance Matching for Wearable Magnetoinductive Waveguides
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Magnetoinductive Waveguides (MIWs) consist of coupled electrically small resonant elements that support the propagation of magnetoinductive waves. By exciting current on an element, a magnetic field is formed, leading to the generation of current on neighboring elements via Faraday's Law. This pattern continues to form a traveling wave. MIWs have been used in wireless power transfer applications, sub-wavelength imaging setups, and as data communication media for applications such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or in challenging Radio-Frequency (RF) environments such as underground, underwater or on the body. In particular, our previous work has focused on their application to wireless body area networks (WBANs) that seamlessly interconnect wearable devices and sensors.

articleTitle: Reconfigurable Transmitarray Design with Generative Adversarial Network
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced innovative approaches for the design of metasurfaces, significantly reducing the reliance on traditional iterative analytical methods based on simulations. Numerous studies (e.g., S. An et al., “Deep Convolutional Neural Networks to Predict Mutual Coupling Effects in Metasurfaces”, Advanced Optical Materials, vol. 10, 2022) have demonstrated substantial advancements by leveraging various deep learning networks to address macroscopic-level challenges, such as beam steering, pattern optimization, and aperture efficiency enhancement. Conversely, there is a growing interest in employing generative AI algorithms to address the more intricate task of designing unit cells, which is crucial to achieving the desired electromagnetic (EM) surface properties (C. Niu et al., “A Diffusion Model for Multi-Layered Metasurface Unit Cell Synthesis”, IEEE Open Journal of Antennas and Propagation, vol. 4, 2023). This unit-cell-level design process has long been recognized as one of the most time-intensive aspects of metasurface development, primarily due to the extensive literature review and the iterative nature of the trial-and-error approach conventionally required for achieving optimal designs. At the meta-atom level, AI-based design methodologies are commonly applied to solve the inverse design problem, where the process begins with the desired surface performance and seeks to generate the appropriate unit-cell geometry. A notable example of this is the work of Sensong An et al. in “A Deep Learning Approach for Objective-Driven All-Dielectric Metasurface Design” (ACS Photonics, vol. 6, issue 12, Nov. 2019), which demonstrated the potential of AI to design passive metasurfaces in a matter of seconds by utilizing variants of generative adversarial networks (GANs) for the rapid and efficient creation of multifunctional passive designs. Reconfigurable metasurfaces with beam-steering capabilities, such as transmitarrays or reflectarrays, traditionally time-consuming to design, are also promising candidates for the application of AI-driven methods. However, unlike passive meta-atom designs, reconfigurable metasurfaces pose significant challenges for AI-based approaches. A major limitation is the difficulty in generating high-quality, effective datasets for training. Moreover, the active structures, which retain fixed geometrical configurations while representing different phase states (or electrical connections), introduce an added complexity in terms of dimensionality, further complicating the AI-based modeling and optimization processes. Nevertheless, it is of great interest to conduct a pilot study on the application of AI-based design approaches for reconfigurable transmitarrays/reflectarrays to evaluate any potential advantages they offer over conventional design techniques.

articleTitle: Reinforcement Learning Controlled Mechanically Reconfigurable Antennas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This work presents a mechanically reconfigurable antenna controlled with a reinforcement learning algorithm developed in an open-source simulation environment and then tested in real world conditions. The simulation is designed with knowledge of the beam characteristics of a low gain planar antenna and the physical range of movement restrictions of the system hardware to create an environment where reinforcement learning methods can be evaluated prior to hardware implementation. Final algorithm results and the results of real-world testing will be presented.

articleTitle: Assessing MR Safety of Cerebral Stents: Insights into RF-Induced Heating and Stent Orientation at 1.5 T and 3 T
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of patients with medical implants can lead to localized tissue heating, primarily due to the interaction of radiofrequency (RF) fields emitted by the RF coil of MRI machine. This heating around implants is quantified through specific absorption rate (SAR) and temperature rise, which can be assessed using Electromagnetic (EM) numerical simulations and in-system measurements. The extent of RF-induced heating varies significantly depending on the design, structure, physical dimensions, and resonant lengths of the implant, as well as its location and orientation within the human body. These variations highlight the complexity of predicting RF-induced heating in patients with different types of implants.

articleTitle: Remote Sensing of Humidity and Temperature from X-Band Radar Measurements in the Marine Atmospheric Surface Layer
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The propagation of electromagnetic (EM) waves at X-band frequencies within the marine atmospheric surface layer (MASL) are influenced by variations in the index of refraction of the air. Variations in the index of refraction cause changes in the direction of propagation of EM waves. In some cases, vertical variations in the index of refraction are significant enough to trap and carry the EM wave energy over longer distances relative to normal atmospheric conditions. The high degree of sensitivity of the EM wave propagation to the index of refraction makes it possible to perform inversions for vertical profiles of atmospheric refractivity based on radar measurements. In the MASL, which extends from the surface to tens of meters above the ocean surface, the index of refraction is sensitive to changes in atmospheric humidity and temperature, especially humidity. Vertical variations of humidity and temperature in the MASL can be significant and complex due to the water vapor and heat exchange with the ocean. Direct measurement of these variations is challenging because of the difficulty in making accurate profile measurements near the ocean surface (e.g., due to platform interference); yet, the vertical distributions of humidity and temperature within the MASL are important to climate science, weather forecasting, as well as a number of civil and military engineering applications. Thus, a remote method of obtaining highresolution vertical profiles of humidity and temperature in the MASL would enable advancement of related science and engineering applications.

articleTitle: Ducting Conditions During the 2024 REDSAW Campaign
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The lowest~100m of the atmosphere is known as the surface layer. Coincidentally, this layer is also the location of many of the U.S. Navy's surface-based sensor platforms. During stable surface layer conditions (determined by a positive air-sea temperature difference), surface layer evaporation duct models such as the Navy's Atmospheric Surface Layer Model (NAVSLaM) is unable to provide a solution. These conditions are often found in regions that are relevant to the U.S. Navy and therefore it is important to characterize the evaporation duct in all conditions to inform tactical decisions regarding radio frequency propagation in the lowest portions of the atmosphere. However, stable surface layers do not often persist for long periods of time, creating a challenge to design a measurement campaign focused on understanding them.

articleTitle: Superconducting Bolometric Detector Technology for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present the design, fabrication plan, and development of detector arrays for the CMB-S4 project. CMB-S4, led by the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation, aims to characterize the polarization of the cosmic microwave background with unprecedented precision. The project's goals include probing primordial gravitational waves, investigating cosmic inflation, exploring the universe's dark sector, studying its evolutionary history, and monitoring mm-wave sky transients.

articleTitle: Neural Network Prediction of Scattering Parameters Based on Voxel Mesh Representation
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In our work, we demonstrate a novel Neural Network (NN) based methodology for generating S-Parameters based on using the meshed and discretized geometry as input to the NN. Our approach would enable a designer to rapidly optimize the performance of vias across an entire substrate. This performance is possible while also achieving a computational time improvement of approximately double that in other NN-based works.

articleTitle: Compact Millimeter Wave Band Button Antenna Design for WBAN Off-Body Communication
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a novel millimeter-wave (mmWave) button antenna designed for off-body communication in Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs). The proposed antenna comprises a circular patch incorporating multiple slots to optimize performance. The antenna's results were investigated in free space and the presence of denim fabric, with measurements conducted on the chest and hand positions. The simulated and measured results demonstrate a satisfactory impedance bandwidth encompassing the 28 GHz mmWave band in all scenarios, with a consistent gain of 6.10 dBi. The radiation patterns indicate minimal influence of the fabric material, and the antenna maintains its broadside radiation. The design's compactness, good matching, stable gain, and good radiation characteristics make it suitable for integration into clothing and other wearable devices.

articleTitle: Towards Harsh Environment Silicon Carbide Based On-Chip Antenna
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents an on-chip dielectric resonator antenna (DRA) based on silicon carbide (SiC). SiC is a semiconductor material known for its large bandgap, high dielectric breakdown, and temperature-stable dielectric properties, making it well-suited for harsh environment electronics. We propose a DRA on a SiC substrate, incorporating a sapphire rectangular resonator bonded to the SiC chip. The fundamental TE111 mode is excited at 29.5 GHz within the resonator via a rectangular aperture on the SiC chip, which is fed by a coplanar waveguide (CPW). An inductive series stub at the feed is used for impedance matching. Simulation results demonstrate a high gain of 7.4 dBi with a radiation efficiency of 84%. Furthermore, we propose a custom probe station with an integrated hot plate and robotic arm for high-temperature testing of the DRA.

articleTitle: Laser Induced Fluorescence Measurements of Flow Velocity in a Rotating Plasma Layer
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Localized transverse electric fields are known to arise in the near-Earth plasma environment. These fields can induce plasma flows perpendicular to the ambient magnetic field and the resulting sheared flow layers can support a variety of plasma instabilities [1]. These phenomena have been the topic of extensive theoretical and experimental study both at the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) and within the broader scientific community. Numerous laboratory experiments have been performed in the Space Physics Simulation Chamber (SPSC) at NRL to study both the associated transverse velocity shear-driven instabilities [2] and, more recently, soliton generation by object immersed in these flows. Traditionally, these experiments have utilized cylindrical ExB flows produced by applying a radial electric field within a larger uniform domain of axial magnetic field. The resulting flow profiles have been determined indirectly from electric field measurements within the flow layer [3]. Recently, experiments have been performed in the SPSC to directly map the velocity distribution function (VDF) in cylindrical flow regions using laser induced fluorescence (LIF). Two co-axial arrays of concentric mesh rings are used to establish a cylindrical domain of plasma flow within the SPSC. The rings are sequentially biased so as to induce a constant radial electric field. The well-known 668.6138nm Ar II LIF scheme beginning with the 3d<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup><inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">F7</inf>/2 metastable state [4] is used to measure the VDF of argon ions, while laser injection and fluorescence collection are implemented using in-vacuum optics mounted to a linear positioning system with mutual focal points aligned to ~1 mm spatial resolution. The flow velocity is mapped as a function of both z and r, as well as with respect to the applied electric and magnetic fields. Preliminary results are compared to the flow velocity predicted indirectly via emissive probe measurements of the electric field, and ramifications of the chosen geometry are discussed.

articleTitle: Beam Maps of the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) Measured with a Drone
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present beam measurements of the CHIME telescope using a radio calibration source deployed on a drone payload. During test flights, the pulsing calibration source and the telescope were synchronized to GPS time, enabling in-situ background subtraction for the full N<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> visibility matrix for one CHIME cylindri- reflector. We use the autocorrelation products to estimate the primary beam width and centroid location, and compare these quantities to solar transit measurements and holographic measurements where they over- on the sky. We find that the drone, solar, and holography data have similar beam parameter evolution across frequency and both spatial coordinates. This paper presents the first drone-based beam measurement of a large cylindrical radio interferometer. Furthermore, the unique analysis and instrumentation described in this paper lays the foundation for near-field measurements of experiments like CHIME.

articleTitle: Using Beam Simulations to Model Mutual Coupling in the MWA Phase II Compact Array
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Measurement of the 21 cm emission of neutral hydrogen in the intergalactic medium probes the era of the first luminous objects and the era of the intergalactic medium becoming fully ionized by the first stars, the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). However, the 21 cm signal is orders of magnitude fainter than astrophysical foregrounds, as well as other sources of radio frequency interference, making it challenging to measure. It is therefore imperative that any instrumental systematic effects which could further distort spectral structure are properly understood and mitigated. Kolopanis et al. (2023) identified a systematic in Phase II data from the MWA which manifests as excess correlation in the 21 cm power spectrum. This introduces a bias that can make foregrounds couple into 21 cm background modes. The source of the systematic is not known but one possible cause is mutual coupling between antennas. There are multiple physical mechanisms which cause mutual coupling, but we have focused on re-radiation for this work. Re-radiation is caused by impedance mismatch at the antenna receiver which causes part of the sky signal to be reflected and re-radiate to the surrounding antennas. This can cause excess correlation in the resulting observation.

articleTitle: Experimental Generation of Biasing Voltage Distribution Along a RIS by Using Standing Wave Control
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A novel method for biasing varactors in a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) has been recently proposed, which uses standing waves on a transmission line (TL) to bias each RIS element, eliminating the need for a complex external biasing network (E. Ayanoglu, F. Capolino, and A. L. Swindlehurst, IEEE Wireless Comm., 29, 4, 86-92, 2022). This method consists of a TL board isolated from the RIS surface to avoid RF interference that supports <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex> resonant standing waves to bias <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex> varactors at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$x_{m}$</tex> with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m=1, \ldots, M$</tex>. Each varactor receives a dc voltage <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v(x_{m})$</tex>, measured at the output of the rectifier, determined by the sum of a base dc voltage, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$W_{0}$</tex>, and the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex> standing waves. This allows for a specific reflection phase distribution, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha_{m}$</tex>, to be created over the RIS to control the reflection pattern. The standing waves are generated using a single port, where a periodic time-domain signal is injected into the TL (M. Saavedra-Melo, K. Rouhi, and F. Capolino, IEEE AP-S/URSI, 2023). This method also uses a unit cell model (D. Hanna, M. Saavedra-Melo, F. Shan, and F. Capolino, IEEE AP-S/URSI, 2022) that accounts for a realistic reflection response of the unit cell, enhancing the method's accuracy.

articleTitle: Application of Weyl Symbol Calculus for Quasilinear Modeling of Waves in Plasmas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Plasmas are fascinatingly complex as dispersive media in that they support a wide variety of waves and these waves can significantly evolve due to background inhomogeneities and nonlinear interactions. This necessitates a particularly systematic approach to wave theory. It has long been recognized that phase-space methods from quantum physics, particularly Weyl symbol calculus and metaplectic transforms, can serve as a foundation for such an approach to classical waves (E. R. Tracy et al., “Ray Tracing and Beyond” (Cambridge Univ. Press, 2014)). These methods have proven useful for reduced modeling of linear-wave propagation and mode conversion in inhomogeneous media. As it turns out, though, they are also helpful for modeling quasilinear (QL) wave effects, specifically, QL diffusion, ponderomotive forces, and structure formation in wave turbulence.

articleTitle: Efficient Use of the Frequency Spectrum and Secure Communications in Consideration to Antenna Design
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In the modern era of wireless communications, particularly as we transition from current communication technologies to 5G and beyond (6G), the efficient use of the frequency spectrum and secure communication are crucial topics. One way to achieve efficient spectrum use is through polarization reconfiguration in antennas, allowing the same frequency bandwidth to be utilized more effectively. Additionally, incorporating frequency reconfiguration, agility, or tunability into antenna designs can further optimize spectrum usage by enabling different applications to share the same frequency band simultaneously. Combining polarization reconfiguration with frequency reconfiguration or agility can enhance spectrum efficiency even further. Moreover, integrating radiation pattern reconfiguration into antenna designs enables a single antenna to offer various radiation patterns within the same frequency spectrum. Again, combining polarization and radiation pattern reconfiguration can result in additional spectrum efficiency gains. Multiple-Input-Multiple-Output (MIMO) antennas and massive arrays are another approach that maximizes spectrum efficiency by delivering high data throughput within a limited frequency bandwidth. Recent research into Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) with polarization and frequency reconfiguration capabilities also demonstrates notable improvements in spectrum utilization. Antennas that support multiple radiating modes offer additional benefits by providing various radiation patterns to meet specific communication needs. For secure communications, null steering antennas (also known as anti-jamming antennas) or antennas with sidelobe and grating lobe control are effective solutions. In this talk, we will showcase several examples of these advanced antenna technologies, drawn both from the presenter's research group and published literature highlighting efficient use of the frequency spectrum and secure communications.

articleTitle: 37 GHz Low-Profile Wideband Antenna with High-Gain Characteristics for Next-Generation Networks
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The expanding demand for high-capacity, ultra-fast wireless communications in emerging 6 G networks has accelerated. As new technologies develop, the need for antennas that provide high bandwidth and gain is critical. The Ka-band (26.5 GHz–40 GHz) has become an essential frequency range for future wireless communication applications, including phone-to-satellite communications. However, achieving both high bandwidth and good gain in a compact, low-profile antenna structure remains a significant challenge. Patch antenna arrays are typically narrowband and often require improved performance in terms of gain.

articleTitle: Plasma Impedance Probes and E Field Sensor Instabilities: Two Sides of the Same Coin
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The design and implementation of double probe electric field sensors and plasma impedance probes for space and laboratory plasma applications has a long and successful history spanning nearly 60 years. While at times the two techniques and communities have overlapped - sharing antennas, spacecraft, or laboratory chambers - the designs and lessons learned by each community have in general remained distinct. Recent laboratory work has clarified and reinforced the connections between these two techniques as they relate in particular to the source and control of electric field sensor instabilities in the heliospheric plasma environment, and to probe-plasma interactions in general.

articleTitle: Using Meter-Wavelength Lunar Polarimetry to Determine the Accuracy of Estimates of the Ionospheric Faraday Rotation Measure
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Earth's magnetized ionosphere causes a rotation of the plane of polarization of propagating radio radiation due to the phenomenon of Faraday rotation. The amount of rotation is given by Δ θ= IFRMλ2 radians, where IFRM is the ionospheric Faraday rotation measure in rad/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, and λ is the wavelength in meters. Typical IFRM values are from 0.5 to 2 rad/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, while values as high as 6 rad/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> during periods of greater solar activity are common. These IFRM values are highly variable, with changes occurring on timescales from hours to minutes.

articleTitle: Pulsar Detection Performance Using Oversampled Spectrometer: Preliminary Indications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Advanced L-Band Phased Array Feed for Astronomy (ALPACA) implements a two-stage “zoom” spectrom-eter to support multiple scientific modes. The first stage coarse spectrometer must be oversampled to avoid spectral degradation near band edges in the second stage fine spectrometer outputs used for HI mode observations. For pulsar studies, however, preliminary results show that using oversampled data may cause a loss of sensitivity in the parameter estimation used by the pulsar search algorithm. To overcome the sensitivity loss, we will implement a resampler following the coarse filterbank to provide critically sampled data when ALPACA is in pulsar search mode.

articleTitle: Storm Chasing with the INCUS Mission
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The overarching goal of the NASA INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) mission is to enhance our understanding of why, when and where tropical convective storms form, and why only some of these storms produce extreme weather. Convective storms transport air and water between Earth's surface and the upper troposphere. This vertical transport of air and water - often referred to as convective mass flux (CMF) - plays a critical role in Earth's weather and climate system through its impacts on large-scale atmospheric circulations, upper tropospheric moistening and high cloud-radiative feedbacks, precipitation rates, and extreme weather. Potential changes to CMF with changing climates may significantly impact these processes. In spite of the critical role of this vertical transport of water and air, representation of CMF remains a major source of error in weather and climate models, thereby limiting our ability to accurately predict convective storms and their impacts in current and future climates. The observations obtained from INCUS will enhance our understanding of tropical convective storm processes and provide guidance for representing these processes in weather and climate models.

articleTitle: Preserving the Shielded Zone of the Moon for Radio Astronomy
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The scientific reach of radio astronomy endeavors on the Earth's surface is severely restricted by heavy spectrum use for radiocommunications among other active services. Protection afforded to radio astronomy by the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) is limited. Historically, the 1420 MHz neutral hydrogen line has enjoyed longstanding protection. While this is one of the most important emission lines for astronomy, modern astronomical telescopes passively access a much broader range of spectrum in order to achieve their science goals. Traditionally, to access this broad spectrum, astronomers have sited their telescopes in remote locations free from terrestrial emissions. However, with the rise of large constellations of satellites for broadband internet, even these remote Earth-based sites are no longer radio quiet. The shielded zone of the moon (SZM) provides a new frontier for radio astronomy with its uniquely radio quiet environment, shielded from Earth-based transmissions across the full electromagnetic spectrum. Additionally, the lack of a lunar ionosphere as well as the lack of appreciable water vapor and oxygen in the lunar environment enables scientific observations that are not possible from Earth. For these reasons, radio telescopes located in the SZM have the potential to provide the most robust measurements of the evolution of structure in the universe. Scientific endeavor in this region is already well underway; NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program delivered the Radiowave Observations at the Lunar Surface of the photoelectron Sheath (ROLSES) to the lunar south pole on February 22, 2024. A number of other radio astronomy missions for the lunar far side have also been proposed and are expected to be carried out well within the next decade.

articleTitle: Quantum Geometry and Transport in Cold Magnetized Plasmas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The structure of the complex projective space for the physical states of a quantum system leads to a natural definition of distance between two quantum states. When the states are indexed by a continuous parameter, such as a wave vector, the distance between quantum states can be related to the distance in parameter space via a complex tensor, the quantum geometric tensor Q. The imaginary part of Q is the well-known Berry curvature whereas the real part is the quantum metric g. In the past two decades a lot of work in condensed matter physics has focused on the effects of the Berry curvature, and, in particular, on the study of the topological phases that can arise due to it. In recent years topological phases and the associated topologically protected edge states, have also been identified in cold-magnetized plasmas. However, the effects arising from the real part of Q, the quantum metric, have so far received much less attention. In this talk we will first give a brief overview of the concept of quantum geometry and its relevance for physical quantities in condensed matter systems. Next we will discuss how, in general, the imaginary part of Q is related to transverse transport properties whereas the real part is related to longitudinal transport properties and nonlinear responses to external fields. We will then present the relevance of quantum geometry for cold magnetized plasmas, and the possible connection between quantum metric, transport properties, and nonlinear responses in these systems.

articleTitle: Large Aperture Telescope High-Throughput Receiver Design
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present the design and development for the receiver for the large aperture telescope (LATs) for the CMB-S4 experiment. The CMB-S4 experiment aims to make measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) with an unprecedented combination of sensitivity, sky area, and angular resolution. The resultant measurements will lead to new discoveries across astrophysics and cosmology, including placing new constraints on cosmic Inflation, the physics of the dark universe, the spatial distribution of matter, and the time-variable millimeter-wavelength sky.

articleTitle: Dynamics of Quantized Signals in Random Media: A Transport Theoretic Model
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: With increased availability of a wide range of good quality sources and receivers of quantized signals, remote sensing of long standoff objects with quantized signals has become a viable reality. This necessitates adequate understanding of the impact of channel fluctuations on quantized signals. In this paper we present a transport theoretic model for this problem.

articleTitle: Overview of Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Division (NSWCDD) Execution of Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in the Stable Atmosphere over Water (REDSAW) Experiment at the Salton Sea, California
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Division (NSWCDD) designed, constructed, and deployed a Radio Frequency (RF) Path Loss Measurement System (PLMS) in support of the Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in the Stable Atmosphere over Water (REDSAW) experiment. The REDSAW experiment was performed overwater in the Salton Sea, California where the goal was to characterize atmospheric effects on RF propagation within a thermally stable boundary layer, with a focus on identification and assessment of evaporation ducting, relative to surface layer modeling utilizing Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory (MOST). Evaporation ducts are a surface layer phenomenon that are difficult to directly measure but have a well-documented effect on RF propagation and are commonly modeled with MOST. However, assumptions in MOST based surface layer models are violated in stable surface layers regimes, which is a common occurrence in the Salton Sea, and can be easily covered by a stable boundary layer.

articleTitle: Performance Showdown: Rydberg Sensors vs. Electrically Small Antennas
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: There is a growing need to develop novel technologies that can enable resilient spectrum operations in complex electromagnetic environments. Traditional antenna-based receivers have limitations in tunability and require specialized filters to reject broadband noise. Rydberg atom electric field sensors are quantum sensors that have a fundamentally different principle of operation than traditional antenna-based receivers. Lasers are used to excite atoms to high-energy Rydberg states, where the atoms behave as electric dipoles and can transduce information from an incident RF field onto the lasers passing through the atoms. These sensors offer ultra-wideband tunability with a single small-size sensing element and provide intrinsic filtering of broadband noise due to the narrowband atomic response. Due to these qualities, these sensors have generated substantial interest for reception at longer wavelengths where their small size compares favorably to impedance-matched antennas.

articleTitle: Unconditionally Stable Time-Marching for Numerical Modeling of Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: While superconducting qubits are one of the most mature technologies for quantum computing, significant scaling is required before they can solve relevant problems. However, the scalability of current superconducting quantum processor designs is limited by the requirement of external interfaces for controlling and measuring each individual qubit. One method to consolidate these external connections is multiplexed readout, where state measurement of multiple qubits can be performed simultaneously using a single readout chain. Enabling multiplexed readout requires using an ultralow-noise amplifier with wide bandwidth, such as a Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier (JTWPA). Despite their promising characteristics, widespread adoption of JTWPAs is inhibited by lackluster accuracy in their fabrication process, which causes critical parameter values to vary substantially across each amplifier. As a result, the performance of individual realizations of a single JTWPA design are wildly inconsistent. To aid designers in addressing that issue, we previously developed a finite element time domain (FETD) based method capable of incorporating arbitrary variations in JTWPA components (S. T. Elkin, M. Haider, and T. E. Roth, “Multiphysics numerical method for modeling Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers,” IEEE Journal on Multiscale and Multiphysics Computational Techniques, vol. 9, pp. 247–257, Jul 2024). That approach used leap-frog time-marching to condense the contributions of nonlinear components into an auxiliary equation, enabling a linear matrix evaluation. While this produced accurate results, it could not enable unconditionally stable time-marching, which is of critical importance for future efforts in full-wave modeling of highly multiscale JTWPAs. Further, the approximate nature of leap-frogging accelerated the growth of late-time instability, requiring the use of specialized methods to counteract this behavior. Here, we develop an alternative approach using the Newton-Raphson method to directly model the nonlinear components. In this method, techniques for modeling nonlinear circuit elements in FETD are utilized to couple those components into the EM system (R. Wang and J.-M. Jin, “A symmetric electromagnetic-circuit simulator based on the extended time-domain finite element method,” IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, vol. 56, no. 12, pp. 2875–2884, 2008). The formulation is amenable to Newmark-beta time-marching, guaranteeing unconditional stability. Further, exact treatment of the nonlinearity inhibits the growth of late-time instability. In Fig. 1, we show strong agreement with an analytical method and our prior leap-frogging method using this approach to simulate a JTWPA.

articleTitle: Mapping the Spatial Distribution of the Auroral Electrojet at HAARP
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: During the 2024 Polar Aeronomy and Radio Science (PARS) summer school held by the University of Alaska Fairbanks, the University of Florida (UF) Ionospheric Radio Lab (IRL) performed a variety of very low frequency (VLF) wave generation experiments. These experiments were performed using the High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program's (HAARP) Ionospheric Research Instrument (IRI). VLF wave generation experiments using the IRI have an extensive history within ionospheric research and our lab (Moore 2007). The focus of this abstract is an experiment that attempts to utilize the VLF suppression effects due to simultaneous heating observed by Moore and Agrawal (Moore 2011) to quantify the contribution of source regions in the auroral electrojet.

articleTitle: ULF Waves in the Subauroral Geospace
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The mesoscale electric field is generated in the nightside equatorial magnetosphere near the plasmapause by the penetration of injected mesoscale plasma flows (MPFs) into the plasmasphere. Once created in the equatorial magnetosphere, the field penetrates into the ionosphere and produces there subauroral polarization streams (SAPS), subauroral ion drifts (SAID), strong thermal emission velocity enhancement (STEVE), stable auroral red (SAR) arcs, and dawnside auroral polarization streams (DAPS). It also drives the Ionospheric Feedback Instability (IFI) generating and amplifying small-scale ULF waves and fieldaligned currents standing along the subauroral magnetic field lines. These fields and currents modify parameters of the ionospheric plasma density and cause field-aligned irregularities and various plasma structures in the ionospheric E and F regions.

articleTitle: Solution of Radiative Transfer Equation for Plane-Parallel Medium Using a Discontinuous Galerkin Method and Adaptive Mesh Refinement
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The discontinuous Galerkin (DG) finite element method (FEM) is employed to solve the radiative transfer equation (RTE) for plane-parallel problems, utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) techniques. In this approach, both spatial and angular directions are discretized using the DG method. This study specifically investigates the impact of AMR on the spatial variability of radiative intensity, aiming to enhance accuracy where it is most needed. To guide mesh refinement, the L-infinity norm is applied for error estimation.
