The space-angle DG method combined with AMR proves to be highly effective, providing accurate and efficient resolution of radiative heat transfer, particularly in regions that require more precise and accurate solutions.

articleTitle: Numerical Optimization of a 3D Multilayer Dielectric Geometry for MRI Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: High-Permittivity Materials (HPM) are used in MRI to improve the radiofrequency <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B 1$</tex> field, resulting in an increase of the SNR and of the transmit efficiency in the tissues. In a previous study, it was shown that the field can be enhanced even more when, instead of a single HPM layer, a multilayer dielectric structure is used. This result was obtained with the optimization of the permittivity of the HPM layers with the fields calculated with a 2D cylindrical analytical solution. Since analytical solutions represent geometries that are not very heterogeneous and complex such as human tissues, in this study we have repeated the optimization with data computed with 3D numerical simulations. The fields were transmitted with a dipole to excite the head of a numerical body model surrounded by spherical dielectric shells. This study confirms that multilayer dielectric shells can enhance the field even more than a single HPM layer, with the improvement quantified as about 6.5 %. However, even if multilayer solutions can enhance the signal, their construction could face manufacturing challenges.

articleTitle: High Power Breakdown Effects in Microwave Components in the Titan Atmosphere
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Saturn's largest moon Titan is characterized as an ocean world with a dense atmosphere. The atmosphere supports hydrological processes that occur on our own planet such as the formation of clouds and rain, and is of great interest to planetary scientists to help uncover fundamental mysteries in early chemical processes. In order to aid scientists in new discoveries of Titan, NASA has funded an ambitious mission, Dragonfly, to explore this moon via a rotorcraft concept, as shown in Fig. 1. The rotorcraft will traverse Titan and land in several locations of interests. The science data will be transmitted from the surface of Titan directly to Earth, a challenging link due to the low angle between Titan and Earth and the proximity of the rotorcraft lander to the ground, leading to transmission fading due to multipath. To overcome these challenges, the telecommunications system utilizes a high-power Traveling Wave Tube Amplifier (TWTA), operating at X-Band. The 100 W TWTA coupled with a dense atmosphere that is not deterministic in its properties (pressure, temperature etc.) increases the susceptibility of ionization breakdown in components from its' output all the way to the antennas.

articleTitle: CPW Fed 28/38 GHz Dual Band Metasurface Flexible MIMO Antenna for Wearable Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a four element dual-band multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) antenna design operating at 28/38 GHz for millimeter wave wearable applications. The antenna incorporates a metasurface-inspired structure on its upper surface and utilizes a coplanar waveguide (CPW) feeding method. The design achieved a high level of isolation exceeding -20 dB between the inter-elements at both frequencies, with minimal impact from bending on the performance. A gain of 5.52 dBi with dual beam characteristics was attained. The MIMO antenna exhibited favorable envelope correlation coefficient (ECC) values below 0.01 and diversity gain (DG) exceeding 9.9 dB at both resonance frequencies. This approach of integrating metasurface with CPW fed in the design of flexible MIMO antennas demonstrates potential applications in wearable devices.

articleTitle: CMB-S4 Feedhorn and Focal Plane Assembly Design
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) offers an unparalleled window into the earliest moments of the universe and its subsequent evolution, including inflation, relativistic particles beyond the standard model, dark energy, dark matter, and neutrino properties. CMB-S4 is a next-generation CMB project that will reach critical thresholds in understanding the fundamental physics of the universe. CMB-S4 is designed to observe the CMB with an unprecedented combination of sky area, depth, and angular resolution across six bands spanning 17–315 GHz.

articleTitle: Precise Small-Scale System Tracking Using Angle of Arrival and Time Stamping Technology and its Use in Guiding Distributed Coherent Beamforming
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a high-accuracy localization system based on Phase Difference of Arrival (PDoA) technology using Decawave Ultra-Wideband (UWB) transceivers. The system leverages multiple antennas and the PDoA technique to estimate the Angle of Arrival (AoA) of wireless signals for real-time location tracking in 3D space. The system determines the direction of incoming signals by measuring the phase difference of incoming signals at two spatially separated antennas and applying the derived PDoA calculation formula. UWB signals offer high time resolution and resistance to multipath interference. Using eqn. (1) and other supporting calculations the location of the source can be estimated with the use of the proposed system.

articleTitle: Co-Site Interference Mitigation in Full-Duplex HF Antenna Arrays Employing Electronically Reconfigurable Impedance Matching and Decoupling Networks
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Co-site radio frequency (RF) interference often occurs when several RF transceivers operate in the vicinity of each other. It can degrade communication quality, particularly when a high-power transmitter is working near a receiver attempting to detect a low-power signal. Co-site interference can be particularly troublesome in the HF band (3–30 MHz) where the wavelengths of electromagnetic waves are large (10–100 m) and large antennas are often needed. The near-field regions of such antennas can extend to long distances away from them encompassing other nearby antennas and transceivers. This close proximity exacerbates the co-site interference issues among different antennas mounted on the same platform. Some traditional methods commonly used to reduce co-site interference are less effective at the HF band. For instance, mechanically movable antennas with directional radiation patterns are harder to realize at HF where real estate on platforms is generally very limited. Moreover, HF communications and over-the-horizon radar systems often experience changes in the HF propagation channel as a function of the time of the day, season, locations of the transmitter/receiver, etc. These changes require the frequency of operation within the 3–30 MHz frequency range to vary over the course of a single day. This frequency agility requirement makes it more challenging to use a fixed frequency allocation strategy for different transceivers to minimize interference. Additionally, fixed filters or other passive interference mitigation techniques have a limited application in such frequency agile applications. Finally, the radiated power levels of many HF systems range from tens to hundreds of Watts for communications systems to kW power levels for over-the-horizon radar systems. In such situations, out-of-band interference caused by high-power emissions of powerful transmitters can cause significant problems to nearby receivers, if not attenuated sufficiently.

articleTitle: Using Plasma Clouds Produced by Dust Impacts on Parker Solar Probe to Search for Anomalous Dust Populations in the Inner Heliosphere
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The densest and most dynamic portion of the zodiacal dust cloud is Sunward of 1 AU. In this region, alpha meteoroids migrating sunward via Poynting-Robertson drag become dense enough for frequent collisions, outward propagating beta meteoroids are created, and dust grains can be efficiently sputtered and sublimated. Finally, the dust trails of comets and asteroids with perihelia under 1 AU stream through this region.

articleTitle: Mutual Coupling Study of Full-Duplex Arrays
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In-band full-duplex (IBFD) phased arrays not only allow for the concurrent use of frequency spectrum, but can also facilitate applications sharing common hardware for directional radiation. These systems require the suppression of both self- and cross-talk interference, which are both influenced by the mutual coupling between elements within the array. This paper presents a study of mutual coupling for linear arrays with patch elements designed to operate at 3.0 GHz. The differences between E- and H-plane coupling as well as a coupling-reduction technique are discussed and simulation results are presented with the intention that this study can inform the design of scalable IBFD arrays.

articleTitle: Comparative Analysis of the Great American Solar Eclipses Data Obtained with the Transportable Dynasonde System
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Dynasonde is uniquely positioned for performing ionospheric observations in the complex environment of a solar eclipse (for a summary of capabilities and additional references see [Zabotin et al., 2017, doi: 1 0.23919/URSIGASS.20 17.8105216]). The technique does not depend on weather and sunlight conditions and may operate continuously and cost-efficiently for any required periods of time. And now, thanks to the AFOSR/DURIP program, we have an implementation of the Dynasonde technique in the Transportable Dynasonde System (TDS), which allows applications of this technique in locations of choice. While ionospheric effects caused by partial solar eclipses can be observed in a broad area, locations within the total eclipse path provide the most favorable conditions for observations.

articleTitle: Development of the SESAR-LITE P-band Synthetic Aperture Radar
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: SESAR-LITE (Space Exploration Synthetic Aperture Radar - Lunar Investigations Targeted Experiment) is lightweight and compact P-band (70 cm wavelength) polarimetric synthetic aperture radar (SAR) being developed at the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). The radar uses a compact deployable antenna, distributed RF electronics, and multi-channel digital processing system to enable a set of focused lunar science and exploration goals called for by the Artemis program. The radar will be capable of measuring the upper 10 m of the lunar subsurface at full polarimetry and at meter-scale resolution, revealing its structure and stratigraphy. These measurements can be used to characterize the physical properties of regolith, locate buried water ice, evaluate landing sites, and identify human-habitable regions of scientific interest, including lava tubes that can potentially serve as shelters for future human explorers.

articleTitle: A Preliminary Comparison of Fast Techniques to Monte Carlo Techniques for Aggregate Modelling
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Wireless engineers have a wide range of readily available tools for constructing frequency-selective systems. For this reason, the traditional way of having different radio frequency (RF) systems operating in the same geographic area is to put them on separate frequency channels, requiring each system to be allocated its own spectrum. With the proliferation of broadband communications devices, the demand for spectrum has become increasingly intense, with multiple services often wanting access to the same bands. This has fueled interest in the concept of spectrum sharing. Under this approach, different systems use the same frequencies, but are managed in such a way that none of them harmfully interferes with another. It is impossible to eliminate all interference issues, but it is generally understood that for all systems to operate effectively and reliably, interference events should be rare.

articleTitle: Reflection by a Coated Parabolic-Cylinder Mirror
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: An exact solution is obtained in closed form for the two-dimensional problem of axial scattering by a coated perfectly conducting (PEC) parabolic-cylinder mirror. The mirror is immersed in a medium that is linear, homogeneous, lossless and isotropic. The coating is made of a lossless, linear, homogeneous and isotropic material that is either isorefractive or anti-isorefractive to the surrounding medium. The boundary separating the coating layer from the surrounding medium is a parabolic-cylinder interface that is confocal to the parabolic-cylinder surface of the PEC mirror. Both cases of incidence on the convex and concave sides of the mirror are considered. The analysis is conducted in the phasor domain with a time-dependence factor <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\exp(+\mathrm{j}\omega\mathrm{t})$</tex> omitted throughout.

articleTitle: Cyclic Spectroscopy in Present and Upcoming Radio Telescope Data
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio pulsar signals are significantly perturbed by their propagation through the ionized interstellar medium. In addition to the frequency-dependent pulse times of arrival due to dispersion, pulse shapes are also distorted and shifted, having been scattered by the inhomogeneous interstellar plasma which affects pulse arrival times. Understanding the degree to which scattering affects pulsar timing is important for gravitational-wave detection with pulsar timing arrays (PTAs), which depend on the reliability of pulsars as stable clocks with an uncertainty of ~ 100 ns or less over ~ 10 yr or more. Scattering can be described as a convolution of the intrinsic pulse shape with an impulse response function representing the effects of multipath propagation. Cyclic spectroscopy has been applied to pulsar signals to deconvolve the effects of scattering from the original emitted signals, increasing the overall timing precision. We present an analysis of simulated data to test the quality of deconvolution using cyclic spectroscopy over a range of parameters characterizing interstellar scattering and pulsar signal-to-noise ratio (S/N). We show that cyclic spectroscopy is most effective for high S/N and/or highly scattered pulsars. We conclude that cyclic spectroscopy could play an important role in scattering correction to distant populations of highly scattered pulsars not currently included in PTAs. For future telescopes and for current instruments such as the Green Bank Telescope upgraded with the ultrawide bandwidth receiver, cyclic spectroscopy could significantly increase the number of PTA-quality pulsars. As full deconvolution is computationally expensive, other approaches to cyclic spectroscopy that do not require full deconvolution are also discussed.

articleTitle: Realtime Geospatial Spectrum Sharing between Earth Exploration Satellite Services and Communication Networks via Geofencing of co-operative 5G/6G transmitters
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Real-time Geo-fencing for Spectrum Sharing (RGSS) is a dynamic, software driven spatiotemporal sharing mechanism which utilises the orbital motion of the EESS satellites relative to the ground, and the rotational motion of the instrument scan-head; in order to automatically schedule cessation of interfering transmissions by co-operative terrestrial 5G/6G networks, during “dark times”. Statistics of the “dark time” periods, for a chosen location within the contiguous US, incorporating - inter alia - duration, and period of recurrence - across all currently operational satellite radiometers; and a demonstration of the RGSS via a web-based API front-end are presented.

articleTitle: Simulating Linear Plasma Waves on Quantum Computers
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Universal quantum computers lend researchers the ability to simulate evolution of physical systems that may otherwise be hard to simulate classically. In particular, approximate time evolution with local lattice spin models is naturally realized with layers of quantum gates on a quantum computer. Here, we develop a local one-dimensional lattice spin model to simulate linear wave phenomena, and use it to study reflection and transmission of plasma waves at a sharp boundary, and propagation of waves through an inhomogeneous plasma. Our quantum simulation maps N spatial lattice points to N qubits, which enables the realization of the spin model with nearest-neighbor connectivity and modest circuit depth, thus making it suitable for current noisy quantum devices.

articleTitle: Cylindrical Dielectric Resonator Antenna Providing Pattern Diversity Using Higher-Order Modes
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Recent advancements in multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) and diversity technologies have significantly improved the data throughput, robustness, and resilience of wireless communication systems. Diversity antennas are particularly crucial in contemporary wireless systems, as they effectively mitigate fading effects and enhance channel capacity without necessitating additional spectrum or power resources. There are three primary types of diversity antennas: spatial, polarization, and pattern diversity. Among these, pattern-diversity antennas are generally more complex to design compared to the other two types. This complexity arises because achieving different radiation patterns requires exciting the antenna in different resonant modes, which often correspond to different frequencies. Most prior works that investigated pattern diversity in dielectric resonator antennas (DRAs) focus on analyzing the electric field of fundamental modes in cylindrical dielectric resonators, such as HEM <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$11\delta, \text{TM}_{01\delta}$</tex> as well as higher-order modes like TM<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">l1</inf> or <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$HEM12\delta$</tex>. The goal is to modify the radiating structure such that the dominant electric field distribution of these modes does not significantly interfere with each other. While exciting higher-order modes can potentially enhance antenna gains, to the best of our knowledge, this approach has not yet been thoroughly investigated due to the complexity of the electric field distributions of such modes.

articleTitle: In-Situ Voltage and Current Assessment for Transmission of Signals with Bandwidth
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: With the wireless spectrum becoming increasingly congested and contested many transmitter systems will need to be designed with frequency-sharing capabilities. These capabilities can include frequency hopping, changing array transmission angles, and reconfigurable hardware. An adaptive system with these capabilities requires a control system to determine the optimal configuration for different transmission states. For a very simple system, it is possible to store the optimal configuration of each transmission state before deployment, but most systems will require an in-situ feedback mechanism to optimize performance while in use.

articleTitle: Space-Borne Doppler Weather Radar Modeling for Radar Design Evaluation
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A model has been developed to predict the reflectivity and Doppler performance of a spaceborne weather radar for atmospheric aerosol and cloud monitoring. The goal is to predict radar sensitivity, resolution, uncertainties and other key performance metrics vs. radar design parameters and hardware nonidealities. Analytical formulas are readily available to predict key performance metrics of a space-borne radar system as a function of design parameters such as antenna size, spacecraft velocity, transmit power, and receive noise figure. Effects of some system nonidealities such as antenna pointing errors, power amplifier nonlinearity and phase noise can be estimated using idealized methods. These analytical formulas use idealized forms of the antenna radiation pattern and weather statistics to predict system performance. However, it is desirable to have a more physical model based on discretized weather volumes in which the particle size distribution, Doppler distribution, and other parameters can be varied to study how the radar hardware design parameters and nonidealities affect the measurement of the weather reflectivity and Doppler characteristics. This would allow the radar designers to have more insight into what is being measured and the hardware parameters and errors that need to be carefully controlled to achieve best radar performance, as well as potential methods to calibrate the system or correct errors.

articleTitle: Development and Testing of the Prototype Configurable Reflectarray Wideband Scanning Radiometer (PT-CREWSR)
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We describe a new observing system funded by the NASA Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO) to improve present capabilities for high-resolution atmospheric sensing from small satellite platforms – the Configurable Reflectarray Wideband Scanning Radiometer (CREWSR) is a high-resolution, lightweight, low-power multiband (23, 31, and 50–58 GHz) radiometer with a deployable scanning reflectarray. CREWSR is envisioned to be fielded on an ESPA-class small satellite platform, with a stowed volume that fits within a 0.61 m x 0.71 m x 0.97 m envelope. Once in orbit, the platform will deploy a large Reconfigurable Reflective Surface (RRS), as well as a multi-feed antenna connected to a multiband radiometer. These components can provide an electronically-scanned beam for radiometric Earth observation. CREWSR would operate with a single, linear polarization, but fully polarimetric operation is also possible in principle. The reflectarray is also compatible with radar use, thereby enabling wide-swath radar from a small satellite. A prototype, small-scale version of CREWSR (PT-CREWSR) is now in the third year of a three-year ESTO Instrument Incubator Program (IIP) to demonstrate the core concept and raise the technology readiness level to an appropriate level for a future flight demonstration. The custom radio frequency integrated circuits (RFICs), three-band antenna patch antennas, panel stack-up, and control electronics have been verified in anticipation of upcoming system-level testing.

articleTitle: V-Band 2SQCC Digital Correlating Spectrometer - Prototype Development and Preliminary Test Results
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Long term direct thermal measurement of the earth's middle and lower tropospheric temperature on a global basis along with the determination of a diurnal temperature climatology is needed to 1) correct historic satellite mid-tropospheric temperature data, 2) estimate the impact of atmospheric greenhouse warming in response to anthropogenic CO2 emissions, 3) inter-calibrate the international fleet of weather satellites, and 4) monitor naturally occurring atmospheric temperature trends. Quantifying anticipated temperature trends on a timely basis requires the globally averaged mid-tropospheric temperature to be observed with a satellite temperature sounding instrument of very high stability and traceability. Stable on-orbit reference instruments are needed to also prevent instrumental drift or deterioration from obscuring trends occurring over several decades. With increased anticipated anthropogenic emission resulting from the imminent deployment of 5G communications electronics and related consumer and defense applications at V -band, radio frequency interference (RFI) detection and mitigation also becomes indispensable for accurate temperature retrievals. Given the historical trend of spectral occupancy doubling every ~6 years, RFI detection and mitigation is critical to future imaging and sounding radiometer architectures.

articleTitle: Efficiency in Measurement-Based Nonlinear Dynamics
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present a quantum algorithm based on repeated measurement to solve initial-value nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The algorithm relies on classical evaluation of a summation over sub-Hamiltonians, weighted by the expectation values of paired observables. Standard quantum Hamiltonian simulation bridges the short times between evaluation of new Hamiltonian matrices. This algorithm requires an ensemble of quantum states, where each step consumes a subset of quantum states, which are used for measurements and are discarded from further time advance. Having demonstrated that our algorithm is capable of solving nontrivial problems, in this work, we explore the question of efficiency: For what class of problems is the algorithm efficient? For a range of problem classes, we use classical simulations to estimate how algorithmic errors scale with simulation time. For problems where the algorithm is efficient, the scaling is polynomial, rather than exponential, indicating that more accurate results is attainable with a small increase of computational resources. We present potential physical systems for the problem classes, providing further analytical analysis.

articleTitle: Theoretical Estimation of Passive HF Signal from a Meteorite Plasma Trail
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The plasma trails of bright meteorites are known to produce HF signals in the 3–300 MHz regime. We explore the possibility that these signals are coherent or partially-coherent Langmuir oscillations of an extended electron cloud along the plasma tail, driven by the differential motion of fast-moving charges through a uniform magnetic field.

articleTitle: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithms for Satellite Swarm Optimization in Non-Terrestrial Networks
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents an efficient hybrid quantum-classical methodology for synthesizing swarm-based antenna arrays in 6G non-terrestrial networks. The approach jointly optimizes satellite element positions and amplitude weights while adhering to engineering constraints like power limitations. The work effectively handles nonlinear objectives and constraints, demonstrating superior sidelobe level (SSL) minimization for large-scale 100-element swarm-based antenna arrays.

articleTitle: Review of a Newly Developed Modular Ionosonde Operating in the Canadian High Arctic
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The ionosphere is a dynamic medium, that interacts with propagating radio waves through a variety of physical mechanisms. The characteristics and extent of the ionosphere's impact varies with season, local time, altitude, geographic and geomagnetic location, as well as helio-, geomagnetic, and terrestrial activity. On the other hand, the operation and reliability of many strategically important communication, navigation, and radar systems are subject to ionospheric conditions. A thorough understanding of physical mechanisms, accurate observation, as well as modeling of the state of the ionosphere are required. The combination of these facilitates the mitigation of detrimental influences on the operation of complex systems, or allow to utilize certain states of the ionosphere to an operational benefit, e.g. for long-range communication, through now- and forecasting of space weather.

articleTitle: Development of an All-Dielectric Quantum-Based RF Field Sensor for Electric Field Calibrations
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The National Institute of Standards and Technology in Boulder, Colorado provides calibration services and participates in international standards intercomparisons of electric field strength. The facility includes a set of standard gain horns operating from 400 MHz - 40 GHz which emit electric fields into an anechoic chamber of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 7$</tex> m x 6 m x 5 m, as shown in Fig. 1 a. The rms electric field <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E$</tex> is given by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E= \sqrt{NFG*P_{net}*Z_{0}/47td^{2}}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$NFG$</tex> is the calculated near field antenna gain, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P_{net}$</tex> is the measured net power delivered to the chamber, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$Z_{0}$</tex> is the free space impedance, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$d$</tex> is the antenna to probe distance. Although our facility provides field strength measurements with uncertainties better than or comparable to similar institutions, the underlying uncertainties from the terms in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E$</tex>, as well as due to multipath reflections in the chamber, lead to an uncertainty of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1$</tex> dB <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\sim 12\%)$</tex> across the frequency range.

articleTitle: Coherent Backscatter from a Vegetation Canopy - Model vs Experiment
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A vegetation canopy can be modeled as a layer of discrete random media over a dielectric halfspace having a rough surface at the interface. The random media consists of scattering objects that have prescribed orientation statistics. These objects can be simple canonical shape s such as thin elliptical discs and cylinders, representing leaves and branches, respectively, or can have complicated geometrical structures with inhomogeneous permittivity properties, representing the vegetation's fruit.

articleTitle: Material Parameter Extraction and Fine-Tuning Techniques for Reducing Overfitting of Deep Neural Networks in Medical Imaging and Diagnostics Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Medical imaging and diagnostic applications of RF systems are often limited by the vast variation in material parameters between different test subjects. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) RF systems, for example, are severely limited by difficulties in modeling, controlling, and designing of RF penetration and absorption in biological tissues due to intersubject variability in material parameters. Additionally, many modern applications of RF systems in the medical field rely on Neural Networks to provide images or other numerical indicators of a patient's condition; due to the vast variation of physical parameters between test subjects and the relative lack of variability in available datasets, these Neural Network models are prone to overfitting, which necessitates model fine-tuning for every new patient.

articleTitle: Interpolating SMAP Soil Moisture to 3 km Using CYGNSS and Spire Reflectivity Observations: Regional Case Study
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study utilizes GNSS-reflectometry (GNSS-R) reflectivity data from Spire Global Inc. and CYGNSS constellations to interpolate SMAP brightness temperature to enhance its resolution from 9-km to 3-km. Previously Behavior Interpolation Method (POBI) is firstly employed to fill spatial gaps of CYGNSS and Spire data gridded at 3-km, which are then used to downscale the SMAP 9-km brightness temperature to achieve a fine resolution. Soil moisture is derived from the enhanced brightness temperature using the tau-omega model. The POBI-processed CYGNSS and Spire datasets are comparable with a mean difference of 0.27 dB across the Southern Continental United States and central America. Our results demonstrate that the 3-km soil moisture maps generated by combining SMAP and Spire/CYGNSS data offer an improved spatial resolution over the standalone SMAP 9 km product and significantly increased spatial coverage compared to CYGNSS measurements.

articleTitle: An Analytical Method for Designing Matching and Decoupling Networks for Three-Element Antenna Arrays with Radiation Pattern Control
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Multi-input-multiple-output (MIMO) antenna arrays have been widely employed to enhance the data throughput of modern wireless communication systems. However, due to the limited space among antenna elements in MIMO arrays, mutual coupling inevitably occurs among these elements, significantly degrading the system's data throughput. One of the most widely used techniques is to connect an antenna array to a matching and decoupling network (MDN) to achieve impedance matched and decoupled ports at the output terminal. Various analytical and optimization-based techniques have been proposed for designing MDNs to address antenna mutual coupling. Optimization-based approaches, while being effective for a variety of design problems, usually have drawbacks such as long computational time and heavy dependence on the initial parameters of the optimization process. On the other hand, analytical methods allow for calculating the S-matrix of an MDN and determining a reactive network of lumped components to realize the MDN's S-matrix. However, extending these analytical methods to design MDNs for antenna arrays with more than two elements <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\mathrm{r}\iota\geq 3)$</tex> is extremely challenging, primarily due to difficulties in the MDN synthesis step to achieve the desired S-matrix for a realistic network consisting of both transmission lines and lumped elements.

articleTitle: 300–900 MHz Midband Array Design for the Lunar Farside Technosignatures and Transients Telescope
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Lunar Farside Technosignatures and Transients Telescope (LFT3) has been proposed to observe radio signals in the shielded zone on the lunar farside. LFT3 will include several low-gain antennas covering frequencies from 1–1800 MHz. The main mission antenna is a phased array on the lander top surface operating from 300–900 MHz, referred to as the LFT3 midband array. Design requirements for the midband array include low power operation, beams formed with near total lunar sky coverage, and sensitivity commensurate with the available aperture size. This paper discusses the design and testing of the midband array.

articleTitle: Evaluating a Convolutional Neural Network Calibration Algorithm Using a 500 GHz Radiometer
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In-orbit calibration of Smallsat and Cubesat sensors can be challenging due to fluctuations arising from sensitivity to solar radiation and imperfect calibration sources. In order to maintain low revisit times and minimize downtime, Cubesat instruments are often powered off during eclipse, or rapidly power cycled on and off to reduce average power consumption. Power cycling during eclipse can result in a steep transient curve when the instrument is powered back on, and while rapid power cycling can produce continuous measurements, it is done so at the cost of increased measurement uncertainty due to the same transient effect at each turn-on.

articleTitle: Qualification of the IMAP X-Band GaN Solid State Power Amplifiers for Near Earth and Deep Space
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In support of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASA's) Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) mission, an X-band GaN Solid State Power Amplifier (SSPA) has been developed at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (IHU/ APL). The SSP A consists of an RF Amplifier box and a Power Converter Unit (PCU), and an inter-box harness to connect the two boxes. The RF Amplifier box consists of three hybrid amplifiers, an output isolator, and DC bias circuitry. The GaN hybrid amplifiers consist of two unique designs, two driver stages and an output stage. The hybrids can operate over the entire International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Near Earth and Deep Space downlink frequency band of 8400–8500 MHz, however the IMAP SSPA hybrids are tuned to maximize RF output power and efficiency in the Deep Space Network (DSN) near-earth downlink frequency band, 8450–8500 MHz (I. R. Dennison et al., “X-band GaN SSPA for Near Earth and Deep Space Missions,” 2022 IEEE Aerospace Conference (AERO), Big Sky, MT, USA, 2022, pp. 01–09, doi: 10.1109/AERO53065.2022.9843728).

articleTitle: Design and Implementation of an E-textile Vivaldi Antenna for Wearable Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: With the recent advancements in 5G and 6G wireless communication technologies, ultra-wideband (UWB) antennas have found extensive use in wearable applications due to their unique advantages, including high data rate transmission, low power consumption, and precise positioning. Various types of UWB antennas have been employed for on-body wireless communication, such as planar monopole and fractal antennas. The Vivaldi antenna is also of interest for its simple design, high directional gain, and excellent radiation efficiency (Tael Saedi et al., “Metamaterial-based Antipodal Vivaldi Wearable UWB Antenna for IoT and 5G Applications,” IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag., Aug. 2020). However, most wearable Vivaldi antenna designs are implemented at millimeter-wave frequencies on rigid substrates. There is a growing need to develop wearable Vivaldi antennas at lower ISM frequency bands using flexible e-textile technology, particularly for biomedical applications

articleTitle: Dual Frequency Improvements to the Time-Series Ratio Algorithm for Soil Moisture Retrievals in the SMEX02 Campaign
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Surface soil moisture is a key variable in Earth's hydrological cycle that describes the exchange of moisture between land, air, and sea. Soil moisture plays an integral role in balancing the exchange of energy between the atmosphere and land surface (evapotranspiration), ecology, infiltration, and runoff. Soil moisture information also influences applications such as agriculture and food security by supporting of crop yield prediction, drought forecasting, and irrigation, water resource management and flood dynamics, and weather forecasting.

articleTitle: Phenomenology of Spatial SEE Variation Depending on Wave Type
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Previous work has demonstrated that different source regions generate various stimulated electromagnetic emissions (SEE) spectral components. A theory has been developed to explain why the different spectral components originate in different regions. An HF array is being proposed to be deployed near the high-frequency active auroral research program (HAARP) facility, to further study these source regions.

articleTitle: GNSS-T Forest Transmissivity Simulations Based on LiDAR-Derived Tree Structure
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this study, we calculate forest transmissivity using Global Navigation Satellite System Transmissometry (GNSS-T) techniques. The SoOp Coherent Bistatic (SCoBi) model is enhanced by incorporating LiDAR-derived tree architectures to simulate forest environments, capturing the detailed structure of trees and their influence on signal attenuation. Using quantitative structure modeling, we generate simplified cylindrical models of trees and simulate forests with varying tree spacing to represent dense and sparse conditions. Two forest models are examined: one focusing on primary tree constituents and another encompassing full tree complexity. Both stationary and moving GNSS-T techniques are employed to assess temporal and spatial variations in forest transmissivity. Additionally, the study investigates the role of the woody volume of different tree parts within the Fresnel zone which is related to water content and responsible for signal attenuation. Preliminary findings suggest notable differences in signal behavior between the forest types, highlighting the importance of tree structure in understanding microwave signal propagation. Overall, this research provides a basis for improving forest transmissivity modeling simulations to support better forest health monitoring.

articleTitle: Large Aperture Telescope Designs for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The CMB-S4 project aims to measure the temperature and polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) with unprecedented sensitivity and precision. The key survey requirements of the project motivated the use of two different types of widefield Large Aperture Telescopes (LATs), each tailored to the needs of one of the two project surveys.

articleTitle: Monofilar Helix with Paraboloid Ground Plane
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A novel paraboloid ground plane is designed and integrated with an X-band coax fed monofilar helical antenna. The antenna assembly is modular, where both the antenna and ground plane are designed to be 3D printed and electroplated. The performance of the paraboloid is compared to the cone ground plane that is extensively covered in literature, and improvements with respect to bandwidth and directivity are shown. Excellent performance with VSWR < 2, and axial ratio < 3 dB over the X-band is demonstrated.

articleTitle: Compact Intracloud Discharges and the Sources Generating Their Low and High Frequency Signatures
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A class of lightning precursor discharges known as compact intracloud discharges (CIDs) are primarily iden-tified by their characteristic wideband (VLF-LF) radio emissions known as narrow bipolar events (NBEs). In addition, there is a growing list of signatures identifying CIDs. In the radio spectrum, the NBE sferic is accompanied by a burst of very strong HF-VHF radiation [Rison et al., Nat. Commun., 7, 10721, 2016], and recent observations from space have identified strong emissions at 337 nm emerging from cloud tops as the optical signature of CIDs [Neubert et al., Nature, 589, 371, 2021], termed as blue luminous events or BLUEs [Li et al., JGR, 128, e2022JD038328, 2023]. The association of CIDs with blue emissions, or pixies, from cloud tops was first made by Lyons et al, [Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., 84, 445–454, 2003]. There is also a growing evidence of CIDs being associated with elves [Neubert et al., 2021]. Recent work has reported a mechanism based on photoelectric feedback in relativistic electron avalanches to explain the production of the source current resulting in the VLF-LF NBE sferic [Pasko et al., manuscript submitted to GRL, 2024GL110623, 2024]. This source current can be remotely sensed from ground based electric field measurements of the NBEs using the method described by Pervez et al. [GRL, 51, e2023GL107789, 2024, doi: 10.1029/2023GL107789], which assumes that the observed radiation is emitted due to polarization of a conducting region in externally applied electric field. The 337 nm optical observations suggest the presence of a system of cold streamers around the CID source, that are also accompanied by strong HF- VHF radiation [Rison et al., 2016]. This suggests the existence of two separate mechanisms driving the low and high frequency radiation associated with CIDs. There are also often quasi-periodic variations superimposed on the opposite polarity overshoot of the bipolar NBE waveform, termed as ringing [Chen et al., JGR, 129, e2023JD040307, 2024]. In this talk we report frequency domain analysis and model interpretation of above described NBE signatures.

articleTitle: A Broadband Metasurface-Based Polarization Converter with Reconfigurable Characteristics for Intelligent Reflecting and Sensing Systems
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper proposes a metasurface-based reflective polarization converter that converts the polarization of incoming electromagnetic (EM) waves from linear-to-linear (LTL) and linear-to-circular (LTC) using varactor diodes (MAVR-011020–11411). This paper aims to address the limitations of previously published polarization converters, which operate in single mode, and to overcome the constraint of limited bandwidth response. The unit cell is implemented on an FR-4 substrate with two staircase lines on the front and a full ground plane on the bottom in Figure 1(a). The biasing layers are sandwiched between two substrates, with a microstrip line (ML) used for DC biasing to enable reconfigurability. The polarization converter metasurface (PCM) demonstrates broadband performance (54.3% fractional bandwidth) centered at 10 GHz, as shown in Figure 1(b). The simulated surface current distribution was analyzed to assess its polarization conversion performance. A 10 × 10 element prototype is designed and fabricated. When the PIN diode is forward biased, LTL polarization is observed, and the LTC polarization occurs when the PIN diodes are off. The proposed polarization converter metasurface is considered a strong candidate for intelligent reflecting surfaces, radar imaging and sensing applications. Since S<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">21</inf> is close to 0 dB as shown in Figure 1(b), the system efficiently converts the entire incident wave to a cross-polarized state, allowing it to distinguish between reflected signals of different polarizations, minimizing interference and improving sensing and imaging clarity. Additionally, the wideband polarization converter, with a 54.3% fractional bandwidth, operates effectively across multiple frequencies, enhancing radar resolution and enabling more detailed imaging under varied conditions.

articleTitle: Precision Data Analysis for 21 cm Cosmology with the OVRO-LWA Stage III
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: 21 cm emission from neutral hydrogen represents a promising probe of the universe's large-scale structure across cosmic time. At near redshift, this emission traces galaxies and the Cosmic Web; during the Epoch of Reionization, it maps ionization of the intergalactic medium by early stars and galaxies. At the highest observable redshifts, 21 cm emission offers a key observable for constraining the Dark Ages and Cosmic Dawn. The Owens Valley Radio Observatory Long Wavelength Array (OVRO-LWA), currently in its Stage III upgrade, could provide the best constraints to date on the 21 cm power spectrum from the Cosmic Dawn, at z~18.

articleTitle: CMB-S4 Science Case and Instrument Overview
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The next generation cosmic microwave background experiment CMB-S4 was conceived by the community as the path forward to realizing the enormous potential of CMB measurements for understanding the origin and evolution of the Universe, from the highest energies at the dawn of time through the growth of structure to the present day. Based on its spectacular and transformative science promise and its technical maturity, CMB-S4 was highly ranked (tied for 2nd priority) by U.S. 2020 Decadal Survey of Astronomy and Astrophysics and was ranked as the highest priority, new large project by the 2023 report of the U.S. Particle Physics Project Prioritization Panel.

articleTitle: A Novel Computational Imaging Method Using Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper proposes and numerically demonstrates a novel method for computational imaging using reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) that combines the benefits of compressive imaging using random patterns with spotlight imaging. In our approach, RISs are programmed to direct their beams toward a region of interest (ROI) where they interfere with each other, resulting in spatially diverse patterns that can multiplex the information within the ROI into a few measurements. Since each RIS produces a directive beam, the resulting speckle pattern is only confined to near the ROI, helping to reduce clutter, a typical issue with using random patterns. Furthermore, our method requires fewer measurements than raster scanning and can work even when RISs are separated, which is useful in practical implementation. The proposed RIS-enabled imaging system can find applications in security screening, user tracking, and activity recognition.

articleTitle: Antennas Made from Transparent Conductive Oxides Require Multiple Optimization Criteria
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Optically transparent antennas allow telecommunications transmission and reception in applications, such as urban areas and vehicle windshields, where blocking visible light is undesirable or unsafe. Depositing a very thin layer of conductive material is one method to accomplish optical transparency. Parasitic resistances resulting from both material properties and conductor thicknesses of thin films increase losses and negatively impact the efficiency of antennas made from these materials. Manufacturing and growth processes for conductive thin films such as screen printing, molecular beam epitaxy, and sputter deposition often limit researchers through high costs and require coplanar designs. Indium Tin Oxide (ITO) on a glass substrate, although still requiring coplanar designs, is a cost effective and readily available optically transparent conductive thin film that allows for simpler transitions to automotive and urban applications. The parasitic resistances inherent in existing optically transparent conductive thin films complicates the antenna design and optimization processes, often resulting in low gain and low efficiency antennas. Parametric simulation of all antenna parameters is impractical due to the large search space. Multi-objective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) allows for efficient optimization of large multi-dimensional search spaces.

articleTitle: Wideband Dual-Circularly Polarized Phased Array Antenna Using a Novel Radiating Element for Ku-Band SATCOM Applications
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this paper, a novel wideband array antenna is proposed for Ku -band satellite communication (SATCOM) applications. The radiating element includes a stacked microstrip patch configuration and has a wide 48 % impedance bandwidth that covers both the downlink (10.7 ‒ 12.7 GHz) and uplink (14 ‒ 14.5 GHz) SATCOM bands. articleTitle: Improving Robustness for Large-Scale Wireless Power Receiver Arrays
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This talk describes 10-GHz patch antenna rectifier arrays with 25 × 25 elements designed using Schottky diodes on 0.127 mm of polyamide and 2 mm of expanded PTFE (ePTFE) on a copper fabric ground plane. These materials were chosen to optimize easy deployment, low cost and easy storage. For this reason, the chosen substrate is flexible and water resistant, ePTFE is a common material used on gaskets and the rectenna arrays can be rolled up like an exercise mat. For the rectifying element, Skyworks SMS7621-079 Schottky diodes are soldered to the metallization (A. Montgomery, J. Molles, C. Scarborough, and Z. articleTitle: Small Aperture Telescope Designs for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A leading science goal of the next generation cosmic microwave background experiment CMB-S4 is to dramatically advance our understanding of cosmic inflation by constraining amplitude of the primordial gravitational waves the process produces, which is quantified by the tensor-to-scalar ratio r. To do this, it must measure the exceedingly faint pattern of B-mode polarization predicted in the CMB from this effect to peak at large angular scales, roughly 2 to 4 degrees. CMB-S4 will meet this goal with a deep, ultra-sensitive survey concentrated on a few percent. Arcminute resolution and sensitivity to measure and remove the gravitational lensing contamination of B-modes from the dominant CMB E-mode polarization will be provided by large aperture telescopes (LATs), while ultra-deep measurements across eight frequency bands from 25 to 280 GHz chosen to separate Galactic emission from the CMB will be made at the essential degree angular scales by an array of small aperture telescopes.

articleTitle: Advancing Understanding of Mid-Latitude L-band Scintillations with Alternative GNSS-based Monitors
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: As we approach the peak of Solar Cycle 25, our ground and space-based technological systems face increased vulnerability to space weather. One critical impact is on Position, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) services provided by the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS). While the effects of space weather on GNSS at low and high latitudes have been well studied, we still seek a better understanding of space weather effects at mid-latitudes. This is, in great part, due to the limited deployment of specialized ionospheric scintillation monitors. In this study, we describe an affordable, easy to deploy and maintain ionospheric scintillation and total electron content monitor that uses low-cost off-the-shelf GNSS receivers. We will also present the application of this low-cost solution to monitor the occurrence and severity of mid-latitude L-band scintillations, addressing the gap in current space weather monitoring capabilities.

articleTitle: Adaptive Beamforming with a Double-Cross Array of Dipole Antennas on a Drone
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Adaptive beamforming from a two-dimensional horizontal array of vertical dipole elements on a drone is considered. The dipole radiating elements are arranged on a fixed “double-cross” horizontal layout that consists of a central dipole element (at the origin, with x = y = 0) surrounded by eight neighboring dipole elements, as shown below in Fig. 1. The horizonal positions of the dipoles in the double-cross array are first determined by an initial simple two-parameter optimization. After the layout is determined (and then kept fixed), the amplitudes and phases of the dipole radiators are then optimized to give patterns that meet various objectives. Pattern objectives may include a single focused beam pointing in an arbitrary (and steerable) direction with low sidelobes, multiple beams, a null in one or more directions, or even an angular null region over which the pattern level is as low as possible.

articleTitle: Low-Power ULF Transmitter Design Using Static Permanent Magnet
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a low-power Ultra Low Frequency (ULF) transmitter design that uses a static, permanent magnet to bring the surrounding magnetic shield near saturation. A low-power control coil modulates this static magnetic field by toggling sections of the shield between saturated and unsaturated states. The transmitter, operating at 400 Hz and tested using a 3D magnetometer, demonstrated an increase of 22.3 dB along the pole at 800 Hz and a 17.7 dB increase at 400 Hz perpendicular to the pole, with a further 33 dB enhancement than the control coil's leakage at 800 Hz. These results highlight a novel method for efficient magnetic field modulation with significantly reduced power requirements compared to traditional approaches. This novel approach reduces power consumption and opens new possibilities for designing scalable, energy-efficient ULF communication systems, with potential applications in areas such as underwater communication, remote sensing, and long-range wireless networks.

articleTitle: Electromagnetic Emissions Associated with the 2024 Perseid Meteor Shower
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: There is evidence dating back to the writings of Edmund Halley (1714) that suggests meteors may generate energy at very low frequencies that propagate much faster than the speed of sound (i.e., the speed of light). Modern scientific inquiry into the phenomena of electromagnetic emissions from meteors began when Kalashnikov (1949) reported that meteors generate magnetic disturbances detected using induction coils at extremely low frequencies. In Khlyustov (1951), reported observations made in the Arctic that bright meteors with visible contrails gave rise to high frequency radio noise which fades as the optical signature of the tail fades. Almost immediately his observations were challenged by Hawkins. Numerous theoretical investigations followed, including Chapman and Ashour (1964) who proposed an extrinsic point of origin to be coupling with the electrojet current by meteor ion trails, to Medvedev (1964) and Bronshtén (1983) who proposed intrinsic mechanisms including ionosphere charge circulation and magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) effects. Shock wave induced plasma deceleration produced by the strong bow shock and cylindrical shock in the trail almost certainly play a role in the production of electromagnetic radiation. Meanwhile, empirical investigations have continued, with the work of Blum and Price (1999), for instance, made observations during the Leonid shower from the Negev Desert, Israel. They reported evidence of electromagnetic emissions time coincident with visual sightings. Guha and Rakesh (2009) reported similar coincidences of very low frequency emissions during 2007 Geminid meteor shower, but others have questioned the rigor of their analysis.

articleTitle: Beneficial Impact of Rocket Engine Burns Over Ground VLF Transmitters for Radiation Belt Remediation
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Currently, there are about 10,000 active space objects in orbit around the earth. Satellites have to avoid collisions by energetic particles that can damage solar panels and electronic components. Whistler and electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) can scatter trapped radiation into the atmospheric loss cone and, thus, reduce energetic particle fluxes. The proliferation of satellite launches and International Space Station (ISS) reboost missions may be used to reduce the populations of harmful radiation. Low frequency (ELF/VLF) waves can be artificially intensified to produce strong electromagnetic (EM) waves (e.g., whistlers). A Rocket Exhaust Driven Amplification (REDA) system has been tested with (1) a ground Navy ELF/VLF transmitter used as coherent wave source, (2) the firing a rocket motor over the transmitter to produce an amplifying medium in the ionosphere and (3) the satellite plasma-wave sensor on the Canadian SWARM-E. Measured wave amplitudes can impact the dynamics in the inner magnetosphere and reduce the lifetime of the radiation belts.

articleTitle: Grid Size Optimization for Soil Moisture Estimation Using UAS-Based GNSS Reflectometry
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The agriculture industry consumes 70% of the world's available freshwater, making efficient water use essential to ensuring sustainable practices. Precision agriculture, through accurate soil moisture (SM) measurements, can play a pivotal role in optimizing irrigation, reducing water wastage, and conserving critical resources. However, obtaining precise SM data across large agricultural areas remains a significant challenge. In-situ invasive SM probes can deliver highly accurate data but are limited to localized, point-based measurements that do not provide complete field coverage. Conversely, satellite-based SM measurements, such as those from the Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS), Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP), etc., offer extensive coverage but at resolutions (in kilometer range) that are insufficient for the high spatio-temporal accuracy required in precision agriculture.

articleTitle: HPG: A High Performance Gridding Library
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: HPG is a portable library for gridding and degridding non-uniformly distributed visibility data for synthetic aperture imaging. The library is designed for performance portability, and is implemented using the Kokkos C++ Performance Portability Ecosystem, a High Performance Software Foundation project that was initially developed under the US Department of Energy's Exascale Computing Project. The HPG implementation uses portable C++, which compiles to optimized code on CPUs as well as GPUs. The library implements general purpose algorithms that can be used with any user-defined convolution kernels, and is thus applicable to most visibility-based gridding algorithms. It is currently being used by groups within the National Radio Astronomy Observatory in the implementation of A-projection, W-projection, AW-projection, full polarization, spectral line, continuum, and mosaic imaging. Performance testing at NRAO has demonstrated a speedup of up to 160x on GPUs versus CASA-based gridding on a single CPU core. Although the algorithms are inherently optimized for GPU execution, the code can be compiled, unchanged, for OpenMP or even serial CPU execution, which provides a significant benefit for code development and debugging. Hooks provided by Kokkos also support fine-grained performance profiling on all architectures, promoting ease of use during performance optimization. The library is currently undergoing an update to merge a variant that was implemented for the DSA-2000 radio camera imaging pipeline software. Early tests of the merged code promise an approximate 2x speedup versus the current version of HPG on a wide range of GPUs. This performance improvement is achieved through various algorithm refinements, including an option to use mixed precision arithmetic, which is targeted to more affordable GPUs having low double precision floating point performance. After the new version of HPG is complete, the identical library will be used by both NRAO and radio camera imaging codes. This talk will present the design of the HPG library and some aspects of its implementation, describe how it is being used by various applications, show results of some performance tests in several applications, discuss the critical imaging parameters that affect performance, and provide an overview of plans for future development.

articleTitle: A Novel Radiometric Scene Generator for Reconfigurable Microwave Remote Sensing
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: There is growing interest within the Earth remote sensing community in developing reconfigurable microwave sensors capable of dynamically adjusting their spectral, radiometric, spatial, and viewing angle properties in real-time. These sensors would adapt to targets of interest within their field of regard, enabling more efficient use of resources. For example, in areas with high spatial frequency, such as tropical storms, the sensor can be configured to observe the region at high spatial resolution, while in calmer weather, where spatial frequency is lower, the sensor can conserve resources by reducing resolution. This adaptive approach enhances the overall performance and efficiency of the sensor.

articleTitle: Scattering Coefficients of Forested Mountainsides at L Band
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study investigates the electromagnetic wave propagation through forests on both non-sloping and sloped terrains, emphasizing the differences in scattering mechanisms between the two. Using a model based on the Foldy-Lax approximation and Distorted Born Approximation (DBA), the study computes bistatic scattering coefficients for forested environments. For non-sloping terrain, the scattering is driven by the azimuthally symmetric distribution of trunks, branches, and leaves. On sloped terrain, this symmetry is disrupted, leading to significant polarization conversion effects. Results are presented, using the ground truth data acquired from the White Mountains, NH, showing azimuthally asymmetric attenuation values and cross-polarization effects on forested mountainsides compared to the non-sloping terrain.

articleTitle: Nonlinear HF Propagation in the Ionosphere above HAARP
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The nature of HF radio wave propagation through the lower ionosphere has significant impact on scientific efforts such as ELF /VLF wave generation and ionospheric sounding, as well as operational efforts e.g. over-the-horizon radar and satellite-to-ground communications. Historical interpretation of propagation within the lower ionosphere centers on D-region absorption models, but observations of polar mesospheric echoes in HF and VHF radars and anomalous absorption in HF cross-modulation experiments highlight the potential for other interactions to impact HF radio wave propagation in the lower ionosphere.

articleTitle: Preliminary Ultra-Wideband Measurements During the Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in Stable Atmosphere Over Water Campaign
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio propagation through stable atmospheric conditions is of great interest in recent literature and is the primary focus of the Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in Stable Atmosphere over Water campaign. Our group deployed the Ultra-Wideband Lower Atmospheric Propagation system, measuring the shore-to-shore propagation loss from 2 to 40 GHz.
