articleTitle: Design and Validation of an In-Situ Downconversion Circuit
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: With the auctioning of the 24 GHz frequency band for fifth-generation (5G) wireless communications, meteorologists predict that 5G transmitters could interfere with passive weather radiometer systems, which would result in inaccurate weather predictions. These passive weather radiometers operate in the 23.6-24.0 GHz range, due to the resonant frequency of water vapor in the atmosphere. The frequency range of 50–58 GHz is also of importance, due to its susceptibility of out of band and harmonic emissions from 5G transmitters. This interference would result in significant delays in accurate weather forecasting, meaning delays in warnings and emergency procedures in the event of natural disasters such as tornadoes and hurricanes. (E. Niller, “5g networks could throw weather forecasting into chaos,” 2019. [Online].).

articleTitle: Evaluation of a Turbulence Characterization Technique Using Fixed-Distanced Commercial Radiosondes: Insights from a 2024 Measurement Campaign
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Troposcatter is often described as a phenomenon driven by turbulence in the atmosphere that allows for over-the-horizon (OTH) radio wave propagation impacting frequencies from around 100 MHz to 18 GHz. Atmospheric turbulence can be characterized by measuring the rapid spatiotemporal fluctuations in temperature and humidity throughout the atmospheric column that dominate the index of refraction at these frequencies. Much of the research undertaken for in situ characterization of atmospheric turbulence has focused on fast response temperature measurements with application to electro-optic and infrared (EO/IR) systems (e.g. thermosondes). These devices typically consist of two fine wire temperature probes spaced one meter apart and connected to circuitry to measure the slight differences in their resistance caused by the mismatch in their respective temperatures. For radio frequency (RF) systems, the effects of humidity dominate the index of refraction compared to EO/IR wavelengths where many systems operate in window regions where the effects are negligible. The fragile nature of fine wire sensors, lack of commercially available thermosondes and need for differential humidity measurements spurred the attempt at a complementary technique: that of using two or more commercial radiosondes attached to a single weather balloon. This is further enabled by recent upgrades in the radiosonde ground station permitting simultaneous reception of multiple radiosondes in flight.

articleTitle: Resonant-Perturbation Method Applied to UHF Cryogenic Dielectric Measurements of Saline Ice
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This year's launch of Europa Clipper and proposals for follow on lander missions to Europa and other ice-covered bodies in the solar system has highlighted the need for a better understanding of the properties of these icy environments. A comprehensive survey paper, published by authors at JPL, (E. Pettinelli, et. al., “Dielectric properties of Jovian satellite ice analogs for subsurface radar exploration: A review,” in Rev. Geophys., 2015, vol. 53, pp. 593- 641, doi:10.1002/2014RG000463) highlights a significant dearth of applicable dielectric measurements for ice in the radio spectrum. More specifically the existing measurements of the complex permittivity of ice do not include either the expected salinities (concentrations up to 4.2×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup> kg/kg) or temperature ranges (as low as 80 K) expected in the Europan cryosphere. This makes interpretation of data from orbiting, surface and subsurface radar and radiometer systems difficult. This abstract proposes and the associated presentation will present the results of a novel experiment to cover this extended parameter range and measure these critical parameters in the UHF radio spectrum.

articleTitle: Quantifying Uncertainty in Space-Borne Radar Estimates of Cloud and Precipitation Properties
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: It is well known that radar measurements of liquid and ice clouds and hydrometeors are sensitive to the assumptions made about the particle size distribution and particle shape. While models of the shape of liquid drops are relatively straightforward, representation of ice is far more complicated, involving a vast diversity of crystal habits and degrees of accumulated frozen liquid drops (rime). Ice crystal shape complexity introduces additional ambiguity into the relationship between radar measurements and cloud properties (mass and number distribution). While the existence of PSD and shape sensitivity is well known, the dependence of the resulting uncertainty on the characteristics of the radar and on the cloudy state being observed is not. In particular, it is not clear whether the degree and characteristics of the uncertainty may vary as a function of the cloud type observed.

articleTitle: DSA-2000 Feed and Antenna System Performance
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Deep Synoptic Array (DSA-2000) will be a world-leading radio astronomical survey telescope with unprecedented survey speed and sensitivity. It is based on an array of 2000 reflector antennas each with 5 m diameter and will span an area of 15 km x 19 km in Nevada, USA (G. Hallinan et al., Astro2020 51(7), 2019). Each antenna will be equipped with a high-sensitivity, low-cost feed package covering 0.7-2 GHz based on a ground-breaking ambient temperature low-noise amplifier (LNA) with 11 K noise temperature (J. Shi & S. Weinreb, IEEE-MTT 2023, pp. 1540–1543). The predicted system noise temperature is less than 25 K.

articleTitle: Updates on the Array of Long Baseline Antennas for Taking Radio Observations from the Seventy-Ninth Parallel
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The cosmic “dark ages” refers to the period when the universe was filled with neutral hydrogen after recombination and prior to the cosmic dawn. This period can be probed via measurements of redshifted 21 cm emissions of neutral hydrogen at ≲ 30 MHz. To date, the dark ages remains unobserved due to the experimental challenges of overcoming Galactic foreground emissions, ionospheric contamination, and terrestrial radio-frequency interference (RFI). The Array of Long Baseline Antennas for Taking Radio Observations from the Seventy-ninth parallel (ALBATROS) aims to characterize Galactic foregrounds at these low radio frequencies with an order of magnitude resolution improvement over existing data below ~30 MHz, paving the way for future observations of the dark ages. The state of the art among ground-based measurements dates from the 1950s, when Reber and Ellis caught brief glimpses of the 2.1 MHz sky at ~ 5° resolution, using an array of 192 dipoles (Reber & Ellis, 1956). With an operating frequency range of 1.2 - 125 MHz, ALBATROS is an interferometric array consisting of multiple independent stations of dual polarization Long Wavelength Array (LWA) dipole antennas connected to back-end readout electronics.

articleTitle: Networked AI for Detection Classification and Localization of RF Signal Emitters
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Spectrum sensing is an important capability for understanding what kind of wireless radio activity is present in frequency bands. This knowledge, or spectrum awareness, enables and enhances a range of applications, from spectrum sharing and mapping to fault detection, security and regulatory monitoring. In wireless systems like 4G LTE, 5G-NR, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth, the frequencies, bandwidths and timeslots are pre-coordinated, meaning that both the transmitter and receiver know which bands have been allocated to them and where to find the signal in the spectrum. This allows the receiver to focus on specific frequency bands and specific protocols (e.g., preambles) for signal detection. When unwanted signals or interferers impair 5G reception, they often do not follow the same predictable patterns and can be very difficult to pinpoint, occurring randomly in time and frequency.

articleTitle: Global Analysis of Mid-latitude Ionospheric Trough Morphology
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study characterizes the midlatitude ionospheric trough (MIT) using a newly implemented detection method applied to ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) data collected over a solar cycle. The MIT is defined as a region of plasma depletion occurring in the nighttime sub-auroral F-region ionosphere. Subsets of over a decade of GNSS-derived ionosphere total electron content (TEC) data were chosen to distinguish behavior under quiet and active geomagnetic conditions and season. The goals of this paper are to characterize MIT dynamics and demonstrate the capability to produce a running synoptic view of the trough. Detection rate and trough position are statistically quantified and visualized.

articleTitle: Propagation of Whistler Mode Waves in Earth's Inner Magnetosphere in the Presence of Field Aligned Irregularities and Geomagnetic Curvature
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Magnetospheric chorus waves play a dominant role in accelerating high energy electrons and in precipitating energetic electrons in the radiation belts. These waves are generated near the geomagnetic equator outside the plasmasphere. The propagation of whistler mode waves along the magnetic field lines can be strongly influenced by magnetospheric ducts or the plasma density anisotropic inhomogeneities. Recent spacecraft observations confirm the existence of field aligned plasma density irregularities and their strong influence on observed whistler mode wave parameters. To investigate chorus wave propagation, numerous simulation techniques have been employed, among which ray tracing theory has been the most utilized method.

articleTitle: A Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface Using Transparent Conductive Oxide
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this work, a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) using a transparent conductive oxide (TCO) will be presented. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces have gained much interest for their potential applications in 5G and emerging 6G communications. At 5G and 6G frequencies with millimeter wavelengths (mmWave), free-space losses are high and many scattering events from structures occur. These two effects cause significant loss to the mmWave signal. RIS structures use various components (e.g., diodes, switches, etc.) to change the reflected signal phase in order to intelligently capture and reflect the signal in selected directions. This effect enables the reduction of signal dead zones and signal power lost from random scattering. In current literature, many RIS solutions have been demonstrated with substrates that are not optically transparent. However, this limits their applications to optically opaque building walls. This is not ideal as it neglects the potential to make use of windows, which are a large area of the building surface. In this vein, this work proposes the use of transparent conductive oxides, which are conductive at radio frequencies and optically transparent, for RIS designs. Such devices can be used on the windows of buildings, increasing the potential area for RIS implementation.

articleTitle: WLAN Protocols Identification Using Machine Learning and Ensemble Models
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The growing demand for wireless communications has caused significant spectrum congestion, requiring multiple WLAN protocols to share limited spectrum resources. To address this, further research is necessary to optimize spectrum sharing and improve coexistence between various wireless technologies and protocols. This study introduces a software defined radio (SDR) and machine learning-based approach for classifying WLAN protocols-specifically IEEE 802.11a, 802.11ac, and 802.11ax-operating in the 5 GHz band. To enhance classification performance, we optimize the hyperparameters of several machine learning and ensemble models. Their performance is evaluated using metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC, providing a comprehensive assessment of the models' effectiveness. Our findings show that the proposed classification method achieves up to 95% accuracy, with Random Forest, KNN, and Gradient Boosting models performing the best. These results are novel as they show that the use of intelligent sensing can achieve satisfactory protocol classification performance with low-cost devices.

articleTitle: Simulation and Theoretical Studies on the Validity of Using Langmuir Probes in Hypervelocity Impact Plasma
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Langmuir probe measurement relies on the understanding of plasma sheath theory. Plasma sheath is a thin region that forms between bulk plasma and a physical boundary such as the probe surface. The behavior of this sheath has only been studied in literature for a limited range of cases, none of which can be applied to hypervelocity impact (HVI) plasma without violating some assumptions. Theoretical studies of plasma sheath are being conducted while relaxing many of the assumptions made in current literature. Preliminary results show that the data interpretation model used for Langmuir probe in many HVI research are indeed not perfectly valid and can cause discrepancies in the final measurement. In this work, 1- D fluid simulation is performed using fluid ions and Boltzmann electrons to study the temporal and long-term behavior of the plasma sheath formed between a bulk, flowing plasma and a current absorbing boundary. Plasma sheath theory for stationary and non-stationary plasma were also derived and compared to the simulation result. This work shows that the stationary plasma sheath theory is not adequate when applied to non-stationary plasma, and further research is needed to justify using Langmuir probe in HVI plasma. The simple 1-D fluid simulation suggests that there is a variation of the ion saturation current corresponding to changes in the incoming bulk flow speed. Specifically, as the flow speed increases, so does the ions saturation current. The results of this are tabulated in table 1. This work also shows that transient formation of the plasma sheath is not an issue when it comes to making transient measurements in HVI, as sheath formation occurs on the order 10–100 times the inverse of the plasma frequency. Further 2-D simulation and theoretical studies are also being conducted to study effect of a non-planar probe geometries in a non-stationary plasma.

articleTitle: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Sporadic E Formations and Their Irregular Structure Based on Dynasonde Analysis
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present a novel imaging approach in studies of the spatiotemporal dynamics of Es events based on Wallops Island Dynasonde data. This may be named a Dynasonde-specific implementation of a “sky maps” technique focused on sporadic E layer and leaving regular E and F regions aside.

articleTitle: The DSA-2000 Radio Camera
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Synthetic aperture imaging for an interferomeric array of antennas traditionally requires the use of deconvolution algorithms that iterate over sets of visibility, or correlation, data. Because the data sets of modern radio telescope arrays exceed the memory capacity of even large supercomputers, those data must be stored prior to the completion of an image. As the rate of visibility data produced by such an array scales with the number of antennas squared, for a very large number of antennas, the storage costs quickly become prohibitive. Despite having a large number of antennas (2000), the DSA-2000 array avoids exorbitant data storage costs by a novel design that circumvents the need to ever persistently store the visibility data. We have named the real time data processing and imaging back-end of the DSA-2000 design the “radio camera”. The radio camera integrates the traditional on-line stages of interferometric data processing - digitization and correlation - with an imaging pipeline that performs flagging and calibration on streaming data, and directly creates images in real time, without the visibility data being written to persistent storage at any point. In particular, visibility domain deconvolution and indeterminate iteration in self-calibration are not done. Note, however, in DSA-2000 image domain deconvolution and other post-processing algorithms may be applied in downstream processing outside the radio camera. In this talk, we begin with a description of the high level architecture of the radio camera, subdivided into two subsystems in the context of the DSA-2000 system design. We follow with an overview of the current design of the radio camera subsystems, both hardware and software, and review the current state of subsystem development. We complete the talk with a focus on the imaging pipeline software, with a brief look at its implementation, and an outline of the remaining steps on the path to a final design. The DSA-2000 is supported by Schmidt Sciences.

articleTitle: Substituting Lattices to Improve Mass Fraction of an Antenna for Stress Testing (SLIMFAST)
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A 0.6 m High-Gain Antenna (HGA) reflector assembly operating over the 17.7 to 31 GHz frequency range was fabricated using a polymer additive manufacturing process. The HGA was optimized for mass, cost, lead time, RF performance, and strength. Using structural inputs from both analytical and measured responses, the supporting structures used in the HGA was topologically optimized to maximize structural integrity. These structures have complex geometries that are difficult to fabricate using conventional machining, but relatively simple using additive manufacturing. The reflectors were coated with a conductive paint to support efficient radiation. The finished HGA assembly was tested in a compact range and show about 2 dB less gain when compared with an equivalent HGA made using conventional fabrication methods. This was attributed to the main reflector warping and the inherent surface roughness for a large reflector. The HGA was then vibration tested until failure in order to validate the structural model.

articleTitle: An Algorithm for Converting PCB Via Structure to a Voxelized Mesh for Artificial Intelligence Models
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Hardware design for radio frequency devices often demands the use of full-wave electromagnetic (EM) field-solvers to extract scattering parameters (S-parameters) for systems that contain discontinuities throughout their printed circuit boards (PCBs) and substrate packages. Using EM field-solvers not only requires extensive EM knowledge during the setup phase, but also demands considerable computational resources. Previously, machine learning (ML) and neural network (NN) models have been used to solve EM fields; however, they tend to use design parameters as input rather than the structure's geometry. Parametric analysis is beneficial when the solution space is well bounded, but it is more desirable to develop the capability of feeding generic and arbitrary geometry into a machine learning model for rapid S-parameter extraction. This work presents an algorithm for converting a sub-section of hardware geometry designed with an electronic design automation (EDA) tool into a dataset suitable for training and validating machine learning models including fully connected NNs and convolutional NNs (CNNs).

articleTitle: A Quantitative Method for Comparing RF Propagation Model Output
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) propagation forecasts are increasingly made using output from mesoscale numerical weather predictions (NWP). These RF forecasts are then used within system-level models for radars, RF communications, and passive RF sensors. Of ultimate interest are the output of these system-level models, which are often complex to run and slow in producing output. A natural question arises in this scenario: can a semi-quantitative measure of system performance be generated at the level of NWP forecasts, circumventing (at least sometimes) the need for system-level model runs? The diversity of applications is broad, and their system-level dependency on meteorological and oceanographic (METOC) data is highly nonlinear. An absolute, semi-quantitative measure is unlikely, but a relative measure between two distinct NWP outputs might be feasible. As the availability of data outpaces computational resources and bandwidth, the need for such an approximation grows. At the core of this need is the ability to meaningfully and robustly quantify the difference between two RF-propagation-model output fields (propagation values versus range and height). Without a propagation-level metric, any chance of succeeding at the METOC level is diminishingly small.

articleTitle: High-Power Dual-Polarized Reconfigurable Reflectarray with All-Metal Antenna and Stacked Phase Shifters
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: High-power all-metal antenna arrays with dual-polarization and wide-angle scanning capabilities are well-suited for directed energy applications. Keeping this in consideration, a dual-polarized reconfigurable reflectarray is proposed to maximize the effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) of a high-power phased array system.

articleTitle: REDSAW Drone-Based Electromagnetic Measurements
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The propagation of electromagnetic waves through the marine boundary layer can be strongly influenced by meteorological states. The Radar and Electromagnetic Ducting in Stable Atmosphere over Water (REDSAW) campaign explores the effects of stable atmospheric conditions on radio frequency propagation. During this experiment, two drone receiver systems were deployed at the Salton Sea Causeway, including a newly-developed tethered quadcopter drone receiver system which can record electromagnetic signals continuously over a span of hours. This allows for closer examination of the vertical electromagnetic (EM) profile and influence of the environment on the profile over long periods of time. The objective of this research is to analyze the relationship between the atmospheric environmental conditions and the characteristics of the EM signals propagating through the Salton Sea. Preliminary results from the deployed drone receiver systems are shown.

articleTitle: A New and Efficient Solution to Matrix Equation Generated by the Method of Moments
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this work, we build upon previous solution procedures to solve the matrix equation generated by the well-known method of moments (MOM). The present procedure is developed to save memory and storage space, and to be computationally efficient. The first step involves generating the MOM matrix equation by conventional method. The second step involves gathering the total number of basis functions into a small number of groups thereby casting the moment matrix into a collection of smaller matrices representing self and mutual interactions between the groups. Third, the procedure generates a new matrix using straight-forward mathematical steps where the blocks residing on either side of the diagonal blocks are set to zero. Fourth, the new matrix equation is solved using modified algebraic steps that is memory efficient compared to repeated matrix vector multiplication. Finally, all of the off-diagonal blocks in the modified matrix are replaced by a simple scalar constant to obtain a very efficient MOM procedure.

articleTitle: Electric Field Detection with High Angular Momentum Rydberg Receivers in the HF/VHF Bands and Beyond
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Atomic systems have been used as sensors of external fields for decades, and recently have gained attention as high-sensitivty receivers of electromagnetic radiation. Specifically, near room-temperature atomic vapor cells demonstrate broad tunability across many decades of the radio frequency (RF) spectrum. Application studies have included sensitivity to electric field polarization, phase, and angle-of-arrival. Generally, Rydberg receivers have operated in the range of tens of GHz. Most recently, investigations have explored the bandwidth of these systems, modulation schemes and their applications, and frequencies below 1 GHz.

articleTitle: Lightning Precursor Discharges and Terrestrial Gamma Ray Flashes
publicationTitle: 2025 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Spectacular naturally occurring bursts of X-rays with tens of mega electron-volt energies are observed in association with lightning activity in the Earth's atmosphere. These events were first discovered in 1994 by NASA's Compton Gamma Ray Observatory [Fishman et al., 1994] and are commonly referred to as terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs). Although since then many other orbital observatories captured these high energy events [Smith et al., 2005; Marisaldi et al., 2010; Briggs et al., 2011; Neubert et al., 2020] and these events have been clearly linked to very intense but short (approximately 10–50 microseconds) bursts of electromagnetic radiation [Ostgaard et al., 2021], the physical nature of these events remains unclear. It is widely recognized that these electromagnetic bursts are also the strongest naturally occurring sources of terrestrial very high frequency (VHF) radiation [Jacobson et al., 2012]. The most puzzling unexplained aspect of these events is that the extreme gamma ray and electromagnetic energy fluxes originate from very compact regions with spatial extent on the order of 100 meters [Lu et al., 2010; Rison et al., 2016; Tilles et al., 2019; Tilles et al., 2020; Kohn et al., 2020; Heumesser et al., 2021], yet they are light-deficient and often even optically undetectable compared to ordinary lightning discharges [Jacobson et al., 2012]. In this work we report on the mechanism that allows precise quantitative explanation of the vast majority of currently accumulated observations of these events at different altitudes in the Earth's atmosphere. The specifics includes TGF fluences and durations, optical darkness, magnitudes and specific waveform characteristics of low and very low frequency radio emissions termed narrow bipolar events and energetic in cloud pulses that are associated with TGFs, the peculiar observations of very fast (typically one tenths of the speed of light) spatial propagation features termed fast positive breakdown in the present literature, pulsing of TGFs, and low fluence TGFs not observable from the orbit.
